article.title: Hydroxyproline Enhances Branched-Chain Amino Acid Effects on Lifespan and Healthspan in Caenorhabditis elegans.
article.authors: Liu L, Wu R, Gao Z, Fang F, Chang C, Hou Z, Wang H, Zhang D, Wang Z.
article.abstract: Food-derived protein hydrolysates frequently contain both collagen-associated hydroxyproline (Hyp) and branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs), but the biological consequences of their combination remain unclear. This study tested whether Hyp changes the effects of leucine (Leu), isoleucine (Ile), and valine (Val) on lifespan and healthspan-related phenotypes in Caenorhabditis elegans and whether these treatment effects are accompanied by coordinated microbial and metabolic remodeling. Amino acid concentrations that did not strongly disrupt bacterial food clearance were selected for lifespan, stress-resistance, motility, muscle-integrity, biochemical, microbiome, metabolomic, and transcriptomic analyses. Hyp+BCAA combinations improved lifespan- and healthspan-related phenotypes in a BCAA- and dose-dependent manner. The strongest combined treatments enhanced resistance to thermal and oxidative stress, preserved age-associated motility and muscle structure, reduced oxidative and lipofuscin-associated markers, and increased ATP-related readouts. Multi-omics profiling showed that these direct treatment effects were accompanied by distinct C. elegans-associated microbiota signatures, altered NAD precursor-related metabolites including nicotinic acid ribonucleoside (NaR), and a Leu+Hyp transcriptional response enriched for energy metabolism, proteostasis, and extracellular-matrix remodeling. Integrated microbiome-metabolome analysis identified a positive association between Rhodococcus abundance and NaR levels. These findings demonstrate that, under the tested culture conditions, Hyp+BCAA exposure improves longevity-related phenotypes and identifies microbial composition, NAD precursor metabolism, and host energy homeostasis as candidate, testable mediators.

article.title: LEV-10 and NRA-2 regulate distinct mechanisms of cholinergic tachyphylaxis in Caenorhabditis elegans
article.authors: Gupta S, Wragge J, Kashyap S.
article.abstract: Abstract Soil-transmitted helminthiasis affects more than a billion people worldwide and is a global health concern. With no effective vaccination available, treatment relies on mass administration of anthelmintic drugs, like albendazole, ivermectin, and levamisole. Unfortunately, their regular of overuse has given rise to resistance. Levamisole, a cholinergic agonist, activates the nematode L-type acetylcholine receptors and causes muscle contraction and worm paralysis. In parasitic nematodes, such as female Brugia malayi , worms paralyze and recover through cholinergic tachyphylaxis. In this study, we dissect the molecular mechanisms behind cholinergic tachyphylaxis using the free-living model, C. elegans . Here, we differentiate between two independent recovery mechanisms: one that is mediated by L-AChR clustering mutants – lev-10 and another, mediated by an ER-resident protein, NRA-2. Cholinergic tachyphylaxis observed in nra-2 mutants can be distinguished from lev-10 mutants using motility assays, transcript analysis, and calcium imaging. nra-2 mutants are more sensitive to levamisole and recover differently than lev-10 mutants. We observe that nra-2 mutants do not show increased calcium influx during their levamisole-mediated recovery. Our study delineates two distinct modes by which worms can adapt and overcome effects of cholinergic anthelmintics.

article.title: Understanding How Actomyosin Dynamics Drive Apical Constriction by Systematically Tagging and Mapping Actin-Binding Proteins
article.authors: Zhang, P.; de Jesus, B. N.; Medwig-Kinney, T. N.; Matus, D. Q.; Yee, C.; Gibney, T.; Pani, A. M.; Goldstein, B.
article.abstract: Apical constriction shapes tissues in fundamental events including gastrulation and neural tube formation. Diverse actin regulators play key roles in shaping cells, but the spatial distribution of most actin regulators in apical constriction is unknown. Here, we describe a systematic approach revealing the endogenous localization of 49 actin regulators in C. elegans gastrulation -- nearly every actin-binding protein (ABP) expressed in the early embryo -- and we use this atlas to test mechanistic hypotheses. We found that many actin regulators localized basolaterally, dependent on the Arp2/3 complex; that linear actin assembly factors enriched apically; and that apically constricting cells had an extra requirement for membrane-cortical linkers present in all cells. These findings answer some key questions about how ABPs function in apical constriction, and they establish a rich resource for investigating actin organization throughout early C. elegans development and a systematic in vivo protein localization reference for the actin cytoskeleton community.

article.title: Staphylococcus warneri MN336185 from Fermented Rice Water: a Multifunctional Probiotic with Anti-pathogenic and Longevity Benefits in C. elegans.
article.authors: Prakash V, Madhavan A, Babu P, Vanuopadath M, Jayakumar A, Raveendran A, Abhinand K, Sain T, Sasidharan NB, Hely S, Alphonse J, Nair BG, Pal S.
article.abstract: Fermented ecosystems serve as critical reservoirs for functionally diverse microorganisms with applications in food safety and nutraceuticals. This study focuses on Staphylococcus warneri MN336185 (SW), a non-traditional probiotic strain isolated from fermented rice water and evaluating its probiotic and bio-preservative properties. SW demonstrated significant gastrointestinal and oxidative stress tolerance, high epithelial cytocompatibility (> 80%), non-hemolytic safety, and an exceptional cholesterol assimilation efficiency of 85%. Moreover, whole-genome sequencing (WGS) confirmed genomic biosafety, establishing the absence of acquired enterotoxins, superantigens, ica-dependent biofilm determinants, and most transmissible antibiotic resistance elements. Studies on the host-microbe interface confirmed strong adherence of SW to HT-29 cells with proportionate competitive anti-adhesion potential against Salmonella enterica and Escherichia coli. The strain could also upregulate tight-junction proteins, claudins and zona occludens, indicating barrier-protective effects. In Caenorhabditis elegans, supplementation of SW as live feed enhanced lifespan, pharyngeal pumping, locomotory abilities, and resistance to pathogens. Further, challenge tests involving incorporation of live cells or cell-free supernatant of SW into rice-based matrices resulted in significant, time-dependent reduction of pathogens with a 4 log₁₀ CFU decrease during refrigerated storage. Collectively, these observations could establish S. warneri MN336185 as a multifunctional probiotic strain with potential application in functional food and natural biopreservation strategies.

article.title: A secreted LEA-like protein functions as a basement membrane stress protectant
article.authors: Brown, B. A.; Lewis, A. L.; Lester, M. K.; Wang, Z.; Hibshman, J. D.
article.abstract: Organisms have evolved to withstand a wide variety of environmental stresses. Survival requires individual cells to mount appropriate responses to combat molecular damage. In animals, multicellularity introduces an additional challenge: how is tissue integrity preserved? Our knowledge of extracellular tissue-level mechanisms of protection remains limited. Here, we report that a late embryogenesis abundant (LEA)-like protein, DUR-1, is secreted and then accumulates in basement membranes, where it acts to promote tissue integrity and stress survival. DUR-1 is strongly upregulated in the stress-tolerant dauer diapause stage of C. elegans and further upregulated upon desiccation. Loss of the protein sensitizes animals to desiccation and osmotic stress. Other LEA proteins have been regarded as strong desicco-protectants, but none have been recognized as components of basement membranes. We show that DUR-1 is important for maintaining the integrity of basement membrane-ensheathed tissues under mechanical stresses associated with drying or osmotic challenge. This work defines a mechanism for extracellular protection and emphasizes the importance of preserving tissue integrity during stress.

article.title: Quinoclamine, a repurposed agricultural algicide, functions as a multi-target quorum sensing inhibitor to attenuate Pseudomonas aeruginosa virulence and potentiate antibiotic efficacy.
article.authors: Zhang Z, Feng M, Fan Y, Liu J, Yuan Y, Hu X, Jiang W, Chu Y, Huang T, Zhao K.
article.abstract: The widespread overuse and misuse of antibiotics have precipitated a global antimicrobial resistance crisis, compounded by a dwindling pipeline of novel antibiotic discovery. As the quorum sensing (QS) system tightly mediates bacterial colonization and pathogenicity in Pseudomonas aeruginosa, QS-targeted anti-virulence therapy has emerged as a promising alternative to conventional antibiotics. In this study, through an integrated approach combining virtual screening and systematic experimental validation, we identified quinoclamine as a candidate QS inhibitor and comprehensively characterized its anti-virulence efficacy via in silico, in vitro, and in vivo assays. Molecular docking analysis predicted that quinoclamine simultaneously interacts with three core QS regulators: LasR, RhlR, and PqsR. In vitro experiments demonstrated that quinoclamine significantly inhibited key QS-controlled virulence factors including pyocyanin and extracellular proteases, as well as biofilm formation and bacterial motility, without affecting bacterial growth. Quantitative real-time PCR confirmed that quinoclamine downregulated QS-associated virulence genes and competitively blocked autoinducer-receptor binding. Furthermore, quinoclamine exhibited synergistic bactericidal activity with five clinical anti-pseudomonal antibiotics. Additionally, quinoclamine has moderate disruptive capacity against pre-formed mature biofilms, and partially potentiates the bactericidal efficacy of ciprofloxacin against sessile bacteria embedded within biofilms. The in vivo protective efficacy was validated across three infection models: C. elegans fast-killing, C. elegans slow-killing, and mouse acute pulmonary infection. Impressively, the combination of quinoclamine and 1/2 × MIC ciprofloxacin further improved host survival in all three models and reduced bacterial burden in mouse lung lesions. Collectively, these findings characterize quinoclamine as a promising QS inhibitor with broad anti-virulence activity, and provide robust experimental support for the development of QS-targeted anti-virulence therapies against P. aeruginosa infections.

article.title: Germ granules function as stress-responsive hubs to protect germ cell resilience
article.authors: Gaylord, O. J.; Armasanaa, M.; Basu, A.; Lee, H.-C.
article.abstract: Biomolecular condensates are dynamic, membrane-less compartments that perform critical cellular functions in the adaptation to environmental stressors. Within germ cells, germ granules are specialized condensates essential for germ cell viability, genome defense, and epigenetic inheritance. Notably, environmental stressors such as heat and starvation can disrupt genome defense and epigenetic inheritance, yet germ cell viability is often preserved. How germ cells adapt to environmental stress and recover viability remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate the impact of heat stress on the biomolecular condensates of adult germ cells in C. elegans. Upon heat stress, we observe extensive remodeling of the germ granule compartments, including reduced enrichment of key genome defense and epigenetic inheritance factors. Adjacent to remodeled germ granules, stress granules and P-bodies robustly assemble, suggesting these distinct condensates may functionally interact during the stress response. Indeed, we find stress granule and P-body formation within germ cells largely requires germ granule assembly factors GLH-1/VASA and MIP-1. Furthermore, we show these germ granule assembly factors and stress granule factors GTBP-1/G3BP1 and TIAR-1/TIA1, are essential for recovery of germ cell viability after heat stress. Intriguingly, stress granule factor TIAR-1/ TIA1 localizes to germ granules with and without stress, indicating germ granules are poised for the stress response. Together, our results support a model in which germ granules function as stress-responsive hubs that reorganize RNA granule networks to promote germline resilience.

article.title: Immune surveillance of cellular damage: lessons from Caenorhabditis elegans.
article.authors: Ghosh A, Singh J.
article.abstract: Innate immune systems must detect infection rapidly and reliably, yet pathogens can often evade direct recognition by host pattern-recognition receptors. An alternative and increasingly appreciated strategy is damage-driven immune surveillance, whereby hosts detect pathogen-induced perturbations to essential cellular and tissue functions rather than microbial molecules themselves. This mode of detection is particularly prominent in Caenorhabditis elegans, which lacks professional immune cells and most canonical innate immune receptors, and therefore relies extensively on monitoring disruptions to core homeostatic pathways. Perturbations to protein translation, proteostasis, mitochondrial function, genome and nucleolar integrity, lysosomal homeostasis, and Golgi function can all trigger immune responses. Recent studies have further uncovered roles for inter-organelle communication, effector-triggered surveillance of lysosome-related organelles, and physiological signals such as intestinal distension in regulating immune activation. Here, we integrate these advances into an organelle- and tissue-centric framework and explore parallels with other organisms to identify emerging and potentially conserved principles of damage sensing in innate immunity. These findings highlight the surveillance of cellular homeostasis as a central strategy for immunity that operates beyond canonical pattern-recognition mechanisms.

article.title: Repurposing the phospholipase A2 inhibitor, darapladib, to combat multidrug-resistant fungal pathogens, including Candida auris.
article.authors: Elgammal Y, Salama EA, Alkashef NM, Lawrence CB, Seleem MN.
article.abstract: Candida auris is an emerging multidrug-resistant fungal pathogen and a major global health threat, highlighting the urgent need for new therapeutics. We screened ~2,600 FDA-approved drugs and clinical compounds and identified darapladib (DAL), a phospholipase A2 inhibitor, as a potent antifungal agent against multidrug-resistant C. auris. DAL exhibited antifungal activity against all tested C. auris isolates and showed broad-spectrum activity against other tested clinically important fungal pathogens, including other Candida, Cryptococcus, and mucormycosis-associated species, with minimum inhibitory concentrations of 4-16 μg/mL. DAL also displayed rapid fungicidal activity against C. auris and synergized with amphotericin B against C. auris and filamentous fungal pathogens. More importantly, serial exposure of C. auris to subinhibitory concentrations of DAL for 16 passages did not result in detectable resistance. Mechanistic studies indicated that DAL acts through an ergosterol-dependent membrane targeting mechanism, as exogenous ergosterol attenuated its activity and ergosterol-related haploinsufficient mutants showed reduced susceptibility. Consistent with this mechanism, DAL increased membrane permeability, nucleic acid leakage, and reactive oxygen species. In a Caenorhabditis elegans-C. auris infection model, DAL reduced the C. auris burden to below the limit of detection. Together, these findings support further investigation of DAL as a repurposed antifungal candidate against drug-resistant fungal infections.

article.title: AKT1-phosphorylated TERT assembles a FOXO3-MYC transcriptional complex that drives ERphagy and proteostasis in post-mitotic RPE.
article.authors: Babu VS, Ghosh S, Bammidi S, Jiwon R, Sharma R, Meyer D, Hose S, Pattabiraman PP, Sahel JA, Kidley NJ, Braz NF, Slater MJ, Lang S, Ghosh A, Handa JT, Yi J, Sripathi S, Kannan RM, Bharti K, Sinha D.
article.abstract: The retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) sustains lifelong proteostasis under chronic stress, yet how post-mitotic cells activate macroautophagy/autophagy when canonical kinase pathways suppress it remains unresolved. Here we demonstrate that AKT1 (protein kinase B alpha), drives autophagy through a non-canonical transcriptional mechanism triggered by isoform imbalance. In RPE and age-related macular degeneration (AMD) models, AKT2 (protein kinase B beta) hyperactivation destabilizes MTORC2 (mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 2) and engages RPS6KB/S6K (ribosomal protein S6 kinase beta) -mediated IRS-1 (insulin Receptor Substrate 1) inhibition, creating a feedforward autophagic arrest. Compensatory AKT1 activation via MTORC2 phosphorylates TERT (telomerase reverse transcriptase) at serine 824, driving nuclear translocation that is independent of telomere maintenance. In the nucleus, TERT assembles with FOXO3 (forkhead Box O3) and MYC (MYC proto-oncogene, bHLH transcription factor) into a tripartite transcriptional complex that occupies the EIF2AK3/PERK promoter (eukaryotic translation initiation factor 2-alpha kinase 3/ protein kinase R-like endoplasmic reticulum kinase), enabling EIF2AK3 transcriptional activation. This activity converts the unfolded protein response from pro-apoptotic to cytoprotective: EIF2AK3-ATF4 (activating transcription factor 4) signaling promotes core autophagy machinery biogenesis and selective ERphagy through the receptors TEX264 (testis expressed 264) and CCPG1(cell cycle progression 1), which prevents pathological EIF2AK3 clustering and preserves tubular ER architecture in diseased RPE. Using C. elegans phosphorylation-deficient mutants, mouse models and AMD patient iPSC-RPE, we establish that AKT1-mediated TERT phosphorylation is an evolutionarily conserved prerequisite for FOXO/DAF-16 nuclear function and lysosomal homeostasis in post-mitotic cells, offering therapeutic potential through targeted pharmacologic inhibition of AKT2. Abbreviations: ACTB: actin, beta; AKT1: AKT serine/threonine kinase 1; AKT2: AKT serine/threonine kinase 2; ALP: autophagy-lysosomal pathway; AMD: age-related macular degeneration, ATF4: activating transcription factor 4; ATG3: autophagy related 3; ATG4B: autophagy related 4B cysteine peptidase; ATG7: autophagy related 7; CCPG1: cell cycle progression 1; CFH: complement factor H; C57BL/6J: C57 black 6J; DMSO: dimethyl sulfoxide; MYC: MYC proto-oncogene, bHLH transcription factor; EIF2A/eIF2α: eukaryotic translation initiation factor 2A; EIF2AK3/PERK: eukaryotic translation initiation factor 2 alpha kinase 3; ER: endoplasmic reticulum; ERN1/IRE-1α: endoplasmic reticulum to nucleus signaling 1; ERphagy: endoplasmic reticulum-selective autophagy; FOXO1: forkhead box O1; FOXO3: forkhead box O3; iPSC-RPE: induced pluripotent stem cell-derived retinal pigment epithelium; ITGB1/integrin β1: integrin subunit beta 1; MAP1LC3/LC3: microtubule associated protein 1 light chain 3; MAPKAP1/SIN1: MAPK associated protein 1; MTOR: mechanistic target of rapamycin kinase; MTORC1: MTOR complex 1; MTORC2: MTOR complex 2; PBS: phosphate-buffered saline; PI3K: phosphoinositide 3-kinase; RICTOR: RPTOR independent companion of MTOR complex 2; RPE: retinal pigment epithelium; RPTOR: regulatory associated protein of MTOR complex 1; SQSTM1/p62: sequestosome 1; TERT: telomerase reverse transcriptase; TEX264: testis expressed 264, ER-phagy receptor; UPR: unfolded protein response; VCL: vinculin; WT: wild type.

article.title: Arsenic promotes MIN6 cells dysfunction via ACO2-αKG-mitophagy pathway.
article.authors: Zhang J, Liu S, Wang Q, Jia Y, Qiu T, Yao X, Bai J, Wang N, Yang G, Sun X.
article.abstract: Arsenite can impair pancreatic β-cell function, but the mechanisms linking mitochondrial metabolic disturbances to this toxicity remain incompletely understood. Therefore, mitophagy, which removes dysfunctional mitochondria by lysosomal degradation, has attracted much attention. Mitochondrial (cis)aconitase 2 (ACO2) is a critical enzyme in the tricarboxylic acid cycle responsible for coordinating mitochondrial functions and is involved in energy metabolism. However, the role of ACO2 in arsenite-induced mitochondrial dysfunction and altered mitophagy in pancreatic β cells remains unclear. In this study, we demonstrated that arsenic exposure leads to the downregulation of mitochondrial ACO2. As expected, ACO2 overexpression reversed the arsenic-induced MIN6 cells dysfunction. In addition, arsenic induced the inhibition of mitophagy in islets β-cells characteristic with the downregulation of PTEN-induced putative kinase 1 (PINK1) , Parkin RBR E3 ubiquitin protein ligase (Parkin) and sequestosome 1 (p62/SQSTM1), accompanied by an increased level of microtubule-associated protein 1 light chain 3-II (LC3-II). ACO2 reversed these alterations in protein expression. Simultaneously, ACO2 overexpression elevated adenosine triphosphate (ATP) and mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP) levels, decreased mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS) production, and alleviated the functional impairment of β-cells induced by arsenic. Moreover, supplementation with α-ketoglutarate (α-KG), a downstream metabolite of ACO2, similarly mitigated arsenic-induced mitophagy inhibition and functional impairment of MIN6 cells. In conclusion, this study identified a novel mechanism by which inorganic arsenic can lead to pancreatic β cell dysfunction via the ACO2-αKG-mitophagy pathway. These findings advance the mechanistic understanding of arsenite-induced β-cell toxicity.

article.title: Prolonged low-salinity stress drives coordinated energy metabolism reprogramming and membrane lipid remodeling in the hepatopancreas of mated female mud crab (Scylla paramamosain): An integrated multi-omics study.
article.authors: Dildar T, Xue Y, Cui W, Waqas W, Ikhwanuddin M, Shen Z, Ma H.
article.abstract: The mud crab Scylla paramamosain is a commercially important euryhaline crustacean, yet the long-term hepatopancreatic response to low salinity remains largely uncharacterized. Adult mated females were exposed to (30, 15, and 5 ppt) salinity for 40 days, and hepatopancreatic responses were assessed using integrated histological, biochemical, transcriptomic, metabolomic, and lipidomic analyses. Low salinity exposure inhibited growth and survival and caused progressive hepatopancreatic injury, from lumen dilation at 15 ppt to severe vacuolization, basement-membrane disruption, and haemocyte infiltration at 5 ppt. Salinity stress elevated superoxide dismutase activity and reduced malondialdehyde content, whereas total protein declined, suggesting antioxidant activation and protein mobilization to meet energetic demands. Transcriptomic and gene set enrichment analyses showed coordinated activation of oxidative phosphorylation, the tricarboxylic acid cycle, ribosome, and proteasome pathways, together with sustained cytochrome p450 and UDP glucuronosyltransferase mediated detoxification. Steroid biosynthesis was selectively suppressed under low salinity. Metabolomic profiling shifted with salinity level, from nutrient-sensing signaling and amino-acid metabolism at 15 ppt to AMPK and HIF-1 signaling, the tricarboxylic acid cycle, and nucleotide metabolism at 5 ppt. Lipidomic evidence revealed extensive glycerophospholipid and cardiolipin remodeling, linking membrane adaptation with mitochondrial energy metabolism. Integrated analysis identified glycolysis/gluconeogenesis as the only significantly co-enriched pathway at 5 ppt, with pyruvate emerging as a key node linking glycolysis and the TCA cycle in the integrated network. Overall, prolonged low-salinity exposure compromises hepatopancreatic integrity while activating coordinated energy mobilization, membrane remodeling, and detoxification responses that support osmotic adaptation in female mud crabs.

article.title: Engineered SHED-EVs delivering FtMt siRNA rescue mitophagy and bone formation in smoking-related osteoporosis.
article.authors: Fang M, Ren Z, Li N, Xu W, Xue Y, Wang R, Zhou J.
article.abstract: Aims Tobacco smoking independently contributes to osteoporosis. Cigarette smoke-derived reactive oxygen species (ROS) and transition metals promote iron accumulation and impair mitophagy in bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs), causing mitochondrial dysfunction, reduced osteogenic differentiation, and iron-induced osteoporosis. The molecular pathways linking smoke exposure to impaired bone formation remain incompletely understood. Materials and methods We established a cigarette smoke extract (CSE)-induced bone-loss model in female C57BL/6J mice ( n = 8/group) and performed femoral transcriptomic profiling. Bone-targeting extracellular vesicles from stem cells from human exfoliated deciduous teeth (SHED-EVs) were loaded with siRNA against mitochondrial ferritin (FtMt; siFtMt) to generate BT-siFtMt@SHED-EVs. The nanoplatform was characterized and tested in vitro and in vivo using micro-CT, JC-1, Alkaline Phosphatase/alizarin red S, immunostaining, RT-qPCR, Western blotting, and in silico docking (ZDOCK/RDOCK). Results CSE upregulated FtMt while suppressing mitophagy and osteogenic differentiation. BT-siFtMt@SHED-EVs restored mitochondrial membrane potential, reinstated mitophagic flux, and rescued BMSC osteogenesis. Systemically administered BT-siFtMt@SHED-EVs restored trabecular microarchitecture and bone mineral density and elevated osteogenic markers in CSE-exposed mice; these benefits were abolished by the mitophagy inhibitor Mdivi-1. Conclusions Targeted FtMt knockdown via bone-homing SHED-EVs reinstates mitochondrial quality control and ameliorates smoke-related bone loss, offering a precision mitochondrial medicine approach to osteoporosis.

article.title: The Blood Is Not the Heart: Clonal Haematopoiesis, Tissue-Restricted Mitochondrial Heteroplasmy and the Bidirectional Error of Cardiogenetic Attribution
article.authors: Biswas B.
article.venue: 预印本平台（数据库未注明）
article.abstract: Purpose: of Review: Cardiovascular genomic interpretation frequently relies upon peripheral-blood DNA, although blood-derived variation does not necessarily represent the genome of diseased cardiac tissue. Conversely, clinically relevant mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) heteroplasmy may be insufficiently represented in blood. This review examines these opposing errors of cardiogenetic attribution and proposes PROVENANCE-CV, a compartment-resolved framework distinguishing variant provenance, pathogenicity, cardiovascular mechanism and clinical utility.Recent Findings: Large-scale genomic investigations published in 2026 demonstrate that numerous age-associated blood mtDNA variants become detectable through haematopoietic clonal expansion, whereas multitissue analyses establish substantial anatomical heterogeneity of mitochondrial variation. Direct human cardiac investigations demonstrate both tissue-localised molecular abnormalities and clinically informative relationships between blood and myocardial measurements. Experimental and human studies additionally implicate selected haematopoietic clones in cardiovascular pathology through mechanisms that do not require the initiating mutation to reside within cardiomyocytes. Summary: Blood-centred interpretation risks attributing haematopoietic variation to intrinsic cardiac disease or excluding tissue-restricted pathogenic variation following a negative blood result. PROVENANCE-CV proposes five independently evaluated evidentiary gates and an uncertainty-aware adjudication protocol. A copy-number-weighted mixture model demonstrates how changes in cellular composition can alter bulk heteroplasmy without corresponding changes in within-lineage mutation burden. Prospective validation against established, guideline-concordant genetic assessment is proposed using independently corroborated classification, reproducibility and clinical utility. The framework is not a validated diagnostic instrument; its principal contribution is a falsifiable method for distinguishing specimen identity from molecular pathogenicity and cardiovascular causation.

article.title: Bacteroides fragilis Enterotoxin Activates NLRP3 Inflammasomes through NF-κB Signaling and Mitophagy Suppression in Intestinal Epithelial Cells.
article.authors: Choi JH, Lee YC, Shin MK, Kim JM.
article.abstract: Background/aims Enterotoxigenic Bacteroides fragilis (ETBF) induces acute and chronic inflammatory pathology through its toxic factor B. fragilis enterotoxin (BFT). Although inflammasomes are critical for maintaining intestinal homeostasis and modulating inflammation, their roles remain poorly characterized during ETBF infection. This study investigated the pathways involved in inflammasome formation in BFT-exposed intestinal epithelial cells (IECs). Methods Human colon epithelial cells HCT-116 and CCD 841 CoN were used as IEC models. To investigate inflammasome formation and activation, BFT-treated cells were analyzed by immunoblotting, disuccinimidyl suberate cross-linking, immunofluorescence microscopy, colocalization assays, and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay. Results BFT stimulation significantly upregulated the expression of NLR family pyrin domain containing 3 (NLRP3), pro-interleukin (IL)-1β, pro-IL-18, and cleaved caspase-1 in both cell lines. Inflammasome complexes were confirmed by apoptosis-associated speck-like protein containing a CARD (ASC) oligomerization and colocalization of ASC with NLRP3, accompanied by increased IL-1β and IL-18 secretion. Two pathways were involved in inflammasome activation: first, nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) signaling regulated NLRP3, pro-IL-1β, and pro-IL-18 expression, promoting caspase-1 activation; second, p53/BAG5 axis activation suppressed Parkin-mediated mitophagy and drove reactive oxygen species accumulation, engaging the inflammasome complex. Conclusions These findings demonstrate that the formation of inflammasomes may occur via two pathways, namely, NF-κB-mediated signaling and p53/BAG5-associated suppression of mitophagy.

article.title: Biomaterials Targeting Mitochondrial NAD + Metabolism for Tissue Regeneration.
article.authors: Ma X, Li M, Ren T, Li Y, Zhu Y, Wang Y, Han L.
article.abstract: Mitochondrial nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD + ) has emerged as a pivotal regulator in tissue regeneration, central to cellular energy metabolism and redox homeostasis. It regulates key mitochondrial processes-including energy production, reactive oxygen species (ROS) scavenging, and cell death-primarily through the tricarboxylic acid cycle (TAC), oxidative phosphorylation, and sirtuin deacetylase activity. This coordinated regulation fosters a favorable metabolic and immune microenvironment conducive to tissue repair. Strategies to increase mitochondrial NAD + levels, such as delivery, precursor supplementation (e.g., NR or NMN), catalytic conversion, and inhibition of NAD + -consuming enzymes, have demonstrated significant efficacy in promoting regeneration across diverse tissues, including bone, cartilage, tooth, skin, myocardium, muscle, nerve, and vascular. There is no review that systematically addresses the latest progress in the advances of biomaterials targeting mitochondrial NAD + metabolism for tissue regeneration. This review fills the gap by outlining the central role of biomaterials targeting mitochondrial NAD + in tissue regeneration. We introduce the biological functions and regulatory mechanisms of mitochondrial NAD + , highlight the intervention strategies to boost NAD + levels, and summarize the applications across diverse regenerative contexts. Finally, we discuss prevailing challenges and future prospects, providing new theoretical and interventional insights for regenerative medicine.

article.title: Assembly of a high-quality reference genome for the rat tapeworm Hymenolepis diminuta.
article.authors: Choudhary SK, Sundaresha N, Ye K, Bergman CM, Rozario T.
article.abstract: The rat tapeworm, Hymenolepis diminuta, is an important laboratory model for uncovering molecular processes that underly the success of tapeworms as parasites. Despite its importance, a high-quality reference genome for this species is lacking. Here we present a highly contiguous and effectively complete genome of H. diminuta assembled from PacBio HiFi long-read sequencing data. Our primary assembly consists of 7 scaffolds (N50 = 29.25 Mb) with total length of 186.53 Mb, has only 7 gaps, and contains 95.7% complete Lophotrochozoan BUSCOs. Our assembly allows us to confirm aspects of Hymenolepis genome organization, such as high repeat content and unusual chromosomal ends, and to show that Hymenolepis genomes encode ∼10,000 genes. Together with annotations of nuclear tRNAs, mtDNA protein coding genes, and mtDNA tRNAs, our assembly currently provides one of the most complete genome resources for a tapeworm species and will enable research on parasitism, animal regeneration, development, and evolution.

article.title: A Hospital-Based Concurrent Hearing and Genetic Screening Study of 39,282 Newborns in Southwest China.
article.authors: Yi H, He L, Yu G, Dong Y.
article.abstract: BackgroundHearing loss is a significant public health concern. This study assessed the carrier frequency of deafness-associated genetic variants and the yield of concurrent newborn hearing and molecular genetic screening in Chongqing, China.MethodsA total of 39,282 newborns underwent hearing screening using both transiently evoked otoacoustic emission (TEOAE) and automated auditory brainstem response (AABR). Additionally, genetic testing was performed via PCR and flow-through hybridization to detect variants in four key deafness-associated genes: GJB2 , GJB3 , SLC26A4 , and mtDNA . Positive results were confirmed by Sanger sequencing. Follow-up telephone interviews were conducted to monitor auditory status, with objective audiological evaluation recommended for screen-positive newborns.ResultsA total of 1,422 newborns carried at least one genetic variant, with a positive genetic screening rate of 3.62%. The most common variant was GJB2 c.235delC, found in approximately 48.80% of carriers. The carrier frequencies for the other genes were GJB2 (2.184%), SLC26A4 (1.018%), GJB3 (0.168%), and mtDNA (0.204%). Four newborns with biallelic GJB2 variants (one homozygous c.235delC and three compound heterozygous c.235delC/c.299_300delAT) had moderate hearing loss and were fitted with hearing aids. In addition, one newborn with compound heterozygous SLC26A4 v ariants (c.919-2A>G and c.2162C>T), identified by follow-up Sanger sequencing, also had moderate hearing loss and received hearing aids. Fifteen newborns carried heterozygous variants in two different recessive deafness genes and had normal hearing at follow-up; Seventy-seven newborns carried mitochondrial variants associated with aminoglycoside ototoxicity and received drug-warning cards.ConclusionThis hospital-based, single-center study characterizes the carrier frequencies of 13 common deafness-associated variants in a voluntary-participation cohort in Chongqing, China. The findings are restricted to the specific variants examined and may not be generalizable to the entire newborn population of Chongqing.

article.title: A Biomimetic PLK1 Nanodelivery System Promotes Migrasome-Mediated Mitocytosis to Restore Efferocytosis and Functional Recovery After Spinal Cord Injury.
article.authors: Hu Z, Wang H, Huang J, Zhou J, Hou J, Miao H, Tan H, Wang Y, Hu H, Li N, Qiu P, Zhang H, He D, Wang Q.
article.abstract: Excessive accumulation and insufficient clearance of apoptotic cells following spinal cord injury (SCI) are key factors contributing to persistent injury. Macrophage efferocytosis is essential for resolving injury but is compromised by mitochondrial dysfunction and lysosomal overload. Maintaining mitochondrial functional homeostasis is therefore crucial for preserving the acidic lysosomal environment, alleviating the cellular lysosomal burden, and sustaining efferocytosis. Common mitochondrial quality control (MQC) pathways such as mitophagy increase the lysosomal burden. Here, we investigated how polo-like kinase 1 (PLK1) regulates macrophage efferocytosis and elucidated the underlying mechanism of migrasome-mediated mitocytosis. We demonstrate that PLK1 regulates TSPAN4-dependent migrasome formation, which drives the selective extrusion of damaged mitochondria, alleviates the lysosomal burden, and increases efferocytic capacity. To enable targeted PLK1 delivery, we engineered macrophage membrane-coated, reactive oxygen species (ROS)-responsive nanocomplexes encapsulating PLK1 plasmids (MM-NPs@PLK1). This biomimetic nanoplatform preferentially accumulates in the injured spinal cord, promotes macrophage-associated PLK1 delivery, enhances mitocytosis and efferocytosis, supports neural tissue repair, and significantly improves locomotor recovery in SCI mice. In summary, our study reveals a PLK1-regulated MQC mechanism that sustains macrophage efferocytosis through migrasome-mediated mitocytosis, providing a promising therapeutic strategy for SCI.

article.title: Probing non-covalent membrane protein-lipid interactions using sheath liquid capillary electrophoresis-native top-down mass spectrometry.
article.authors: Pathak K, Brinkman D, Walters S, Perrotti G, Fuglestad B, Gomes FP.
article.abstract: Probing non-covalent membrane protein-lipid interactions remains challenging due to the high hydrophobicity and aggregation propensity of membrane proteins. Here, we present a sheath liquid capillary electrophoresis-native top-down mass spectrometry (CE-nTDMS) platform that enables reproducible infusion of aquaporin Z-cardiolipin assemblies and preserves their non-covalent electrostatic interactions during top-down fragmentation. This workflow generated a diagnostic fragment ion that localizes a lipid-binding region within the protein backbone. Notably, charge-reduced precursor fragment ions of the lipid-bound assembly exhibited asymmetrical isotopic distributions following collisional activation, while corresponding apo precursors displayed symmetrical isotopic distributions. These findings demonstrate the utility of CE-nTDMS for reliable analysis of membrane protein-lipid assemblies and provide new insight into the behavior of lipid-bound fragments during collisional activation.

article.title: Mechanisms of Traditional Chinese Medicine-Derived Active Components in the Treatment of Alzheimer's Disease: A Comprehensive Review.
article.authors: Tian Y, Guo J, Lin X, Zhang F, Xie J, Hou X, Deng J, Hao E, Du Z.
article.abstract: Ethnopharmacological relevance Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive cognitive decline and multifactorial pathology. Because AD involves interacting pathological processes, the limited efficacy of conventional single-target therapies has increased interest in traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) and other natural medicines with multi-target pharmacological actions. TCM-derived active components originate from medicinal materials used in traditional practice and are evaluated using modern pharmacological approaches. Their source medicines have diverse traditional-use backgrounds. Some have historical associations with memory or cognitive symptoms, whereas many others were traditionally used for broader deficiency, phlegm, blood-stasis, heat, or related syndromic patterns. These records provide ethnopharmacological context for the source medicines but should not be taken as historical evidence for the anti-AD activity of their isolated constituents. Aim of the review This review synthesizes current evidence on the mechanisms of TCM-derived bioactive components in AD while incorporating relevant traditional-use information on their source medicines. Particular attention is given to their multi-target actions and emerging mechanisms involving ferroptosis, mitophagy, and the gut-brain axis. Materials and methods Mechanistic literature published between January 2019 and November 2025 was retrieved from Ovid MEDLINE, PubMed, ScienceDirect, and Web of Science. Ovid MEDLINE and PubMed were searched separately to maximize retrieval across indexed and additional PubMed records, with overlapping records removed during deduplication. Traditional-use information was evaluated separately for the source medicines. A targeted search of PubMed and ClinicalTrials.gov was also conducted to assess human interventional evidence for compounds covered in the review, with trial-registration information updated through August 2026. Results Current preclinical findings suggest that TCM active components may produce coordinated preclinical pharmacological effects through multiple pathways, including the inhibition of β-amyloid (Aβ) production and deposition, regulation of tau aggregation and phosphorylation, alleviation of neuroinflammation and oxidative stress, improvement of mitophagy and iron metabolism disorders, and modulation of gut microbiota homeostasis. Among these components, saponins show broad mechanistic coverage. Flavonoids, polysaccharides, and other bioactive substances have likewise shown anti-inflammatory and antioxidant activities, together with protective effects on synaptic function, in preclinical models. These mechanistic findings were derived predominantly from cellular and animal studies, with computational analyses providing mainly hypothesis-generating support. Human evidence was available for only a small subset of compounds and was not uniformly positive. Huperzine A has progressed to controlled clinical testing but has shown mixed efficacy findings; resveratrol demonstrated CNS exposure and biomarker activity without consistent cognitive benefit; curcumin did not show efficacy in a placebo-controlled AD trial; and favorable signals from ginseng studies were limited by open-label designs and the use of whole preparations rather than isolated ginsenosides. Conclusions The available evidence supports broad preclinical activity of TCM-derived components across several interconnected AD-related processes, but the strength of mechanistic support varies markedly among compounds and pathways. Human translation remains limited and inconsistent, and current clinical data do not establish disease-modifying efficacy for the compounds reviewed. Further development should therefore be guided by the main uncertainty surrounding each candidate-whether mechanistic causality, reproducibility, systemic or CNS exposure, preparation standardization, or clinical efficacy-rather than by a fixed sequence of technologies.

article.title: Phagocytosis without mitochondria is a lineage trait of planctomycetal bacteria of prey
article.authors: Wurzbacher, C. E.; Hammer, J.; Haufschild, T.; Buyuktarakci, B. S.; Jimenez Gonzales, A.; Bouderka, F.; Soares, A.; Mueller, J. M.; Muriel Millan, L. F.; Ferrelli, M. L.; Hotter, V. S.; Taubert, M.; Kuesel, K.; Devos, D.; Klingl, A.; Probst, A. J.; Andersson, S. G. E.; Kallscheuer, N.; Jogler, C.
article.abstract: Phagocytosis is considered energetically out of reach for prokaryotes. Mitochondria-first models of eukaryogenesis therefore suggest a non-phagocytic archaeal host. Yet two recently described planctomycetes lack mitochondria and engulf entire bacteria. Whether this mode of predation is an oddity of two isolates or the hallmark of a bacterial lineage remained unresolved. Here, we report eight additional predatory Planctomycetota from three aquatic habitats. The ten cultured strains now span two classes of the phylum Planctomycetota,"Candidatus Uabimicrobiia" and one newly proposed class. Using engineered fluorescent prey, we show that nine strains internalize prey into fully sealed compartments whereas one digests its prey externally, a non-engulfing predator for comparison. The strains additionally divide by two distinct modes, however, not correlating with their feeding behavior. Sequence- and structure-based searches detect no eukaryotic phagocytosis protein conserved across the engulfing strains. The actin homologue previously proposed to mediate uptake occurs only in three engulfing strains. Routine engulfment by aerobic bacteria without mitochondria thus unsettles a premise of mitochondria-first models and reopens the question of which cell plans could have hosted the mitochondrial endosymbiont.

article.title: Metabolic profiling of declining ovarian reserve based on non-targeted metabolomics
article.authors: Zhao T, Huang T, Shi H, Xiao X, Yang G, Zhou L, Yuan T.
article.abstract: Abstract Objective To explore serum metabolic profiles and identify key pathways and markers associated with disease progression across different clinical stages of premature ovarian insufficiency (POI). Methods Sixty patients with POI were included in this study and divided into four groups (A, B, C, and D) based on their serum follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH), and oestradiol levels and FSH/LH ratio (15 patients per group). A healthy control group (15 participants) was also included. Non-targeted metabolomics was performed using UPLC–MS/MS to systematically compare differences in metabolites and metabolic pathways among the groups. Results As the disease progressed, FSH levels increased in a stepwise manner, whereas AMH and sex hormone levels progressively decreased. The metabolic profiles showed stage-specific characteristics: Group A was mainly characterised by impaired mitochondrial energy metabolism and exposure to exogenous substances; Group B exhibited altered sphingolipid and arachidonic acid metabolism; Group C showed a widespread increase in acylcarnitine levels; and Group D exhibited elevated levels of bile acid intermediates and sphingolipid reprogramming. Pathway enrichment analysis identified methionine, vitamin/porphyrin, bile acid/one-carbon, and sphingolipid/serotonin metabolic pathways. Conclusion Different clinical stages of POI have distinct serum metabolic fingerprints. Serum acylcarnitine profiles, sphingolipid metabolites, and bile acid intermediates are potential biomarkers for evaluating POI progression and could provide metabolomic evidence to support clinical staging and stage-specific intervention strategies.

article.title: Mitochondrial and bioenergetic processes are enriched in large-but are reciprocally depleted in small extracellular vesicles
article.authors: Achanta, N.; Soundara Manickam, D.
article.abstract: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are a promising class of drug delivery carriers for a broad range of therapeutic applications. We have previously demonstrated that brain endothelial cell (BEC)-derived large EVs (>200 nm in particle diameter) increased mitochondrial function in recipient BECs and improved therapeutic outcomes in a mouse model of ischemic stroke. In the current study, we demonstrate using size-resolved quantitative proteomics and gene-set enrichment analysis that mitochondrial and bioenergetic processes are enriched in large- but are reciprocally depleted in small EVs (exosomes, <200 nm in particle diameter). These results are striking and reveal the selective packaging of mitochondrial cargo in large but not small EVs. These strong mechanistic data anchor the rationale for the continued development of large EV mitochondria as a potential approach for the treatment of multiple diseases associated with mitochondrial dysfunction.

article.title: Cross-cohort kinship in the Critically Endangered Largetooth Sawfish (Pristis pristis) from a northern Australian river
article.authors: Amini S, Feutry P, Malak Rangers M, Pillans R, Davies C, Kyne P.
article.venue: 预印本平台（数据库未注明）
article.abstract: The sawfishes (family Pristidae) are one of the most threatened groups of vertebrates in the world. Global declines are associated with overfishing, habitat loss, and their K-selected life histories. The Largetooth Sawfish (Pristis pristis) is the only euryhaline sawfish, with the last stronghold for this species being found in the remote waters of northern Australia. Using thousands of genome-wide single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and long-read mitochondrial data, we examined the patterns of relatedness in 113 individuals collected over 13-years from the Daly River, Northern Territory. We identified 20 full- and 55 half-sibling pairs, with most half-siblings sharing a mitochondrial haplotype. Estimates of both the effective number of breeders per cohort and the generational effective population size were low (85.7–318.0 and <600 individuals, respectively). We reveal that relatedness is positively associated with both pairwise capture year and capture location. These findings provide further evidence for female reproductive philopatry and highlight the vulnerability of P. pristis to local extinction from the Daly River, a critical nursery area, as it falls under increasing anthropogenic pressures.

article.title: A specialized SUV3 RNA helicase is involved in plant mitochondrial DNA repair
article.authors: Rodriguez, M. G.; Raygoza, C. D.; Martinez Hottovy, A. M.; Campbell, D. M.; Purfeerst, E. R.; Brieba de castro, L. G.; Christensen, A. C.
article.abstract: Synonymous substitution rates in the coding regions of land plant mitochondrial genomes are substantially lower than those in the nucleus. In contrast, non-coding regions are difficult or impossible to align except among very closely related species, suggesting that point mutation rates in these regions are considerably higher. Rearrangement breakpoints occur frequently within non-coding DNA, generating duplications, deletions, and inversions. To reconcile these contradictory patterns of genome evolution, it has been proposed that DNA damage is converted into double-strand breaks that are repaired through a combination of template-directed mechanisms and non-homologous end joining, while purifying selection preserves the integrity of coding sequences. Here we characterized AtSUV3, a mitochondrially targeted RNA helicase encoded by Arabidopsis thaliana At4g14790, a gene previously proposed to function as part of the plant mitochondrial degradosome. Mutations in AtSUV3 confer hypersensitivity to ciprofloxacin-induced mitochondrial DNA damage, CRISPR- knockout lines display increased ectopic recombination in the mitochondrial genome, and recombinant AtSUV3 exhibits ATP-dependent RNA helicase activity with a preference for 3'-ended substrates. Together, these findings identify AtSUV3 as a factor involved in mitochondrial dsDNA break repair. Consistent with our results, Arabidopsis and other plants encode an uncharacterized gene, AT5G39840.1, with 75% amino acid similarity with AtSUV3, dubbed herein as SUV3-like. We hypothesize that the AtSUV3 paralog has undergone specialization towards DNA repair, whereas AtSUV3-like protein may play a role in the plant organellar degradosome. Collectively, these findings identify AtSUV3 as a previously unrecognized factor involved in mitochondrial dsDNA break repair and provide a framework for understanding the diversification of DNA repair proteins during plant evolution.

article.title: CEP-IP with CMRF in SEA-AD Microglia: A Mitochondrial Co-expression Module Linked to Cognition
article.authors: Wong, K. K.
article.abstract: Single-nucleus RNA-seq (snRNA-seq) studies of Alzheimer's disease (AD) routinely filter nuclei by mitochondrial percentage (%MT) or remove mitochondrial genes, yet whether these reads carry information about cognition is rarely examined. In the SEA-AD microglia snRNA-seq dataset, a transcriptome-wide screen identified a module of MT-CO3 and eight co-expressed mitochondrial genes. Three microglial populations were analyzed: M4 (Mic.13-like), PVM_3, and PVM_1, with a housekeeping-gene control in M4 cells. The CEP-IP pipeline with a copula monotone recovery filter (CMRF) used per-cell Spearman and Kendall scores, an inflection point (IP), and a cross-validated copula space boundary to isolate MT-CO3 Module cells. The donor percentage of Module cells past the IP (Module post-IP%) was significantly associated with worse cognition (MMSE and CASI; FDR<0.05) in all three populations. In M4 and PVM_3, these associations remained significant after adjustment for tissue quality, plaque burden, tangle burden, and contamination, and after doublet removal. M4 and PVM_3 Module post-IP% repeated in each donor's regions beyond chance, and no per-cell %MT cutoff reproduced the Module cells. However, at the donor level, Module post-IP% could not be separated from mean %MT, and the source of the mitochondrial transcripts (e.g., retained cytoplasm or a true change in mitochondrial content) remains unresolved. Routine %MT filtering in AD snRNA-seq may therefore remove cells that carry information about cognition. The full pipeline code, software container, processed data, and the R package cepip are publicly available, and reruns of the full pipeline in the container reproduced the original findings.

article.title: Plant Organellar Homologous Recombination Depends on Accessory Factors for Recombinase Activity
article.authors: Mora-Garduno, J.; Peralta Castro, A.; Aguilar Granados, A.; Raygoza, C. D.; Diaz Quezada, C.; Brieba, L. G.
article.abstract: Plant mitochondrial and plastid genomes rely on homologous recombination (HR) for error-free DNA repair of double strand breaks. Here, we reconstructed the homologous recombination pathway of plant organelles from Arabidopsis, aiming to understand how proteins of diverse evolutionary origins assemble into a functional repair pathway. We found that the three bacterial-derived recombinases, AtRecAs assemble D-loop intermediates, but only chloroplast AtRecA1 independently execute end-joining recombination on large DNA substrates. AtRecA1-mediated end-joining recombination is enhanced by plant-unique single-stranded DNA-binding proteins of the Whirly and Organellar Single-Stranded Binding (OSB) families, in contrast these proteins are mandatory for the recombination activities of the dual-targeted AtRecA2 and mitochondrial AtRecA3. Recombinational intermediates generated by AtRecAs are resolved by a bacterial-like RadA helicase but not bacterial-like RecG. Finally, AtRecX inhibits the recombinase activities of AtRecA2, while the activities of AtRecA1 and AtRecA3 remains largely insensitive. Collectively, our results provide an integrative reconstitution of the plant organellar homologous recombination machinery, revealing that homologous recombination arises from a complex system of bacterial, phage-derived, plant-specific, and eukaryotic components. Plant-specific ssDNA-binding proteins emerge as key regulators of this process, promoting recombination efficiency and genome stability, that supports the essential functions of homologous recombination in DNA repair and DNA replication maintenance.

article.title: From micro-architecture to networks: canonical neurobiological architecture of functional brain organization across the lifespan and in psychopathology
article.authors: Feng, G.; Chen, J.; Iraji, A.; Sendi, M. S. E.; Fu, Z.; Calhoun, V. D.
article.abstract: Understanding how macroscale functional network connectivity (FNC) across the lifespan and in psychopathology is spatially organized with respect to microscale neurobiological architecture remains a challenge. Here, we constructed a cross-omics mapping framework by linking resting-state fMRI data (5,349 individuals, 6-80 years) with 49 neurobiological markers (24 cell types, 19 neurotransmitters, 6 mitochondria). We show that FNC development and aging unfold along cellular and molecular gradients. Specifically, spatial correspondence between age-related FNC changes and neurobiological microprofile networks varied by life stage, peaking for cell types in adolescence, neurotransmitter systems in mid-young adulthood and mitochondrial phenotypes in early adulthood. Applying normative modeling to 5 psychiatric disorders (schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, major depressive disorder, autism, and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder), we identified disorder-specific and cross-disorder FNC phenotypes spatially associated with neurobiological architecture. Together, these findings provide a hypothesis-generating framework linking functional brain organization and dysfunction to canonical neurobiological architecture across the lifespan and psychiatric disorders.

article.title: Chromosome-scale nuclear and mitochondrial genome assemblies reveal extreme genome compartmentalization in the hazelnut pathogen Anisogramma anomala
article.authors: Zaccaron, A. Z.; Sondreli, K. L.; LeBoldus, J. M.; Weisberg, A. J.
article.abstract: Anisogramma anomala is an obligate biotrophic ascomycete and the causal agent of Eastern filbert blight, the most economically important disease of hazelnut in the United States. Here, we generated a chromosome-scale reference genome for A. anomala isolate OR-Ennis-d and characterized its nuclear and mitochondrial genome architecture. The 344-Mb nuclear genome was resolved into 9 predicted chromosomes and is repeat-rich, with transposable elements comprising 88.8% of the assembly. Although transposable elements are abundant, their divergence landscape and low retention of conserved protein domains support a history of past extensive transposon proliferation followed by widespread degeneration. Repeat accumulation was highly uneven and generated pronounced genome compartmentalization. Approximately half of predicted genes occur in compact, TE-poor regions with short flanking intergenic regions that are enriched for conserved BUSCO orthologs. In contrast, genes in TE-rich, gene-sparse regions with long flanking intergenic regions are enriched for carbohydrate-active enzymes, secreted proteins, and candidate secreted effector proteins, consistent with a two-speed-like genome architecture. The 462-kb mitochondrial genome is among the largest reported for ascomycetes and contains 117 introns, including an intron adjacent to cob codon 143 that may prevent acquisition of the p.G143A substitution associated with resistance to quinone outside inhibitor fungicides. Finally, we identified mitochondrial DNA insertions at 20 nuclear loci totaling at least 616.9 kb, an unusually extensive amount for a fungal genome. This chromosome-scale genome resource reveals the extreme nuclear and mitochondrial genome architecture in A. anomala and provides a foundation for investigating genome evolution and adaptation to hazelnut resistance.

article.title: Morphologic description and molecular characterization of Trichobilharzia species (Digenea: Schistosomatidae) infection in field-collected Radix auricularia (Linnaeus, 1758) in North of Iran
article.authors: Kenarsari AA, Yakhchali M, Fashi KA, Sharifdini M.
article.abstract: Abstract Lymnaeid snails are considered as intermediate hosts of Trichobilharzia species, the causal agents of avian schistosomiasis in wild and domestic birds in Iran and worldwide. The aim of the present study was to evaluate Trichobilharzia infection in field-collected snails of Radix auricularia (Linnaeus, 1758) in Guilan Province, northern Iran. The collected snails were examined for the cercarial stage of Trichobilharzia infection using the cercariae shedding method. Genomic DNA was extracted from collected cercariae and the soft tissue of R. auricularia . Cercariae were identified by sequencing and phylogenetic analysis of the nuclear internal transcribed spacer 1 (ITS-1) region and the mitochondrial cytochrome oxidase 1 ( cox 1) gene. Snail hosts belonging to the genus Radix were identified based on sequencing and phylogenetic analysis of a partial fragment of the ITS-2 region of ribosomal DNA. Microscopically, R. auricularia snails were found to be infected with the cercarial stage of Trichobilharzia species (1%). Molecularly, 0.89% and 0.11% of the examined snails were found to be infected with T. franki and T. regenti , respectively. Based on the ribosomal loci, T. franki and T. regenti exhibited eight and seven haplotypes, respectively, whereas analysis of the mitochondrial gene revealed eight haplotypes in T. franki and two in T. regenti . These findings indicated R. auricularia served as an important role in maintaining the transmission cycle of T. franki and T. regenti in the region. Therefore, it is recommended to investigate the role of migratory waterfowl in the transmission of Trichobilharzia infection to native birds, as well as to implement preventive measures among the residents in the region.

article.title: Auditory Epigenetic Transduction: Acoustic Perception Drives the c-Fos–SIRT6–SIRT3–Dicer Axis to Extend Health span
article.authors: Lakshmanane B.
article.abstract: Abstract While non-invasive circuit modulation and sensory perception dynamically influence cognitive states and memory consolidation, the precise sub-cellular transducers linking central acoustic perception to chromatin remodeling, microRNA biogenesis, and somatic lifespan have remained uncharacterized. Here, we identify the Auditory c-Fos–GATA2–SIRT6–SIRT3–Dicer Epigenetic Transduction Engine. We demonstrate that central acoustic wave perception (music listening) engages cortical and subcortical integration ensembles to drive high-amplitude nuclear pulses of immediate-early gene factors: c-Fos (AP-1 complex) and GATA2. Nuclear c-Fos directly transactivates Sirtuin 6 (SIRT6), while GATA2 and c-Fos act additively at an intronic Variable Number Tandem Repeat (VNTR) enhancer to boost mitochondrial Sirtuin 3 (SIRT3). Downstream of this multi-Sirtuin activation, SIRT6 stabilizes NRF2 to quench reactive oxygen species (ROS), deacetylates FOXO3a to reboot autophagic clearance, and co-activates the tumor suppressor network (p53/TAp63/TAp73) to directly transactivate Dicer1 through promoter p53-Response Elements (p53-REs). This host-encoded mechanism preserves Dicer-dependent microRNA processing against age-dependent octogenarian decay and pathogen-induced (SARS-CoV-2 N-protein/svRNA) autophagic degradation. We formalize this non-pharmacological sensory-behavioral-dietary cascade into a 9-variable non-linear Ordinary Differential Equation (ODE) system, establishing the quantitative computational proof that music perception—acting synergistically with aerobic exercise (The Treadmill Prescription) and dietary lycopene—restores BDNF-mediated frontoparietal network connectivity, preserves the centenarian-like Dicer longevity phenotype, and extends human healthspan

article.title: Multi-omic causal discovery uncovers a mitochondrial-epigenetic feedback loop in Parkinson’s disease
article.authors: Kang J, Chun H.
article.abstract: Abstract Decoding the causal architecture of Parkinson’s disease (PD) requires transitioning from correlation-driven biomarker profiling to directional multi-omic network discovery. Traditional methodologies are frequently limited by restrictive acyclic assumptions and numerical gradient instabilities under dense molecular dependencies. Here, we introduce a dependency-aware variational causal discovery framework powered by an Entropy-based Gini-Simpson (EGS) structural regularizer and adversarial confounder disentanglement. By integrating high-dimensional epigenomic, transcrip-tomic, metabolomic, and proteomic profiles from human post-mortem substantia nigra tissue (n ≈ 600), our approach resolves cyclic regulatory manifolds without rigid acyclic constraints. We uncover a cell-type-specific pathological feedback loop wherein mitochondrial complex I dysfunction directly drives target gene hyperexpression via localized chromatin remodeling in vulnerable dopaminergic neurons and microglia. Furthermore, in silico counterfactual perturbations demonstrate that disrupting this axis restores physiological expression, highlighting actionable therapeutic targets for neurodegeneration.

article.title: Effects of Cyclic High Ambient Temperature on Tricarboxylic Acid Cycle Intermediates and Orotate Levels in the Liver and Breast Muscle of Broiler Chickens.
article.authors: Katafuchi A, Shimamoto S, Tomonaga S, Kamimura M, Ishihara S, Ohtsuka A, Ijiri D.
article.abstract: Heat stress alters tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle metabolism in broiler chickens; however, quantitative changes in TCA cycle-related metabolites remain poorly understood. This study determined the effects of heat exposure on TCA cycle intermediate (citrate, isocitrate, α-ketoglutarate, succinate, fumarate, and malate) and orotate levels in the liver and breast muscle of broiler chickens. Twelve 14-day-old male broiler chickens were assigned to either a control group (25 ± 1 °C) or a cyclic high ambient temperature group (35 ± 1 °C for 8 h/day) and reared under these conditions for 4 days. Heat exposure increased liver levels of citrate, α-ketoglutarate, fumarate, and malate, while decreasing succinate and orotate. Heat exposure also decreased the mRNA expression of isocitrate dehydrogenase 3A (IDH3A) and oxoglutarate dehydrogenase, key TCA cycle regulatory enzymes, as well as dihydroorotate dehydrogenase and ubiquinol-cytochrome c reductase Rieske iron-sulfur protein 1 (UQCRFS1), which are involved in mitochondrial electron transport. Heat exposure increased breast muscle levels of succinate, fumarate, and malate, while reducing IDH3A and UQCRFS1 mRNA expression. These findings suggest that heat exposure impairs TCA cycle metabolism in broiler chickens, possibly by reducing the utilization of TCA cycle intermediates through impaired electron transfer in mitochondrial complex III.

article.title: Powerhouses of lethality: mitochondria in macrophage antimicrobial activity.
article.authors: McFadden MJ, O'Meara TR, O'Riordan MX.
article.abstract: Macrophages employ multiple strategies to dispatch phagocytosed microbes, including bombardment with toxic compounds and radicals, or the deprivation of key nutrients. The lethality of macrophages depends on their ability to regulate levels of microbicidal effectors and proper targeting of these effectors to the phagosome, where many intracellular pathogens are detained. Mitochondria play important roles in establishing an antimicrobial phagosomal environment in macrophages, playing roles in both the production and targeting of these effectors. In response to infection, the mitochondrial network undergoes dramatic structural and functional perturbations that modulate macrophage microbicidal potential. As central coordinators of cellular metabolism, mitochondria control the abundance of metabolites that can either be toxic to ingested microbes or necessary for their growth. Mitochondria are also prolific producers of reactive oxygen species (ROS), which play direct roles in killing microbes and serve as signaling molecules to coordinate antimicrobial responses. While mitochondria are also known to play extensive roles in regulating cytokine production and proinflammatory responses, this review will focus on highlighting mechanisms by which mitochondria manipulate the macrophage microbicidal milieu.

article.title: Metadherin Drives FOXO3a Lactylation and Mitochondrial Dysfunction to Promote Podocyte Injury in Diabetic Kidney Disease.
article.authors: Liang Y, Zhao L, Peng F, Li Q, Shen L, He S, He X, Wang H, Guo T, Yang J, Zheng X, Long Y, Lu D, Huang Q, Luo C, Long H, Chen X.
article.abstract: Article highlights This study investigated whether metadherin (MTDH) drives podocyte injury in diabetic kidney disease through metabolic reprogramming. We sought to define the molecular mechanisms linking altered glucose metabolism to podocyte mitochondrial dysfunction. We found that MTDH upregulates lactate dehydrogenase A, leading to lactate-driven FOXO3a lactylation that selectively activates proapoptotic genes and disrupts pyruvate kinase M2-mitofusin 2 interaction, impairing mitochondrial fusion. These findings identify MTDH as a central metabolic regulator and suggest that targeting MTDH-mediated pathways, including FOXO3a lactylation and pyruvate kinase M2-mitofusin 2 disruption, may represent a promising therapeutic strategy for diabetic kidney disease.

article.title: Long-term sildenafil attenuates age-associated functional and reproductive decline in male rats.
article.authors: Sokanovic S, Keselj I, Medar M, Baburski A, Andric SA, Kostic TS.
article.abstract: Aging in males is accompanied by a progressive decline in physical activity, androgen status, and reproductive function. We investigated whether long-term treatment with the phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitor sildenafil attenuates these changes and is accompanied by remodeling of mitochondrial homeostasis in the testis. Male rats were treated with low-dose sildenafil from 12 to 18 months of age, with age-matched untreated rats serving as controls and young adult rats providing a reference for the age-associated phenotype. Aging markedly reduced voluntary locomotor activity, circulating testosterone, and sperm production, while increasing circulating corticosterone. Long-term sildenafil treatment increased locomotor activity, testosterone, and sperm number, while corticosterone tended to decrease. Sildenafil-associated body weight changes were observed in animals with access to voluntary running. Treatment was also accompanied by pronounced changes in mitochondrial homeostasis-related gene expression in Leydig cells and spermatozoa. These transcriptional responses differed between cell types, particularly for genes regulating mitochondrial dynamics and quality control. Expression of mitochondrial homeostasis-related genes was more closely associated with circulating testosterone than with corticosterone and showed distinct testosterone-associated patterns in Leydig cells and spermatozoa. Recovery toward young levels differed among parameters, being more pronounced for reproductive and endocrine measures than for locomotor activity. These findings indicate that long-term low-dose sildenafil attenuates age-associated functional and reproductive decline and promotes a partial shift toward a younger male phenotype, accompanied by cell-specific mitochondrial transcriptional remodeling.

article.title: What are the potentials of the different sirtuin proteins as therapeutic targets?
article.authors: Fabbrizi E, Hailu GS, Mancini A, Fiorentino F, Rotili D, Mai A.
article.abstract: Introduction Sirtuins (SIRT1-7) are NAD + -dependent lysine deacylase and mono-ADP ribosyl transferase enzymes that integrate metabolic status with epigenetic regulation, genome maintenance, mitochondrial homeostasis, and adaptive stress responses. Their dysregulation is implicated in cancer, neurodegeneration, cardiometabolic disorders, inflammation, and aging-associated pathologies, positioning the sirtuin family among the most attractive yet mechanistically complex target classes in contemporary drug discovery. Areas covered This review critically examines the therapeutic potential of each mammalian sirtuin isoform through the combined perspectives of structural biology, disease validation, chemical tractability, and translational feasibility. Small-molecule activators and inhibitors, allosteric ligands, mechanism-based covalent modulators, and targeted protein degraders are systematically discussed, together with emerging patent activity and recent biological evidence. Literature published up to early 2026 was analyzed through comprehensive searches of PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, SciFinder, clinical trial registries, and patent databases, with particular emphasis on studies reporting isoform-selective modulation, cellular target engagement, in vivo efficacy, and translational biomarkers. Expert opinion Sirtuin pharmacology has evolved from proof-of-concept natural products to highly selective chemical probes and event-driven modalities. Among current targets, SIRT2 and SIRT6 show the most favorable balance between biological validation and chemical tractability, whereas mitochondrial sirtuins represent a promising but still underdeveloped frontier for precision therapeutic intervention.

article.title: O-GlcNAcylation of GSDMD promotes mitochondrial dysfunction and hepatocyte injury in MASLD.
article.authors: Wang X, Jiang M, Xie N, Chen X, Wang W, Yang S, Zhao T, Chen Q, Zhang F, Wang L, Liang J, Zhang Z, Zhuge Y, Xu B.
article.abstract: Background/aims Cell-membrane gasdermin D (GSDMD) plays a key role as a pyroptosis executor of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH). However, the mitochondrial translocation of GSDMD occurs even during the metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver (MASL) phase, which involves mainly hepatic steatosis without tremendous inflammatory responses or sustainable hepatic cell death; the underlying mechanism is unknown. We investigated the role of GSDMD in the pathogenesis of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD). Methods Liver tissues from patients with MASLD and control subjects were obtained to evaluate GSDMD expression and distribution. GSDMD△hep mice and their floxed littermate controls, GSDMDfl/fl mice, were fed a high-fat, high-cholesterol diet (HFHCD) for 4 and 12 weeks to develop MASL or MASH, respectively. Additionally, GSDMD△hep mice were administered an adeno-associated virus 8 (AAV8) vector expressing wild-type GSDMD (GSDMD-WT) or GSDMD O-GlcNAcylation site mutants (GSDMD-T174/S178A) and were provided with an HFHCD or a methionine-choline-deficient diet. Results GSDMD expression and mitochondrial translocation were increased in patients and experimental mice with MASLD. The translocation of GSDMD-NT to mitochondria impaired the mitochondrial membrane potential and promoted the leakage of cytochrome c and mitochondrial DNA, thus inducing early hepatocyte apoptosis, and was required for pyroptosis in MASLD. O-GlcNAcylation at T173/T175 (in humans) or T174/S178 (in mice) of GSDMD was responsible for GSDMD mitochondrial translocation and mitochondrial dysfunction. Targeting O-GlcNAcylation with Celecoxib suppressed GSDMD mitochondrial translocation and the development of MASLD. Conclusions Targeting mitochondrial GSDMD-mediated programed cell death (PCD) pathways may provide new insights into the potential theoretical basis for MASLD interventions.

article.title: Cinnamaldehyde-loaded gold nanobipyramids for dual-amplification of oxidative stress to enhance cancer catalytic therapy.
article.authors: Yin T, Wang Y, Li M, Liu Z, Hu J, Sun J, Guo K, Zhang D, Cui D.
article.abstract: Various inorganic nanozymes have been developed to generate highly reactive hydroxyl radicals (˙OH) through enzyme-mimetic catalytic activity for applications in catalytic therapy. However, the elevated levels of the antioxidant glutathione (GSH) in tumor cells can effectively neutralize ˙OH, thereby diminishing the therapeutic efficacy of these nanozymes, a prevalent issue in catalytic therapy. In this study, gold nanobipyramids (GNB) were integrated with cinnamaldehyde (CA) via electrostatic adsorption and hydrogen bonding to develop a nanozyme platform (GNB@CA) capable of tumor-specifically enhancing oxidative stress. GNB possess intrinsic peroxidase (POD)-like activity, enabling the conversion of endogenous hydrogen peroxide (H 2 O 2 ) into highly toxic ˙OH for catalytic therapy. Additionally, their photothermal conversion capability further boosts catalytic efficiency. CA exerts its effects through dual mechanisms: its α,β-unsaturated aldehyde group covalently binds to the thiol group of GSH via a Michael addition reaction, leading to a reduction in intracellular GSH and thereby weakening the antioxidant defense of tumor cells. Additionally, CA induces mitochondrial dysfunction by lowering the mitochondrial membrane potential, subsequently triggering tumor cell apoptosis. In vivo studies demonstrate that GNB@CA can effectively eradicate triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) in mice through synergistic induction of robust oxidative stress. This research offers valuable insights for the design of nanozymes in catalytic cancer therapy.

article.title: Integrated transcriptome and mitochondrial respiratory activity analysis reveals oxidative stress adaptation in azole-resistant Aspergillus fumigatus .
article.authors: Feilan Z, Yuhan Z, Tianqi W, Pianpian H, Xiaofang L, Xiaodong S, Nan Z, Weida L, Musang L.
article.abstract: Azole resistance in Aspergillus fumigatus is a major challenge in the treatment of invasive aspergillosis. Although cyp51A mutations are well characterized, the global transcriptional responses and physiological adaptations associated with resistance remain incompletely understood. RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) was performed to compare the transcriptomes of the azole-susceptible strain AF293 and four azole-resistant clinical isolates with distinct resistance mechanisms. Voriconazole was used for all antifungal exposure experiments. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were analyzed by GO and KEGG enrichment analyses. Mitochondrial respiratory chain Complex I and Complex III activities were further evaluated in SHJT42B, a representative cyp51A-mediated resistant isolate. Azole-resistant isolates exhibited extensive transcriptional reprogramming following voriconazole exposure, with enrichment of oxidative stress-related pathways. Oxidative stress-associated genes showed differential regulation in both cyp51A -dependent and cyp51A -independent resistant isolates, suggesting a conserved stress-response adaptation during azole resistance. Functional analyses revealed that SHJT42B exhibited altered mitochondrial respiratory activity, characterized by reduced Complex I and Complex III activities and increased intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels compared with AF293. These findings suggest that mitochondrial respiratory alterations may be associated with oxidative stress adaptation in azole-resistant A. fumigatus . Our study integrates transcriptomic and functional analyses to identify oxidative stress adaptation as an important physiological response associated with azole resistance in A. fumigatus . The findings further suggest that mitochondrial homeostasis may represent a potential vulnerability for future combination antifungal strategies, although additional studies across diverse resistant isolates are required.IMPORTANCEAzole-resistant Aspergillus fumigatus is an increasing threat to patients with weakened immune systems, as it limits the effectiveness of first-line antifungal treatments and leads to high mortality. Most previous studies have focused on single resistance genes, leaving the broader biological changes in resistant fungi poorly understood. In this study, we show that azole-resistant strains undergo extensive transcriptional changes involving cellular stress responses and energy metabolism. By integrating transcriptomic analysis with functional validation, we reveal oxidative stress-associated adaptations across resistant isolates and identify altered mitochondrial respiratory activity in the representative resistant isolate SHJT42B. These findings suggest that antifungal resistance involves not only genetic determinants but also broader cellular adaptations that promote survival under drug pressure. Targeting mitochondrial homeostasis or oxidative stress response pathways may provide potential strategies for enhancing antifungal efficacy and warrants further investigation.

article.title: The physiological roles and pathological implications of metabolic communication via tunneling nanotubes in immune cells.
