article.authors: Chen B, Wang D, Hu R, Zhou X, Zhang H.
article.abstract: The traditional paradigm of intercellular communication is rapidly evolving. Tunneling nanotubes (TNTs) represent a distinct mode of intercellular communication, enabling the transfer of organelles, signaling molecules, and metabolic resources between spatially separated cells. Unlike soluble factor-mediated communication, TNTs establish direct physical connections that can support rapid and directional cargo transport, including mitochondrial transfer, with consequences for recipient-cell metabolism and function. In the immune system, TNT-mediated mitochondrial and other cargo transfer has been implicated in macrophage functional polarization, T-cell metabolic fitness, and natural killer (NK) cell-mediated immunity. In this review, we summarize the molecular characteristics of TNTs in immune cells, the regulation of their formation under inflammatory and metabolic stress, and the mechanisms and consequences of cargo transfer. We further examine the context-dependent nature of TNT-mediated communication, including its potential roles in host defense, tissue repair, tumor immune evasion, and pathogen dissemination. Finally, we critically evaluate transfer kinetics, quantitative scale, prevalence, in vivo evidence, and the technical limitations that currently constrain causal attribution and therapeutic translation.

article.title: The AMPK signaling pathway in cell metabolism and human diseases.
article.authors: Zhang Z, Gu Y, He H, Qiao S, Shao Y, Long X, Huang J, Zhang L, Zhou F.
article.abstract: Adenosine 5'-monophosphate-activated protein kinase (AMPK), a highly conserved energy-sensing kinase, plays a central role in maintaining cellular metabolic homeostasis, such as glucose/lipid metabolism, mitochondrial biogenesis, and autophagy, to counteract energetic stress. Beyond the canonical adenylate-dependent activation of AMPK by sensing the ATP:AMP/ADP ratio, emerging evidence reveals noncanonical activation mechanisms. Proper AMPK signaling is essential for physiological functions, whereas its dysregulation underlies various pathologies, including metabolic diseases, immune disorders, and cancer. This review systematically recapitulates the historical background and landmark discoveries of the AMPK field, including the discovery of AMPK, the structure of AMPK complex, upstream regulators and downstream substrates, and the transcriptional/posttranscriptional and posttranslational regulatory mechanisms. Furthermore, we delineate its roles in maintaining metabolic equilibrium, mitochondrial integrity, and immune competence across organ systems and highlight how dysregulated AMPK activity contributes to pathological diseases, encompassing alterations in its expression levels, intrinsic kinase activity, subcellular localization or upstream regulatory signaling cascades. Specifically, we focus on knock-in or knockout mouse models utilized to study AMPK-associated human diseases and the translational potential of AMPK-targeting agonists or antagonists across diverse pathological conditions. A deep understanding of the multidimensional regulatory network of AMPK and mechanistic insights with therapeutic innovations that we provide with this review will help address the challenges of complex metabolic diseases.

article.title: Complete mitochondrial genome sequence of the green alga Mychonastes koreanus MKSC25 (Chlorophyta).
article.authors: Kang NS, Jo CR, Kim SY, Tran BT, Lee T, Heo JS, Back J, Kim K-Y, An SM.
article.abstract: The complete mitochondrial genome of the green alga Mychonastes koreanus MKSC25 is 23,905 bp long, with a GC content of 44.88%. It contains 13 protein-coding genes, 22 tRNA genes, 2 rRNA genes fragmented into 7 segments, 1 putative open reading frame ( orf158 ), and a 299-bp group I intron interrupting rrnL4 .

article.title: Identification and experimental validation of phospholipase D family member 6 (PLD6) as a mitochondria-related candidate gene in knee osteoarthritis.
article.authors: Zhang J, Wang Q, Zhou J, Wei J, Zhang X, Li B, Liu L.
article.abstract: Mitochondrial dysfunction contributes to cartilage degeneration in knee osteoarthritis (KOA), but the role of phospholipase D family member 6 (PLD6), a mitochondrial outer membrane phospholipase, remains unclear. This study combined transcriptomic analyses and functional experiments to investigate PLD6 in KOA. Integrated analysis of three human cartilage transcriptomic datasets identified eight mitochondria-related candidate genes through differential expression and weighted gene co-expression network analyses. Machine learning, external human validation, and cross-species evaluation prioritized PLD6 for further investigation. PLD6 expression was reduced in damaged cartilage compared with paired macroscopically intact cartilage from patients with KOA, in cartilage from mice subjected to destabilization of the medial meniscus, and in interleukin-1β (IL-1β)-treated primary murine chondrocytes. In primary murine chondrocytes, PLD6 knockdown reduced type II collagen expression, mitochondrial membrane potential, and mitochondrial respiration, while increasing matrix metalloproteinase 13 (MMP13) expression, the Bax/Bcl-2 ratio, and reactive oxygen species levels. PLD6 overexpression under IL-1β stimulation reduced MMP13 expression and the Bax/Bcl-2 ratio and partially restored mitochondrial respiration. These findings suggest that PLD6 downregulation may contribute to chondrocyte mitochondrial dysfunction and cartilage degeneration, supporting PLD6 as a candidate target for further investigation in KOA.

article.title: Role of Leu and Val synthesis in sensing mitochondrial nutrient and energy availability.
article.authors: Phan J, Gay L, Dokládal L, De Virgilio C, Salcedo L, Tha S, Wandvik C, Babst M.
article.abstract: How cells integrate nutrient availability to coordinate metabolism and growth remains poorly understood. Here, we identify branched-chain amino acid (BCAA) synthesis as a metabolic sensing system linking mitochondrial activity to translational and transcriptional control. Yeast limits Leu and Val import and instead relies on their synthesis, allowing BCAA production to reflect mitochondrial anabolic capacity. Reduced Val synthesis activates Gcn2, whereas reduced Leu synthesis inhibits TORC1, together decreasing translation efficiency and restricting growth. This response lowers levels of the transcriptional repressor Mig1, suppressing the Warburg/Crabtree effect and promoting alternative carbon source utilization. Remarkably, pharmacological inhibition of Leu/Val synthesis induces this metabolic reprogramming even in nutrient-rich medium, indicating that mitochondrial BCAA synthesis can partially override other nutrient-sensing pathways. Thus, BCAA synthesis couples mitochondrial anabolic capacity to Gcn2 and TORC1 activity and, through translational control of transcription factor abundance, shapes cellular metabolism.

article.title: SLC25A39: A key regulator of mitochondrial metabolism and a promising therapeutic target in cancer.
article.authors: Tian T, Jin Y, Cui P, Lan S.
article.abstract: The mitochondrial solute carrier (SLC25) family regulates solute transport across the mitochondrial inner membrane. Among them, SLC25A39 has emerged as a critical player in tumor biology, primarily through its dual role in mediating mitochondrial glutathione (mGSH) transport and maintaining iron-sulfur cluster homeostasis. Recent evidence implies that SLC25A39 dysfunction disrupts mGSH metabolism, thereby influencing iron-sulfur cluster synthesis and driving metabolic reprogramming in tumors. Notably, SLC25A39 is governed by a GSH-Fe-S-AFG3L2 feedback circuit, a feature not shared by its closest homolog SLC25A40. Additionally, upregulation of SLC25A39 is frequently observed in multiple malignancies, including colorectal, pancreatic, and liver cancers, where it correlates with enhanced proliferation, metastasis, and poor prognosis. Furthermore, SLC25A39 expression is intricately associated with remodeling of the tumor immune microenvironment and the development of therapeutic resistance, although these associations are primarily based on correlative evidence and require functional validation before causal conclusions can be drawn. This review synthesizes current knowledge on the molecular mechanisms by which SLC25A39 integrates mGSH transport with iron metabolism, and critically evaluates its emerging roles across different cancer types. We propose that beyond serving as a candidate prognostic biomarker, SLC25A39 represents a potential therapeutic target whose clinical utility remains to be established, and we discuss key unanswered questions regarding its tissue-specific functions and the translational challenges that lie ahead.

article.title: Telmisartan attenuates gentamicin-induced ototoxicity and modulates oxidative stress and RhoA/ROCK-associated signaling in mice.
article.authors: Vishwakarma KK, Payasi A, Lather V, Sharma B.
article.abstract: Gentamicin-induced ototoxicity involves oxidative stress, inflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and cochlear hair-cell injury. This study evaluated the protective effects of telmisartan and their association with RhoA/ROCK signaling in mice. Male C57BL/6J mice were assigned to normal control, gentamicin control, gentamicin plus fasudil (2 mg/kg), or gentamicin plus telmisartan (5, 10, or 20 mg/kg) groups (n = 10). Auditory function was assessed by auditory brainstem response, while locomotor and gait performance were evaluated using open-field and gait tests. Cochlear oxidative stress, inflammatory biomarkers, RhoA activation, ROCK1/2 mRNA expression, and ROCK-associated protein phosphorylation were assessed using colorimetric assays, ELISA, fluorescence imaging, qRT-PCR, and Western blotting. Hair-cell integrity was evaluated by MYO7A immunofluorescence, quantitative counting, and histopathology. Gentamicin elevated auditory thresholds, prolonged shock-avoidance response latencies, impaired locomotor and gait performance, increased intracellular and mitochondrial reactive oxygen species, and reduced antioxidant defenses. It also increased iNOS, NF-κB, active RhoA, ROCK1/2 expression, and phosphorylation of ROCK-associated proteins while reducing MYO7A-positive hair-cell density. Fasudil and telmisartan attenuated these alterations, with higher telmisartan doses generally providing greater protection, although responses were not uniformly dose-dependent. Telmisartan also preserved sensory epithelial organization and cochlear hair-cell density. Telmisartan attenuated gentamicin-associated auditory and cochlear injury, with effects associated with reduced oxidative and inflammatory stress and modulation of RhoA/ROCK-related signaling. Further pathway-specific and clinically relevant studies are required.

article.title: AMPK-dependent mechanisms mediate the protective effects of grape pomace extract in obesity-associated chronic renal disease in mice.
article.authors: Figueras TS, Cacciamani VE, Gil Lorenzo AF, Suhaiman L, Antoniolli AN, Perdicaro DJ, Vazquez Prieto MA, Costantino VV.
article.abstract: Obesity-associated kidney disease involves metabolic dysfunction accompanied by lipotoxicity, inflammation, and fibrosis. We previously showed that grape pomace extract (GPE), a polyphenol-rich byproduct of winemaking, exerts renoprotective effects in obese mice; however, the underlying mechanisms remain incompletely understood. This study aims to investigate whether adenosine monophosphate-activated protein kinase (AMPK) mediates the protective effects of dietary GPE supplementation in high-fat diet (HF)-induced obese mice. Male C57BL/6J mice were fed a standard diet (16% calories from fat) or a HF (60% calories from fat) with or without GPE (300 mg per kg body weight per day) for 16 weeks. A subset of animals was treated with compound C (CC), a widely used AMPK inhibitor, during the last 4 weeks. GPE attenuated HF-induced body weight gain, visceral adiposity, dyslipidemia, glucose intolerance, and renal dysfunction, while improving histopathological alterations. Mechanistically, GPE restored renal AMPK phosphorylation, increased autophagy markers (increased LC3-II/LC3-I ratio and Beclin-1 levels) and reduced renal lipid accumulation. In addition, GPE enhanced levels of the mitochondrial biogenesis regulator PGC-1α, while attenuating oxidative stress (Nox4, 4-HNE, and oxidant species production), inflammatory signaling (NF-κB-NLRP3 pathway), and renal fibrosis. Notably, pharmacological AMPK inhibition reversed the GPE effect, leading to worsening of renal injury, autophagy impairment, increased lipid deposition, and exacerbation of fibrotic and inflammatory markers. These findings demonstrate that AMPK activation is a mediator of the metabolic and renoprotective effects of GPE, positioning GPE as a promising functional food ingredient for attenuation of obesity-associated kidney disease.

article.title: Melatonin attenuates diquat-induced acute liver injury by modulating Nrf2-Associated antioxidant signaling and ferroptosis-related processes.
article.authors: Xia L, Liu G, Duan Y, Dong Y, Chen F, Li Z, Liu Y, Shou S.
article.abstract: ObjectiveDiquat (DQ) poisoning can cause severe acute liver injury associated with oxidative stress. This experimental animal study investigated the involvement of ferroptosis-related processes and Nrf2-associated antioxidant signaling in the protective effects of melatonin against DQ-induced liver injury.MethodsMale C57BL/6J mice were used in an experimental DQ-induced acute liver injury model. DQ was administered intraperitoneally, with an LD 50 of 42.70 mg/kg and 24 h selected as the peak-injury time point. Liver injury, inflammation, oxidative stress, iron homeostasis, mitochondrial damage, ferroptosis-related markers, and Nrf2 signaling were assessed. RSL3 and ML385 were used to challenge ferroptosis-related protection and inhibit Nrf2 signaling, respectively. Nrf2 nuclear accumulation, HO-1, NQO1, SLC7A11, and FSP1 were additionally evaluated. A post-exposure experiment tested melatonin administered 2 h after DQ.ResultsDQ increased serum ALT and AST, inflammatory cytokines, ROS, lipid peroxidation, and hepatic Fe 2+ accumulation, while decreasing GSH and impairing mitochondrial function and morphology (all P 2+ accumulation, MDA, GSH, and GPX4. ML385 similarly attenuated Nrf2 nuclear accumulation, HO-1/NQO1 expression, restoration of SLC7A11 and FSP1, and protection against liver injury and ferroptosis-related alterations (P < 0.05 vs. FMDQ). Post-exposure melatonin also reduced ALT, AST, and histological liver injury.ConclusionsMelatonin attenuates DQ-induced acute liver injury. Pharmacological findings support contributions of Nrf2-associated antioxidant signaling and suppression of oxidative stress and ferroptosis-related processes, although they do not establish an exclusive causal pathway. Post-exposure efficacy further supports the potential translational relevance of melatonin.

article.title: A well-resolved phylogeny of Cuscuta subgenus Monogynella based on data drawn from all three plant genomes.
article.authors: Albal A, Stefanović S.
article.abstract: Premise Cuscuta (dodders) consists of ~200 species circumscribed into four subgenera (Monogynella, Cuscuta, Pachystigma, and Grammica) and is the only parasitic genus in Convolvulaceae (the morning-glory family). This group shows a significant diversity in plastid functionality and represents a rare mixotrophic system among parasitic plants. Apart from a few placeholders in broadscale phylogenies, subg. Monogynella had not been extensively examined until a recent molecular systematics study. Despite this effort, a few lineages still remained poorly resolved and some backbone relationships lacked support. Methods To obtain greater resolution and support for the phylogeny alongside studying the effect of hemiparasitism on different organellar genomes, we selected 31 samples, chosen to represent the phylogenetic diversity of each clade, and sequenced them using high-throughput sequencing. We assembled plastid genomes and retrieved mitochondrial genes and nuclear ribosomal arrays (NRAs) for phylogenomic analyses. Results Plastomes in this subgenus show similar lengths and gene composition and retain the bulk of photosynthesis genes. About 33 mitochondrial genes were recovered from assemblies and are more conserved in comparison to plastid genes. In addition, complete NRAs were also found to be well maintained. The members of subg. Monogynella show no evidence of hybridization. Trees obtained from all three matrices corroborate previously published molecular phylogenies with increased resolution and backbone support across the board. Conclusions These results characterize the state of the organellar genomes and particularly plastomes in subg. Monogynella, bridging the gap in this field of study of Cuscuta and allowing us to compare these patterns across other heterotrophic lineages.

article.title: Antifungal terpenoids from Neopallasia pectinata and in vivo activity of 4-terpineol against rice sheath blight.
article.authors: Lan Z, Bao Z, Yi S, Zhu L, Zhang Y, Qin J, Cui X.
article.abstract: Background Oryza sativa L. (rice) sheath blight, caused by Rhizoctonia solani Kühn, is a major disease threatening rice production. This study identifies antifungal constituents from Neopallasia pectinata (Pall.) Poljakov and characterizes 4-terpineol against R. solani using in vitro, in vivo, and mechanistic approaches. Results Five compounds were isolated from N. pectinata. 4-Terpineol (3) inhibited R. solani with an EC 50 of 220.7 μg mL -1 and a minimum inhibitory concentration of 500 μg mL -1 . At 500 μg mL -1 , 4-terpineol achieved protective and curative efficacies of 42.29% and 55.43%, respectively, in rice plants. Transcriptomic and physiological analyses showed impaired membrane integrity and extensive remodeling of sterol and fatty-acid metabolism, accompanied by strong Pleiotropic Drug Resistance (PDR)-associated responses. 4-Terpineol also perturbed mitochondrial membrane-potential homeostasis and induced glutathione- and glutathione S-transferase-associated responses without detectable reactive oxygen species accumulation under the tested conditions. Conclusion 4-Terpineol induces membrane-associated disturbance and extensive adaptive responses in R. solani. Its in planta activity, practical availability from alternative sources, and chemically modifiable structure support its potential as a natural-product-derived lead scaffold for further optimization against rice sheath blight. © 2026 Society of Chemical Industry.

article.title: Exercise alleviates skeletal muscle dysfunction in COPD by regulating mitochondrial function via apelin/AMPK signaling.
article.authors: Chen S, Chen X, Weng K, Lin R, Lai X, Wan Z.
article.abstract: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a common respiratory disorder characterized by persistent airflow limitation, with skeletal muscle dysfunction (SMD) representing a major extrapulmonary manifestation. Exercise training has positive effects on skeletal muscle strength, mass, and physical activity in patients with COPD, although the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we investigated whether apelin mediates the protective effects of exercise on COPD-related SMD. Mouse models of COPD with SMD and cigarette smoke extract (CSE)-treated C2C12 cells were established. Mice underwent exercise or adeno-associated virus (AAV)-shApln intervention, while CSE-treated C2C12 cells were subjected to apelin overexpression and/or AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) knockdown. Muscle function, skeletal muscle mass, histopathology, apelin expression, cell viability, ATP production, mitochondrial function, and related protein expression were evaluated. Apelin expression was significantly downregulated in mice with COPD complicated by SMD and in CSE-treated cells. Apelin overexpression rescued the CSE-induced decrease in cell viability, ATP levels, mitochondrial content, and citrate synthase activity and the downregulation of PGC-1α and Tom20 expression via AMPK activation. Exercise increased apelin expression, improved muscle function and mitochondrial activity, and reduced Atrogin-1/MuRF1 expression; these effects were abolished by apelin knockdown. Collectively, these findings suggest that exercise alleviates COPD-related SMD by enhancing mitochondrial function through the apelin/AMPK pathway, highlighting this pathway as a potential therapeutic target for COPD-associated SMD.

article.title: Phenylacetylglutamine restrains epithelial ferroptosis in intestinal ischemia-reperfusion by coupling lipid droplet-mitochondria remodeling to metabolic execution.
article.authors: Weng X, Yin Y, Xia Z, Zheng M, Wang S, Chen D, Li X, Liu H, Chen R, Meng Q.
article.abstract: Background Intestinal ischemia-reperfusion injury (IIR) involves epithelial barrier failure, oxidative stress, and ferroptosis-associated lipid damage, yet how lipid droplet-mitochondria coupling influences ferroptotic susceptibility remains incompletely understood. Methods Untargeted plasma metabolomics was combined with murine IIR and Caco-2 oxygen-glucose deprivation/reoxygenation models. Epithelial injury, lipid peroxidation, mitochondrial function, lipid droplet-mitochondria association, and fluorescent fatty-acid analogue localization were assessed. Ferrostatin-1 (Fer-1), etomoxir, PLIN5 silencing, and the ADRB2 antagonist ICI-118551 were used for mechanistic interrogation, together with molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulations, and cellular thermal shift assays. Results Untargeted plasma metabolomics identified phenylacetylglutamine (PAGln) as an IIR-responsive circulating metabolite. Exogenous PAGln pretreatment attenuated epithelial injury, lipid peroxidation, and ferroptosis-associated alterations. PAGln restored perilipin 5 (PLIN5)-associated lipid droplet-mitochondria remodeling, increased the relative colocalization of a fluorescent fatty-acid analogue with mitochondria, and improved mitochondrial metabolic activity. Etomoxir markedly attenuated mitochondrial metabolic recovery, lipid peroxide control, and epithelial protection while largely preserving PAGln-induced organelle remodeling, whereas PLIN5 silencing disrupted both spatial remodeling and its downstream metabolic consequences. Upstream, PAGln engaged β2-adrenergic receptor (ADRB2)-dependent cyclic adenosine monophosphate/protein kinase A signaling. ADRB2 blockade attenuated PLIN5 restoration and organelle remodeling in vitro and weakened mitochondrial metabolic recovery and epithelial protection in both cell and animal models. Computational analyses and cellular thermal shift assays further supported a functional PAGln-ADRB2 relationship. Conclusion PAGln restrains ferroptosis-associated epithelial injury through an ADRB2-PLIN5-regulated organelle program in which lipid droplet-mitochondria spatial remodeling must be coupled to downstream mitochondrial fatty-acid utilization. These findings functionally distinguish spatial remodeling from metabolic execution and identify organelle-level fatty-acid handling as a regulatory layer of ferroptotic susceptibility in IIR.

article.title: A multi-responsive fluorescent probe for simultaneous detection of mitochondrial esterase and viscosity.
article.authors: Yue J, Chen H, Xu X, Wu Y, Zhang W, Yang Y, Qian J.
article.venue: Analytical methods : advancing methods and applications
article.abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is one of the most lethal malignancies worldwide, with early detection severely hampered by its asymptomatic progression. Carboxylesterases (CEs) are significantly upregulated in HCC cells, making them promising biomarkers for cancer diagnosis. Herein, we report a tri-lock fluorescent probe, CMA, capable of simultaneous detection of mitochondrial CE - an enzyme closely linked to metabolism and drug resistance - and viscosity for early cancer diagnosis. The probe incorporates a CE-cleavable benzoate ester and a molecular rotor formed by an indolium-coumarin conjugated system. Upon hydrolysis of the benzoate ester, the released product displays enhanced fluorescence with red-shifted absorption through strengthened ICT. High viscosity restricts intramolecular rotation and suppresses the TICT pathway, whereas the alkaline mitochondrial pH further modulates the emission via deprotonation of the phenolic hydroxyl group. These three orthogonal stimuli converge to produce a 654-fold fluorescence enhancement under coexistent conditions. Cell imaging confirms that CMA effectively differentiates HCC cells from normal cells and detects drug-induced viscosity changes, suggesting its potential for early-stage liver cancer diagnosis.

article.title: Beyond Acid Suppression: Vonoprazan as a Multi-Target Modulator in Experimental Colitis from Oxidative Stress to Mitochondrial Rescue.
article.authors: El-Waseif EG, Nader MA, El-Waseif AG, Abdelmageed ME.
article.abstract: Ulcerative colitis (UC); as one of the inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD), arises from chronic inflammation of the intestinal tract. In this study, we addressed the possible protective mechanisms of vonoprazan, as a potassium-competitive acid blocker, on dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-mediated UC. Therefore, male BALB-c mice administered oral vonoprazan (10 or 20 mg/kg/day) for 10 days and received drinking water containing 3% w/v DSS for 7 days from day 4. Vonoprazan exhibited a promising effect against UC by increasing mice body weight, colon length, and spleen weight, decreasing serum C-reactive protein (CRP) concentration and the disease activity index (DAI), and alleviating colonic histopathological changes. Colonic tissue antioxidants increased significantly in vonoprazan-treated groups. Additionally, colonic tissue oxidative stress was significantly ameliorated in vonoprazan-treated mice. Furthermore, vonoprazan preserved the integrity of intestinal mucosal barrier function and attenuated UC by decreasing the levels of immuno-inflammatory cells, inflammation-related proteins, and pro-inflammatory cytokines, elevating the tight junction proteins levels, and ameliorating mitochondrial energy metabolism. Taken together, vonoprazan protected against DSS-mediated UC in mice via antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activities that maintained tight junction architecture.

article.title: A Rare Sugar, D-Allulose, Attenuates Cognitive Impairment and Brain Pathologies in D-Galactose-Accelerated Aging Rats.
article.authors: Huang Y, Thonusin C, Lu D, Arunsak B, Maneechote C, Pintana H, Chunchai T, Tokuda M, Chattipakorn N, Chattipakorn SC.
article.abstract: Background Aging is the major risk factor for cognitive impairment via aging-induced neuronal dysfunction. D-allulose, a low-calorie rare sugar, has been shown to provide beneficial effects in the obese-insulin-resistant brain. However, its beneficial effects on the aging brain have never been investigated. Objective This study investigated whether D-allulose could attenuate cognitive impairment and brain pathological alterations in a D-galactose-accelerated aging model. Methods Thirty-two 5-month-old male Wistar rats were randomly allocated by cage drawing lots into four groups (n = 8 rats/group): control (Con), D-galactose (D-gal), D-galactose + inulin (D-gal + Inu), and D-galactose + D-allulose (D-gal + Allu). The control group received normal saline solution (NSS; 1 mL/kg/day, s.c.), whereas the other three groups received D-galactose (150 mg/kg/day, s.c.) for 20 weeks. Beginning at week 9, the D-gal-treated groups additionally received NSS, inulin (2.0 g/kg/day), or D-allulose (1.9 g/kg/day), respectively, by oral gavage for 12 weeks. Following the treatment, spatial learning and memory were assessed using the Morris water maze. Brain pathological alterations were evaluated using Western blot, RT-qPCR, immunofluorescence staining, mitochondrial functional assessments, and electrophysiological recordings. Results D-galactose exposure reduced target quadrant entries in the Morris Water Maze (5.6 ± 0.89 vs 7.6 ± 0.42, P = 0.021) and lowered the mean normalized hippocampal fEPSP slope (99.0% ± 1.86% vs 162.0% ± 21.79%, P = 0.009) compared with controls. D-allulose increased target quadrant entries (7.4 ± 0.50 vs 5.6 ± 0.89, P = 0.042) and the mean normalized hippocampal fEPSP slope (155.5% ± 8.95% vs 99.0% ± 1.86%, P = 0.018) compared with the D-gal group. However, inulin did not significantly alter these outcomes. Mitochondrial ROS production and brain MDA levels were also lower in D-gal + Allu group than in D-gal group (P = 0.023 and P = 0.013, respectively). Conclusion D-allulose mitigates aging-associated brain dysfunction and pathological alterations in D-galactose-accelerated aging model.

article.title: The mitochondrial genomes of the endemic and endangered South Philippine Hawk-eagle Nisaetus pinskeri and other Nisaetus Hawk-eagles (Aves, Accipitriformes).
article.authors: Perdon DM, Egana JM, Tablizo F, Mantaring RJ, Punayan K, Araiza SM, Llames JH, Abad MC, Ibañez J, Saloma CP.
article.abstract: Southeast Asia is home to 22 endemic raptors, and almost all are classified as "Endangered" or higher by the International Union for Conservation of Nature and Natural Resources (IUCN). The limited range and fragmented distribution of some Southeast Asian raptors from the genus Nisaetus hinder the characterization of these endangered birds. This study presents the mitochondrial sequences of the Pinsker's Hawk-eagle (Nisaetus pinskeri) and Changeable Hawk-eagle (Nisaetus cirrhatus) and conducts a comparative mitogenome analysis across Accipitriformes. The partial mitogenome lengths of N. pinskeri and N. cirrhatus are 18,654 bp and 17,874 bp, with a GC content of 46.4% and 47.4%, respectively. An extra cytosine at position 174 of the nad3 gene was present in both mitogenomes, which was not previously observed in other Nisaetus species. Phylogenetic analysis recapitulated the topology of the order Accipitriformes. It showed that N. pinskeri and N. cirrhatus are closely related to each other and sister to the rest of the Nisaetus representatives. Moreover, the trees based on concatenated mitochondrial protein-coding genes were closer to the latest reported phylogenies than single-gene trees using conventional mitochondrial markers. The selection pressure analysis showed that all protein-coding genes experienced purifying selection, with the highest in atp8 and the lowest in cox1. As the first report of the near-complete mitogenomes of these raptors, this study expands the available genomic resources for these understudied raptors and provides a foundation for future population genetic research.

article.title: Distinct mitochondrial states modulate α-synuclein toxicity.
article.authors: Haider I, Almazan AVP, Gillespie B, Yadav S, Santhanakrishnan R, Almazan RBP, Biswas K, Minassian C, Ju S, Zhong Q.
article.abstract: Abnormal α-synuclein (α-syn) accumulation and mitochondrial dysfunction are central features of Parkinson's disease (PD), and increasing evidence suggests that these processes are closely connected. Using yeast models to manipulate mitochondrial metabolic states, we investigated how mitochondrial activity may affect α-syn accumulation and toxicity. Under the fermentative growth condition, we found that α-syn localized predominantly to the plasma membrane and was non-toxic. Respiratory growth induced cytoplasmic α-syn accumulation, mitochondrial abnormalities, and marked toxicity dependent on α-syn expression and membrane binding. Surprisingly, genetic disruption of mitochondrial respiration also enhanced α-syn toxicity despite causing little α-syn accumulation, indicating that both increased demand of mitochondrial respiratory function and compromised respiratory capacity can sensitize cells to α-syn toxicity. Overexpression of HAP4 , a master regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis and respiratory gene expression, suppressed α-syn toxicity, but this protection required functional mitochondria. Together, these findings demonstrate that distinct mitochondrial functional states exert markedly different effects on α-syn toxicity and reveal a complex relationship between mitochondrial function and cellular response to α-syn expression. These models provide a new system for investigating how changes in mitochondrial function contribute to α-syn-induced cellular stress.

article.title: HOG pathway-dependent protection against impaired complex sphingolipid biosynthesis involves Fmp48-mediated suppression of mitochondria-dependent ROS accumulation.
article.authors: Sudo T, Sakamoto R, Yamanaka K, Sugihara S, Tani M.
article.abstract: Complex sphingolipids are required for normal growth of the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae . Repression of AUR1 , which encodes inositol phosphorylceramide synthase, disrupts sphingolipid homeostasis by reducing complex sphingolipid levels and promoting ceramide accumulation, ultimately causing growth inhibition and cell death. We previously showed that the high-osmolarity glycerol (HOG) pathway is activated under AUR1 -repressive conditions and alleviates the resulting growth defect. In this study, among genes induced in a HOG pathway-dependent manner, we identified FMP48, UIP4 , and MGA1 , whose overexpression suppressed cell death caused by AUR1 repression. Simultaneous deletion of these genes had modest effects under AUR1 repression alone but more clearly impaired cytoprotection when HOG pathway signaling was enhanced. Neither deletion nor overexpression of these genes restored complex sphingolipid levels or prevented ceramide accumulation. AUR1 repression promoted mitochondria-dependent ROS accumulation, and the associated cell death was markedly reduced when mitochondrial electron transport was impaired. Loss of HOG1 further enhanced ROS accumulation. FMP48 overexpression suppressed ROS accumulation and cell death under AUR1 -repressive conditions but did not further reduce cell death when mitochondrial electron transport was impaired. Together, these findings identify FMP48 , UIP4 , and MGA1 as contributors to HOG-dependent cytoprotection.

article.title: Integrated Multi-Omic Characterization of Hexokinase-1 Deficiency in Red Blood Cells Reveals Altered Redox Homeostasis, Membrane Remodeling, and Features of Incomplete Erythroid Maturation.
article.authors: Haiman ZB, Anastasiadi AT, Delaporta P, Stephenson D, Dzieciatkowska M, Nemkov T, Page GP, Chouliara V, Glentis S, Adam AS, Keele GR, Deng X, Busch MP, Norris PJ, Kattamis A, Tzounakas VL, D'Alessandro A.
article.abstract: Hexokinase 1 (HK1) deficiency is a rare cause of hereditary nonspherocytic hemolytic anemia characterized by impaired erythrocyte glycolysis, but its broader molecular consequences of HK1 dysfunction remain poorly understood. We integrated population-scale genetics, hemolytic testing, and multi-omic data from the REDS RBC-Omics cohorts with comprehensive clinical, metabolomic, lipidomic, oxylipin, and proteomic profiling of erythrocytes and plasma from an individual carrying the HK1 p.Arg12Ter variant, predicted to cause complete loss-of-function of the erythroid-specific HK1-R isoform. Population-scale analyses identified multiple HK1 variants associated with erythrocyte metabolism and susceptibility to osmotic hemolysis. In the affected individual, multi-omic characterization of HK1 deficiency revealed disruption of glycolysis, the pentose phosphate pathway, and glutathione metabolism, accompanied by ATP depletion, impaired antioxidant defenses, susceptibility to oxidative challenge, and ongoing hemolysis. Lipidomic analyses revealed extensive membrane remodeling with increased oxidized phospholipids, lysophospholipids, oxylipins, and triglycerides, and altered phospholipid remodeling pathways. Proteomics identified signatures of redox imbalance, altered proteostasis, and enrichment of mitochondrial proteins. Reticulocytosis, increased CD235a + CD71 - mitochondria-positive erythrocytes, elevated acylcarnitines, tricarboxylic acid cycle intermediates, and polyamines suggested severe erythropoietic stress and incomplete reticulocyte maturation. Thus, HK1 deficiency extends beyond impaired glycolysis and ATP depletion to encompass altered redox homeostasis, widespread metabolic and membrane remodeling, disrupted proteostasis, and persistence of immature erythroid characteristics. Together, these findings provide the first integrated multi-omic characterization of HK1 deficiency, define a phenotype of HK1 dysfunction, chronic hemolysis, and compensatory erythropoiesis, and establish a framework linking common and rare HK1 variation to molecular phenotypes in human erythrocytes.

article.title: Circadian aging and neurodegeneration: the emerging role of the melatonin-cortisol axis in brain homeostasis, disease progression, and precision chronomedicine.
article.authors: Chakraborty W, Anand A, Kumar S, Roy KK.
article.abstract: Circadian aging may promote neurodegenerative illnesses by dysregulating the melatonin-cortisol axis. Low nighttime melatonin synthesis, blunted cortisol circadian cycles, abnormal clock-gene oscillation patterns, and sleep-wake architecture undermine central and peripheral circadian equilibrium with age. Neuroendocrine alterations produce oxidative stress, mitochondrial failure, pervasive neuroinflammation (CNS immune function loss), and proteostasis. Increasing Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, ALS, Huntington's, frontotemporal dementia, Lewy body disease, PTSD, and vascular cognitive impairment due to impaired glymphatic axonal clearance/blood-brain barrier dysregulation/synaptic degeneration/pathoproteopathic protein We examine how clock genes, melatonin signaling, hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis administration, microglia reactivity, and immune-mediated metabolic dysregulation affect dementia. New endocrine, transcriptomic, multi-omics, and wearable-derived digital biomarkers, chronopharmacology (including melatonin receptor agonists), bright-light therapy, time-restricted eating with exercise chronotherapy guidance/synchronization, sleep optimization, and gut microbiota modulation This study addressed inter-individual circadian variability, genetic susceptibility to therapy timing, biomarker standardization, and clinical trial design. The melatonin-cortisol axis may identify and treat age-related neurodegenerative diseases with tailored treatment.

article.title: Biphasic tRF-31 dynamics regulate HIPK2-mediated dual-track lens epithelial injury under oxidative stress in age-related cataract.
article.authors: Pan Z, Jin Y, Zhang C, Yu Y.
article.abstract: Age-related cataract (ARC) develops through cumulative oxidative stress and progressive loss of lens epithelial homeostasis, but the small-RNA mechanisms that distinguish an adaptive response from sustained injury remain unclear. Using a time-resolved H 2 O 2 model in HLEC-B3 cells, we identified tRF-31, a 31-nt 5' tRNA-Ala-derived small RNA, as a biphasic stress-responsive regulator that increased during an early oxidative-response state with preserved viability but declined during sustained sublethal injury. N-acetylcysteine blunted the early increase and counteracted the later decrease in tRF-31, whereas the full-length parental tRNA-Ala pool remained stable and quantitative immunofluorescence showed stress-dependent angiogenin redistribution that was temporally associated with tRF-31 expression. Functionally, tRF-31 replenishment reduced apoptosis and mitochondrial depolarization while supporting post-stress epithelial recovery and DNA synthesis, whereas tRF-31 inhibition aggravated apoptotic and mitochondrial injury after endogenous tRF-31 had declined. Transcriptomic profiling, target prediction, quantitative PCR validation, and wild-type and mutant 3'untranslated region reporter assays supported homeodomain-interacting protein kinase 2 (HIPK2) as a direct target of tRF-31. tRF-31 suppressed HIPK2 and p53 Ser46 phosphorylation, reduced BAX, BAD, p21, and cleaved caspase-3, and preserved Bcl-2, RB phosphorylation, CCNE2, and PCNA. HIPK2 overexpression counteracted the anti-apoptotic and pro-recovery effects of tRF-31 mimic. In 92 ARC anterior capsule specimens, lower tRF-31, higher HIPK2 and CDKN1A expression, and a higher BAX/Bcl-2 ratio were associated with greater nuclear hardness and poorer preoperative visual acuity after adjustment for age. These findings identify a temporally regulated tRF-31/HIPK2-p53 axis that links oxidative stress responses to lens epithelial injury and impaired recovery in ARC.

article.title: Structural and biochemical characterization of disease-associated mutations in the human mitochondrial processing peptidase α-subunit.
article.authors: Simons DM, Qin S, Munro K, Matthews LA, Thibodeaux CJ, Trempe JF.
article.abstract: The mitochondrial processing peptidase (MPP) is an essential heterodimeric protease responsible for cleavage of N-terminal mitochondrial targeting sequences (N-MTSs) from most nuclear-encoded mitochondrial proteins following import into the mitochondrial matrix. Pathogenic variants in the α-subunit of MPP (PMPCA) cause a spectrum of mitochondrial disorders, including spinocerebellar ataxia type 2 (SCAR2), encephalopathy, and severe neurodevelopmental disease; however, the molecular mechanisms underlying these phenotypes remain poorly understood. Here, we combined biochemical and structural approaches to characterize five disease-associated PMPCA variants (S96L, R185W, R268W, A377T, and G515R). Enzymatic analyses revealed variant-specific defects in substrate processing, with most mutations severely impairing cleavage of the rapidly processed substrate malate dehydrogenase 2. In contrast, several variants exhibited only modest impairment in the processing of the slowly cleaved substrate PINK1. Mass photometry demonstrated reduced heterodimerization of all variants, whereas circular dichroism identified varying degrees of structural destabilization, particularly for S96L and G515R. To define the structural basis of these defects, hydrogen-deuterium exchange mass spectrometry was performed on wild type MPP and selected variants. Pathogenic mutations altered substrate-induced conformational changes within previously characterized substrate-recognition elements, including the glycine-rich loop. Furthermore, we identified a previously unrecognized region, termed the INS loop, that exhibited substrate-dependent protection uniquely in the wild type enzyme but was consistently disrupted across pathogenic variants. Together, these findings demonstrate that PMPCA mutations impair MPP function through diverse mechanisms involving protein stability, dimerization, substrate selectivity, and allosteric conformational dynamics. Our work provides a mechanistic framework for understanding genotype-phenotype relationships in PMPCA-associated disease.

article.title: Snapshots of ATP-driven substrate translocation by the mitochondrial AAA+ protease AFG3L2.
article.authors: Dai Y, Hong S, Wu Y, Xiong R, Guan Z, Zhang D, Wang Q, Yin P.
article.abstract: AFG3L2, located in the mitochondrial inner membrane, is an ATP-fueled protease responsible for protein degradation, and its dysfunction has been implicated in multiple neurodegenerative disorders. However, the structural basis underlying its ATP-driven substrate translocation remains incompletely understood. Here, we purified full-length human AFG3L2 and determined its cryo-EM structures in four distinct conformational states (Con1-Con4), revealing substrate engagement in the core catalytic domain despite weak EM density for its transmembrane domain. These structures display an asymmetric spiral-staircase architecture in which the six protomers are arranged around a central pore that accommodates a polypeptide substrate. The four conformational states jointly reveal a substrate translocation mechanism in which ATP binding by the uppermost protomer promotes substrate engagement, whereas ATP hydrolysis by the lowermost ATP-bound protomer leads to substrate release. Our findings provide snapshots of ATP-driven substrate translocation by AFG3L2 and refine the hand-over-hand translocation mechanism by revealing substrate capture and release during an ordered ATPase cycle.

article.title: The antimicrobial peptide pileup promotes enterocyte shedding to maintain gut homeostasis in aging Drosophila.
article.authors: Lee JH, Kim SH, Kim EK, Lee KA, Bhin J, Hwang D, Lee DG, Bahn YS, Lee WJ.
article.abstract: Cellular turnover is a fundamental biological process that counteracts aging by activating stem cells to replace aging cells. This process is especially critical for maintaining the intestinal epithelium, one of the most rapidly renewing tissues in the body. However, the replacement of aging enterocytes cannot be explained solely by the generation of new cells from intestinal stem cells (ISCs); it also requires the complementary process of physically removing aging enterocytes through shedding. Compared with the well-characterized regulation of ISCs, the mechanisms governing enterocyte shedding remain poorly understood. Here, we identify pileup, a novel age-associated antimicrobial peptide (AMP) in Drosophila, as both a genetic marker and a key regulator of enterocyte shedding. Reactive oxygen species (ROS) generated through age-related mitochondrial dysfunction, a process facilitated by Autophagy-related gene 1 (ATG1) kinase, activate hypoxia-inducible factor 1α, which induces pileup expression specifically in aging enterocytes. Pileup then compromises the membrane of these cells and triggers c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) activation, which we propose promotes their shedding. Notably, pileup has three homologs, and loss of all four genes leads to tumorous cell accumulation, gut barrier dysfunction, microbiome dysbiosis, and premature death. Our findings reveal a previously unrecognized role for AMPs in the turnover of aging host cells, extending their classical function beyond microbial defense. This work provides new mechanistic insights into enterocyte shedding and underscores its essential role in preserving gut homeostasis during aging.

article.title: Cardiovascular resilience in centenarians.
article.authors: Carrera-Bastos P, Plaza-Florido A, Pérez-Prieto I, Radom-Aizik S, Franceschi C, Rodríguez-López C, Serra-Rexach JA, Emanuele E, Lucia A.
article.abstract: Centenarians - individuals aged ≥100 years - provide a unique human model for understanding resilience to cardiovascular ageing. Although cardiovascular and metabolic diseases, including hypertension, heart failure, atrial fibrillation and chronic kidney disease, are common in centenarians, their onset is typically delayed relative to that in individuals aged 80-100 years. Centenarians characteristically have structural changes in the heart and vessels, including concentric left ventricular remodelling, increased myocardial stiffness and vascular ageing, but often without the expected burden of myocardial infarction or overt heart failure. Their cardiometabolic profile is generally favourable, marked by preserved insulin sensitivity in cohorts with a low prevalence of diabetes mellitus, mid-range lipid levels and a low prevalence of obesity. Centenarians also have a distinctive inflammatory and gastrointestinal phenotype, characterized by chronic low-grade inflammation with elevated anti-inflammatory signalling, a gut microbiome that more closely resembles that of younger adults, and preserved intestinal barrier integrity. Genetically and epigenetically, exceptional longevity reflects highly polygenic contributions, selective maintenance of genomic stability and markedly younger epigenetic age compared with chronological age. In this Review, we summarize data on the cardiovascular system among centenarians by framing observations of longevity as a composite of delayed pathology, adaptive compensation and survivorship selection. Understanding the biological, behavioural and environmental mechanisms underlying cardiovascular resilience in extreme longevity might inform strategies to extend cardiovascular healthspan across all ages.

article.title: Integrated chemical profiling, transcriptomics and functional validation elucidate the multifunctional benefits of a triple-ferment filtrate complex for skin aging intervention.
article.authors: Gao P, Xiao X, Zhang H, Tu F, Gu X.
article.abstract: Objective Skin aging is driven by interconnected hallmarks including oxidative stress and chronic low-grade inflammation, cellular senescence, impaired epidermal function and extracellular matrix (ECM) degradation. Fermentation-derived cosmetic ingredients have attracted increasing interest as multifunctional actives; however, their underlying mechanisms often remain poorly understood. This study aimed to systematically characterize the biological activities and mechanisms of a triple-ferment filtrate complex (TF Complex) derived from fermented rice, green tea and algae. Methods An integrated approach combining chemical profiling, transcriptomic analysis and functional validation across multiple in vitro skin models was employed. Chemical constituents were characterized using UPLC-Q-Orbitrap-MS. Transcriptomic responses of human keratinocytes treated with TF Complex at different time points were evaluated by RNA sequencing. Functional activities were assessed in keratinocytes, fibroblasts and reconstructed human skin models relevant to skin aging. Results Chemical profiling revealed a compositionally complex mixture containing diverse bioactive constituents. Transcriptomic analysis revealed a time-dependent response characterized by early activation of antioxidant defence pathways, followed by induction of epidermal differentiation related programmes. Functional studies showed that TF Complex promoted wound closure and attenuated UVB-induced inflammatory responses. Furthermore, selected representative constituents, turanose, caffeine and p-hydroxybenzaldehyde, enhanced antioxidant and keratinocyte differentiation-associated gene expression while down-regulating inflammation-related gene expression in skin cells. In H 2 O 2 -induced senescent fibroblasts, TF Complex reduced senescence-associated β-gal activity and p16/γH2AX levels while increasing SOD2 expression. In a reconstructed full-thickness inflammaging skin model, TF Complex restored epidermal thickness and filaggrin expression, preserved dermal-epidermal junction integrity and dermal ECM proteins and reduced the release of MMP-1, MMP-9 and IL-1α. Conclusions TF Complex exerts multifunctional activities relevant to skin aging intervention through coordinated regulation of oxidative stress responses, inflammation and epidermal homeostasis. These findings provide a comprehensive mechanistic framework supporting the development and application of fermentation-derived cosmetic actives for healthy skin aging.

article.title: TREM2/IGF-1 Signaling Axis-induced microglial senescence Underlies Benzo[a]pyrene-associated Parkinson's Disease-like Lesions.
article.authors: Wu Y, Shi Y, Xiao F, Liu A, Li X, Xia N, Zhang H.
article.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most prevalent neurodegenerative disorder worldwide. Accumulating evidence has linked environmental polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), with benzo[a]pyrene (B[a]P) as a representative ubiquitous member, to elevated PD risk and disease pathogenesis. The present study aimed to investigate whether B[a]P can trigger typical PD-like lesions in mice, and further dissects the functional role of microglial senescence as well as its underlying regulatory mechanism, using complementary systems in vivo mouse model and in vitro BV2 microglia cell. Behavioral assessments revealed that B[a]P exposure induced significant, dose-dependent impairments in motor coordination and cognitive function compared with the control group. Moreover, the degree of functional impairments measured in the high-dose B[a]P group was comparable to that observed in the MPTP positive-control group. Following B[a]P treatment, brain-resident microglia cells exhibited signs of cell senescence, as evidenced by typical ultrastructural alterations, increased senescence-associated β-galactosidase (SA-β-gal) activity, and elevated expression of the core senescence markers p16, p21, and p53 proteins. Consistent with these in vivo observations, B[a]P was confirmed to also induce cell cycle arrest in cultured BV2 microglia cells. This pro-senescent effect was significnatly attenuated by Triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells 2 (TREM2) overexpression, whereas it was markedly exacerbated following TREM2 knockout. Subsequent experiments further validated that insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1), as a direct downstream effector regulated by TREM2, is functionally required for B[a]P-triggered microglial senescence. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that B[a]P exposure can induce PD-like lesions and microglial senescence, and which is primarily mediated via the TREM2/IGF-1 signaling axis.

article.title: T cell metabolic ageing as a factor for therapeutic research.
article.authors: King E, Zinali Sohanaki B, Schurich A.
article.abstract: Ageing is an important determinant of immune function across the lifespan, yet it remains underappreciated in the design and interpretation of much basic T cell research. As the immune system ages, T cell responses become less diverse, less efficient, and less adaptable, with consequences for infection control, vaccine responsiveness, cancer immunosurveillance, and the performance of T cell-based immunotherapies. This issue is particularly acute because many fundamental studies still rely on T cells from, mostly, healthy young donors. These controls are indispensable, but the field has built much of its pre-clinical logic on immune systems that are younger, fitter, and biologically distinct from the patients for whom T cell therapies are intended. We argue that this mismatch between experimental systems and clinical reality could be overcome by considering age as a routine variable from the start.

article.title: Functional and Structural Brain Age Gaps as Complementary Predictive Markers for Cognitive Performance
article.authors: Crocetta, A.; Morandini, M.; Bittner, N.; Caspers, S.; Cauda, F.; Brovelli, A.; Gilson, M.
article.abstract: Cognitive decline is characterized by substantial inter-individual variability across the lifespan, even among clinically healthy adults. However, it is unclear how structural and functional brain organization jointly relate to differences in cognitive performance within the typical populations. We considered a multimodal brain age framework by predicting for each subject its age from either structural MRI or resting-state functional MRI, after training on the 1000BRAINS cohort (901 participants, 18-85 years). Following, a structural and a functional brain age gap markers were defined as the deviations with respect to the real chronological age. We then used the markers to characterize the interplay between structure and function in shaping cognitive performances. Our findings reveal that the functional marker is as important to predict global cognitive performance as the structural marker. The most accurate prediction was found for global cognition, executive functions and episodic memory, followed by working memory, attention and language. In particular, the structural marker was contributing to all domains, except for working memory, whereas the functional marker had the highest contribution. Overall, structural and functional brain age models together provide a meaningful subject-level summary of brain information for predicting cognition, supporting a multidimensional view of typical aging.

article.title: Steam explosion-induced structural remodeling of Auricularia auricula polysaccharides enhances anti-aging efficacy in Drosophila melanogaster .
article.authors: Huang Z, Zhang S, Qiang Y, Luo X, Zhang Y, Guo Z, Zheng B.
article.abstract: This paper studied the physicochemical properties and bioactivity of Auricularia auricula polysaccharides (AAPs) before and after steam explosion (SE) pretreatment. AAPs consisted mainly of mannose, galactose, and glucose; SE pretreatment shifted monosaccharide proportions and reduced the weight-average molecular weight to 3.37 × 10 5 Da. Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy showed that SE did not alter the fundamental functional groups of the polysaccharides. Thermal stability was enhanced after SE, as evidenced by scanning electron microscopy, which revealed a transition from a dense architecture to a more open, stratified microstructure with increased surface roughness. Compared with the control (AAP-CK), the SE-treated group (AAP-SE) exhibited enhanced in vitro antioxidant capacity. Dietary supplementation with 0.0312% AAP-SE significantly extended the average lifespan of Drosophila melanogaster by 28.44% in females and 22.08% in males. In fruit flies, AAP-SE enhanced antioxidant enzyme activities, increasing superoxide dismutase by 67.32% and glutathione peroxidase by 2.61-fold in males, while reducing malondialdehyde levels by 42.75% in females. Furthermore, fruit flies fed AAP-SE showed improved resistance to hydrogen peroxide-induced oxidative stress and starvation stress, with gender-specific effects. These results suggested that SE pretreatment effectively enhanced the antioxidant and anti-aging activities of AAPs, suggesting their potential as natural lifespan-extending antioxidants.

article.title: Natural Killer Cell TGF-β Signaling Regulates Postnatal Lung Development.
article.authors: Gainer DJ, Coyle KM, Rätsep MT, Quilty D, Tran Van BL, Skebo S, VandenBroek MM, Laverty KJ, Deng Y, Alalouf JF, Shirazi SP, Brady HJM, Sucre JMS, Vivier E, Shrestha N, Wong HC, Stewart DJ, Domnik NJ, Ormiston ML.
article.abstract: Background Bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD) is a disease of neonatal lung development that is linked to impaired pulmonary vascularization, dysregulated TGF-β (transforming growth factor-β) signaling, and the accumulation of senescent cells. Despite the established role of TGF-β signaling in promoting vascular remodeling and suppressing the senolytic activity of natural killer (NK) cells, the contribution of NK cell TGF-β signaling to postnatal lung patterning and the pathogenesis of BPD remains unclear. Methods Mice bearing an NK cell-selective deletion of the type-II TGF-β receptor ( Tgfbr2 NK- /- ) were analyzed for vascular and alveolar structure, lung NK cell infiltration, senescence markers, and lung function testing across neonatal and adult time points. Lung tissue from both neonatal mice and human infants with BPD was assessed by single-cell RNA sequencing. The effects of enhanced NK cell activity in a hyperoxia-induced model of BPD were examined in Tgfbr2 NK-/- neonates, as well as pharmacologically, using the TGF-β ligand trap/IL-15 superagonist, HCW9218. Results Neonatal Tgfbr2 NK-/- mice exhibited a baseline reduction in distal arteriolar density, impaired alveolarization, and sex-specific deficits in long-term lung function. Single-cell RNA sequencing identified excessive clearance of senescent endothelial cells by TGF-β-insensitive NK cells in the lungs of Tgfbr2 NK-/- neonates. This enhanced NK cell activity promoted a BPD-like phenotype in naïve Tgfbr2 NK-/- mice but protected these animals from impaired lung development under hyperoxia. Sequencing of lung tissue from human infants with BPD confirmed excessive TGF-β signaling and cytotoxic impairment in NK cells. Treatment with HCW9218 prevented senescent cell accumulation and rescued lung development in the hyperoxia mouse model. Conclusions TGF-β is a tunable regulator of NK cell senolytic activity that is essential for normal postnatal lung development. Excessive NK cell TGF-β signaling contributes to impaired lung development with neonatal hyperoxia and may serve as a viable therapeutic target in human BPD.

article.title: DNA damage at Lamina-Associated Domains triggers nuclear envelope reorganization and chromatin detachment to prevent nuclear envelope blebbing and genome instability.
article.authors: Rubio-Contreras, D.; Audibert, S.; Fernandez, J.; Lambuta, R. A.; Pateraki, N.; Meaburn, K.; Wootton, J.; Carreira, R.; Parnandi, N.; Gonzalez-Mendez, R.; Boulton, S. J.; Kozik, Z.; Papathanasiou, S.; Soutoglou, E.
article.abstract: The nuclear periphery anchors large, transcriptionally silent chromatin domains to the nuclear envelope and plays a central role in maintaining genome stability, acting as a dynamic hub for DNA repair. Nevertheless, how cells process DNA damage within lamina-associated domains (LADs), which reside in this environment, remains poorly understood, despite their relevance to nuclear architecture, aging, and senescence. By employing systems for temporally controlled and spatially precise induction of DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) within LADs, we show that DSBs within LADs trigger remodeling of the nuclear lamina and the dynamic detachment of damaged LADs from the nuclear envelope, resulting in their relocalization to the nuclear interior. This process is orchestrated by the ATM/{gamma}H2AX/MDC1/RNF168/53BP1 axis and requires the linker of nucleoskeleton and cytoskeleton (LINC) complex and cytoskeletal components while leaving DNA repair pathway choice unchanged. Persistent tethering of damaged LADs at the nuclear periphery delays the DNA damage response and repair, elevates genomic instability, and drives chromatin extrusion through nuclear blebs directly linking failed repair to dysregulation of nuclear integrity. These findings reveal a protective mechanism in which ATM-driven LAD dynamics and nuclear envelope remodeling might relieve mechanical stress, facilitate repair, and safeguard both genome stability and nuclear architecture.

article.title: Structural characterization and antioxidant-associated anti-aging effects of polysaccharides from the aerial parts of Bupleurum chinense DC.: Insights from cellular and Drosophila models.
article.authors: Li D, Chen R, Xu J, Lu X, Liu C, Du C, Gao Y, Gao P, Liu X.
article.abstract: Bupleurum chinense DC. is a traditional medicinal plant, but the relationship between structural heterogeneity of its polysaccharides and oxidative stress-related biological activities remains unclear. In this study, two polysaccharide fractions, BCPS-1 and BCPS-2, were obtained from aerial parts of B. chinense. Their molecular characteristics, monosaccharide compositions, glycosidic linkage patterns, and conformational features were systematically characterized using chromatographic and spectroscopic approaches. BCPS-1 exhibited stronger in vitro antioxidant activity than BCPS-2, which was correlated with its higher uronic acid content and unique structural characteristics. In H₂O₂-induced SH-SY5Y cell injury models, BCPS-1 significantly improved cell viability, enhanced antioxidant defense capacity by increasing T-AOC, SOD, and GSH-Px activities, and reduced MDA accumulation. Furthermore, BCPS-1 treatment increased Nrf2 and HO-1 expression, while inhibition of Nrf2 partially attenuated its protective effect, suggesting that the Nrf2/HO-1 antioxidant response may contribute to its cytoprotective activity. In Drosophila melanogaster, dietary supplementation with BCPS-1 increased lifespan parameters and improved antioxidant-related indices under the tested experimental conditions. Collectively, this study reveals a correlative structure-function relationship between acidic polysaccharide characteristics and oxidative stress-associated bioactivities of B. chinense polysaccharides, highlighting BCPS-1 as a promising candidate for further development as a functional polysaccharide ingredient associated with oxidative stress regulation and healthy aging.

article.title: Astatine-211 injury induces an immunostimulatory melanoma-cell state and promotes systemic antitumor immunity
article.authors: Mayusumi, K.; Magara, S.; Huang, X.; Kaneda-Nakashima, K.; Ooe, K.; Murakami, M.; Toyoshima, A.; Haba, H.; Yin, X.; Fukase, K.; Shimoyama, A.; Kabayama, K.
article.abstract: Targeted alpha therapy is generally evaluated by absorbed dose and direct tumor-cell killing, but whether alpha-particle-injured tumor cells can induce systemic antitumor immunity remains poorly defined. We investigated the immunogenic consequences of astatine-211 (211At) injury in a prophylactic melanoma vaccination-challenge model. B16F10 cells were exposed ex vivo to 211At, etoposide, or ultraviolet irradiation under conditions that reduced viable-cell counts at 24 hours to approximately 40% of untreated controls. Injured cells were administered subcutaneously to syngeneic C57BL/6J mice before intravenous challenge with viable B16F10 cells. Vaccination with cells exposed to 1 MBq/mL 211At suppressed pulmonary metastasis, reduced regulatory T-cell proportions, and elicited tumor-reactive interferon-{gamma} responses and antibodies. Transcriptomic profiling revealed enrichment of type I interferon, inflammatory, and chemokine-related signatures, together with suppression of cell-cycle, translation, and metabolic programs. At the cellular level, 211At injury was accompanied by {gamma}H2AX accumulation, G2/M arrest, increased reactive oxygen species and cytosolic double-stranded DNA, and senescence-like changes. These features arose without consistent increases in classical damage-associated molecular patterns or prominent induction of senescence-associated secretory phenotype factors at 1 MBq/mL. In vivo pharmacologic inhibition of stimulator of interferon genes (STING) signaling attenuated the antimetastatic effect of vaccination. Together, these findings demonstrate that 211At injury can generate an immunostimulatory tumor-cell state characterized by DNA damage and altered inflammatory signaling. STING contributes to the resulting immune protection, highlighting immunogenic tumor-cell conversion as a consideration in the design of targeted alpha therapies.

article.title: Evaluation of prolonged in vitro incubation of human sperm at room temperature.
article.authors: Xu M, Chan CPS, Chung JPW, Chan DYL.
article.abstract: The longevity in vitro of viability and motility of spermatozoa from a single ejaculate is seldom studied. The physiological decay of human sperm under room temperature in vitro remains a critical yet under-explored area. While standard clinical procedures typically involve short-term sperm handling, the development of novel techniques demands a deeper understanding of 'shelf-life' of sperm. This pilot study aimed to characterise human sperm longevity at room temperature by longitudinally assessing motility, viability and DNA fragmentation, and to evaluate whether culture medium replacement could extend in vitro sperm motility. Twenty-six semen samples with sperm concentration ≥ 15 million/ml and motility ≥ 40% were collected and motile sperm were concentrated using discontinuous gradient centrifugation. A subset of 20 samples was evaluated to determine the longitudinal dynamics of motility and viability. To establish the temporal profile of DNA damage, processed samples were collected using the swim-up method at Days 0, 3, 6, 9 and 12. The remaining 6 samples were used for motility parameter observations using computer-assisted semen analysis both with and without culture medium replacement. Following initial processing, the samples exhibited a baseline motility of 91.2 ± 3.4% and viability of 94.6 ± 3.5%. During 20-day incubation, sperm motility and viability declined in a time-dependent manner, with motility decreasing more rapidly than viability. Motility persisted for an average of 13.4 days. The 20 samples showed viability of 13.4 ± 4.4% at D20. In 10 samples that were fully observed for viability, the longevity range being 35-50 days. The D3 (2.4 ± 1.4%) and D6 (5.7 ± 5.8%) DNA fragmentation levels of progressively motile sperm showed no differences with D0 levels (3.9 ± 2.8%), but at later time points, progressively motile sperm showed increased DNA fragmentation, reaching 9% at D9 (p = 0.003) and 11.2% at D12 (p = 0.01). Additionally, processed sperm exposed to regular culture medium replacement showed prolonged longevity in regard to motility. In this pilot study, after routine processing in vitro and left at room temperature, human sperm had a motility longevity of between 8 and 18 days and a viability longevity of between 35 and 50 days, although after D9 progressively motile sperm displayed significantly increased DNA damage. Regular replacement of culture medium could support and prolong sperm motility longevity.

article.title: Fast Motor Unit Deterioration as a Potential Primary Driver of Systemic Biological Aging
article.authors: Ruggia T.
article.venue: 预印本平台（数据库未注明）
article.abstract: Fast motor units allow muscles to produce force quickly, but their function can deteriorate with age. This paper examines the hypothesis that progressive impairment and eventual loss of these units may contribute to biological aging beyond the muscles themselves. A motor unit consists of a motor neuron and the muscle fibers it controls. When its nerve signals become less effective, its connections deteriorate, or the neuron is lost, the affected muscle may change how it contracts, uses energy, and communicates with other tissues. Extracellular vesicles (EVs)—small membrane-enclosed particles released by cells—are one possible means of communication. Human studies document age-related differences in motor unit properties, while bed-rest experiments show that neuromuscular function can change over relatively short periods. In mice, experimental enlargement of fast muscle fibers has improved measures of metabolism outside the muscle. Laboratory-grown neuromuscular preparations also suggest that nerve connections influence the substances muscle cells release. Animal experiments provide additional evidence that muscle-derived vesicles can affect tissues such as bone and the nervous system. These findings support parts of the proposed mechanism, but they do not establish the complete sequence. No study reviewed here has shown that age-related loss of identified fast motor units changes muscle-derived vesicles and thereby causes widespread biological aging. The proposed pathway must also account for compensatory reinnervation, potentially protective responses to denervation, differences between muscle types, and signals traveling from other organs back to muscle. The hypothesis is therefore presented as a testable model, not an established explanation of aging. Experiments that separately measure motor unit integrity, muscle activity, vesicle origin and contents, and responses in distant tissues will be needed to determine whether the proposed causal chain is correct.

article.title: Identification of TAS2R-targeting bioactive compounds against metabolic decline: A novel ex vivo methodology based on enteroendocrine and inflammatory readouts.
article.authors: Vilalta A, Descamps-Solà M, Feliu-Villarò F, Rodríguez-Gallego E, Beltrán-Debón R, Blay M, Pinent M, Ardévol A, Terra X.
article.abstract: Obesity and ageing disrupt intestinal homeostasis. Bitter taste receptors (TAS2Rs) regulate gut hormone secretion and inflammatory responses. This study aimed to identify intestinal TAS2Rs most affected by obesity and ageing and characterise their receptor-specific responses in ex vivo intestinal explants from Wistar rats. We have integrated previously published transcriptomic and metabolic datasets to identify intestinal TAS2R subtypes differentially modulated by obesity, ageing, and the combination of obesity and ageing. Receptor selection was based on associations with inflammatory, metabolic and enteroendocrine readouts. Subtype-selective agonists were identified through ligand affinity databases and literature screening, and their functional effects were characterised ex vivo in jejunal and ileal explants from Wistar rats. Enterohormone assays revealed receptor- and dose-dependent effects on GLP-1, GIP and CCK secretion, including both stimulatory and inhibitory responses. In Dextran Sulphate Sodium (DSS)-inflamed tissue, bitter agonists exerted divergent immunomodulatory effects on TNF-α, IL-1β and IL-18. Overall, rTas2r108, rTas2r119, rTas2r140 and rTas2r143, activated by amarogentin, costunolide, resveratrol and ethylpyrazine, respectively, emerged as functionally relevant targets. This study establishes an ex vivo platform for profiling intestinal TAS2R agonists, revealing subtype-specific effects on enterohormonal and inflammatory responses. This framework supports the identification of receptor-selective agonists to modulate gut homeostasis in obesity and ageing.

article.title: Regularized logistic regression-based gene selection for functional analysis of heterogeneous scRNA-seq macrophage populations in muscle aging and regeneration.
article.authors: Costa, T. M.; Lopes, M. B.; Neves, J.; Sousa-Victor, P.; Vinga, S.
article.abstract: Background: Single-cell RNA sequencing enables the characterization of heterogeneous cellular responses across experimental conditions. However, feature-selection methods often prioritize genes associated with global condition differences while overlooking subgroup-specific transcriptional structure. This limitation is particularly relevant in complex tissues, where distinct cell states may contribute differently to disease, aging, or regeneration. Regularized logistic regression provides an interpretable framework for sparse gene selection, but standard penalties do not explicitly account for differences in gene-gene correlation patterns across annotated subgroups. Results: We introduce DisTwiner, a subgroup-aware extension of the twiner correlation-based regularization framework for binary classification problems with multiple annotated groups. DisTwiner computes pairwise angular scores between feature-correlation profiles across subgroup labels and incorporates the resulting feature-specific weights into an Elastic Net-regularized logistic regression model. We evaluated DisTwiner using simulated data and a single-cell RNA-seq dataset of macrophage populations isolated from young and aged regenerating murine skeletal muscle. In simulated data, alternative aggregation and transformation strategies showed comparable classification performance, with minimum-based exponential weighting producing the greatest dispersion of feature penalties. In the macrophage dataset, DisTwiner achieved classification performance comparable to standard Elastic Net logistic regression and higher than Random Forest under the evaluated setting. Although predictive accuracy was similar to Elastic Net, DisTwiner selected genes with more heterogeneous fold-change and correlation patterns across macrophage subpopulations. Downstream enrichment analyses showed that DisTwiner-selected features captured biologically relevant aging-associated pathways, including interferon-response signatures in specific macrophage populations, and could serve as an additional filtering layer after differential expression analysis. Conclusions: DisTwiner extends correlation-based regularization to binary classification settings with multiple annotated subgroups, enabling feature selection that accounts for subgroup-specific correlation structure. Applied to single-cell macrophage data, the method preserved competitive classification performance while prioritizing genes with cell-population-dependent expression patterns, supporting its use for interpretable subgroup-aware feature selection in high-dimensional omics data.

article.title: Background Histological Lesions in Aged African Green Monkeys ( Chlorocebus sabaeus ) From St. Kitts.
article.authors: Zayas S, Beierschmitt A, Palmour R, Bolfa P.
article.abstract: The Caribbean African Green Monkey ( Chlorocebus sabaeus ) (AGM) represents a valuable nonhuman primate model for the study of age-related pathology, with an average lifespan of over 20 years. We describe histological background and common lesions in 44 aged AGMs, >15 years, 20 males and 24 females, 26 colony-born and 18 wild-caught from a primate research facility. The most frequent cardiovascular lesion was myocardial fibrosis (54.5%), characterized by multifocal myocardial fibrosis, cardiomyocyte degeneration/necrosis, lipofuscin accumulation, and frequent concurrent vascular hyalinization affecting small to medium-sized arteries across multiple organs. Chronic kidney disease was highly prevalent, marked by lymphoplasmacytic infiltration, interstitial and glomerular fibrosis, tubular degeneration, mineralization, and calcium oxalate crystal deposition; unique renal findings included intratubular iron concretions with foreign body reactions. Hepatic lesions were dominated by lymphoplasmacytic infiltration and widespread hemosiderosis, indicating systemic iron overload. In the respiratory system, silica-laden macrophages (SLM) were the most common finding, alongside diverse forms of pneumonia and occasional cryptogenic organizing pneumonia. Additional aging-related changes included adrenal nodular hyperplasia, uterine pregnancy-associated vascular remodeling (PAVR) (uterine hyaline deposits), and Sarcocystis infection in skeletal muscle. This retrospective, descriptive study provides initial data on age-related background histopathology in the aged AGM.

article.title: Maternal sleep deprivation is associated with fetal hypothalamic-hepatic remodeling and long-term metabolic and behavioral alterations in offspring.
article.authors: Gong J, Liu S, Chen P, Gao X, Bai L, Huang H, Pan J, Liu X.
article.abstract: Maternal sleep deprivation (MSD) is increasingly prevalent during pregnancy; however, its long-term developmental impact on offspring health remains incompletely defined. Here, we identify MSD as a prenatal stressor that is associated with coordinated alterations in fetal hypothalamic-hepatic neuro-metabolic pathways, potentially contributing to increased vulnerability to metabolic and affective disorders later in life. Using a mouse model of chronic gestational sleep deprivation, we perform longitudinal metabolic and behavioral phenotyping in offspring combined with transcriptomic profiling of the fetal hypothalamus and liver and integrative analyses extending into adulthood. Female MSD offspring exhibit delayed-onset glucose intolerance, insulin resistance, and altered lipid utilization during aging, whereas male offspring display only mild metabolic alterations. MSD offspring also demonstrate alterations in anxiety-like and helplessness-related behavioral indices, which are further exacerbated by chronic stress exposure. Transcriptomic analyses reveal coordinated remodeling of hypothalamic neurodevelopmental and neurotransmitter pathways alongside hepatic metabolic programs during fetal development, suggesting early alterations of hypothalamic-liver coupling. Comparative analyses between fetal and adult liver samples demonstrate persistent dysregulation of metabolic pathways. Collectively, these findings suggest that MSD is associated with reconfiguration of fetal central-peripheral regulatory networks, which may contribute to a maladaptive neuro-metabolic trajectory linking metabolic and emotional dysfunction across the lifespan. These results identify prenatal sleep as a modifiable determinant of offspring health and provide insight into potential mechanisms underlying the shared developmental origins of metabolic and affective disorders.
