article.title: A Unified Continuous Time Framework for Adaptive Smartphone Battery Drain Prediction with Finite Horizon Error Analysis
article.authors: Wang C, Li X, Sun Y, Liu S, Zhang H.
article.abstract: Abstract Smartphone battery prediction requires a consistent connection between hardware demand, electrical dynamics and capacity aging. We develop a unified continuous-time framework that integrates a second-order equivalent circuit, a temperature-dependent resistance model, empirical aging and adaptive load calibration. A finite-horizon error analysis connects current bias and capacity uncertainty to state-of-charge drift, while exact interval updates provide a reference for numerical verification. Evaluation combines new Android telemetry, 1000 public smartphone workload profiles and five laboratory cell trajectories. On a later ZTE session, static scale calibration reduces power mean absolute error from 1.582 to 0.232 W; a predict-before-update recursive comparator achieves 0.117 W. Across 17 forward temporal blocks, the recursive method yields a pooled error of 0.155 W, with condition-dependent failures. On public Pixel 8 profiles, linear hardware features explain 89.4% of variation in a nominal-voltage power proxy. Dual-exponential capacity extrapolation achieves 0.00651 Ah root-mean-square error on the UCL cell, but offers no general advantage over simpler models on four NASA cells. The results establish a reproducible route from load calibration to charge-balance error assessment and identify the conditions governing model deployment. Complete-discharge validation remains necessary to quantify end-to-end runtime accuracy.

article.title: Postsynaptic TAK1-GluN2B axis supports hippocampal synaptic integrity and cognitive function during aging
article.authors: Liu, Y.; Huang, M.-Q.; Zhang, Y.-C.; Jia, Z.-R.; Min, X.; Zhou, Z.-Y.; Chen, J.-Y.; Zong, F.-J.; Gao, J.; Xu, Y.-W.; Wang, T.; Zhang, Y.-Y.; He, K.-W.
article.abstract: Transforming growth factor {beta}-activated kinase 1 (TAK1) is a serine/threonine kinase best known for its roles in immune and stress-response signaling, yet its physiological function in mature neurons remains poorly understood. Here we identify neuronal TAK1 as a regulator of excitatory synaptic integrity, hippocampal plasticity and memory. Conditional reduction of TAK1 in forebrain excitatory neurons impaired short- and long-term memory and was accompanied by attenuated long-term potentiation in the hippocampus. At the cellular level, TAK1 deficiency reduced dendritic spine density and suppressed excitatory synaptic transmission, whereas genetic or pharmacological disruption of TAK1 kinase activity recapitulated these synaptic deficits. Mechanistically, TAK1 localized to the postsynaptic compartment of excitatory synapses and associated with PSD-95. Phosphoproteomic analysis of isolated postsynaptic density fractions revealed coordinated changes in synaptic phosphorylation following TAK1 reduction, including decreased phosphorylation of the NMDA receptor subunit GluN2B at serine 920. Analyses of phosphodeficient and phosphomimetic GluN2B mutants supported a role for S920 phosphorylation downstream of TAK1 in maintaining dendritic spine density, excitatory synaptic transmission and spontaneous synaptic calcium activity. Notably, synaptic TAK1 level was reduced in the aged hippocampus. Re-expressing neuronal TAK1 in aged mice increased dendritic spine density, enhanced hippocampal synaptic plasticity, and improved memory performance. Together, these findings define a postsynaptic TAK1-GluN2B signaling axis that supports excitatory synaptic function and suggest that reduced synaptic TAK1 signaling may contribute to hippocampal vulnerability during aging.

article.title: Uterine function and reproduction aging. I. Molecular and structural alterations associated with impaired decidualization in aged mouse uteri.
article.authors: Cummings MJ, Liu B, Paudel S, Wang X, Sgouridis S, Peng X, Hu G, Wang X.
article.abstract: Reproductive aging is associated with reduced fertility and increased risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes, including miscarriage, placental dysfunction, and fetal growth restriction. While age-related decline in oocyte quality contributes to early pregnancy loss, uterine dysfunction is recognized as a critical determinant of pregnancy success, particularly for complications arising after implantation of blastocysts. However, the mechanisms by which uterine aging impairs post-implantation blastocyst development remain unclear. We tested the hypothesis that reproductive aging limits decidual growth through impaired progesterone (P4) responsiveness and fibrotic remodeling. An artificial decidualization model with young and aged virgin mice was used to isolate uterine-specific effects independent of ovarian and embryonic factors. The results indicate that reproductive aging markedly reduced decidual expansion. Aged decidualized uteri exhibited impaired progesterone receptor (PGR) expression and spatial dysregulation and reduced expression of P4-responsive genes. Transcriptomic profiling of decidualized uteri revealed coordinated suppression of stromal differentiation, cell-cycle, growth-factor, and extracellular matrix (ECM)-remodeling programs together with broader changes in stress, immune, and metabolic pathways. Primary stromal cells from aged uteri showed reduced proliferative capacity and attenuated induction of decidualization-associated genes. Histological analyses demonstrated increased accumulation of fibrillar Type I and III collagens and impaired ECM remodeling. These findings provide an integrated molecular, cellular, and structural framework linking impaired P4 responsiveness, stromal dysfunction, and fibrotic remodeling to reduced decidual growth during reproductive aging. Supplementary information The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1186/s44494-026-00007-9.

article.title: Alternate non-metallic implants in fracture care - A review.
article.authors: Fritz T, Osche D, Liodakis E, Orth M.
article.abstract: The use of implants in the treatment of fractures evolved over the last decades. Until today, most implant designs are based on metallic alloys such as Titanium or stainless steel. However, the global ageing population with increasing numbers of fragility and pathological fractures challenges current implant designs regarding stress shielding, fragile soft tissue and advanced demands like reduced imaging artefacts for radiotherapy planning. Therefore, alternative non-metallic implants that more closely resemble the mechanical properties of bone or provide additional stability as intramedullary augmentation have become available. This narrative-review summarizes the current available (2026) technology, biomechanical properties, clinical applications, outcomes and complications of CFR-PEEK implants and photodynamic bone stabilization implants in fracture management. In total n = 100 publications were taken into consideration for this narrative-review. Non-metallic-implants for fracture care are still a niche product in the treatment of fractures. However, with the ageing population and the increasing number of impaired bone quality and stability, these methods could help reduce stress shielding and force distribution comparable to physiological bone (CFR-PEEK implants) or allow additional augmentation (photodynamic bone stabilization) in reduced bone quality.

article.title: The Cervical Mechanical Bottleneck of the Lymphatic–Glymphatic Clearance Chain: Conditional Coupling Between the Investing Cervical Fascia and the Carotid Sheath and the Intrasheath Lymph Node Hypothesis
article.authors: Huang X.
article.venue: 预印本平台（数据库未注明）
article.abstract: Central clearance dysfunction in neurodegenerative diseases has long been regarded as an intracerebral event. However, the final outlet for cerebral metabolic waste—the deep cervical lymphatic system—shares the same mechanical space as the vascular and neural structures within the carotid sheath. This article proposes a hypothesis of conditional coupling between the investing layer of the deep cervical fascia (investing fascia) and the carotid sheath, centered on the lymph node within the carotid sheath (intrasheath lymph node). The central proposition is that chronic forward head posture, aging, and low-grade inflammation synergistically drive investing fascia fibrosis and reduce its elastic buffering capacity. Abnormal shear forces are then transmitted to the carotid sheath through composite pathways involving the deep cervical fascia, visceral fascia, or interstitial tissue pressure, thereby altering the conditional mechanical environment of lymphatic structures within the sheath. Six functional domains—arterial perfusion, venous return, deep cervical lymphatic drainage, lymphatic-glymphatic coupling, sympathetic tone, and the vagal anti-inflammatory pathway—are conditionally co-susceptible under shared mechanical boundaries, but they are not assumed to be equally affected, equally weighted, or involved in an identical sequence. The lymphatic and glymphatic systems constitute a serial clearance chain. Within the carotid sheath region, the intrasheath lymph node is the core structure and the conditional shared bottleneck at the cervical level. Functional stenosis, as defined here, refers to functional limitation of lymphatic structures within the sheath under a conditional mechanical environment; it does not presuppose homogeneous sheath-wall narrowing or constant direct fibrous continuity. Its downstream outcome should be described as altered clearance function (reduction or pathological redistribution) rather than a decline in a single clearance measure. Existing evidence is uneven across nodes of the chain. Meningeal lymphatic anatomy and functional necessity are independently validated; glymphatic driving and coupling frameworks are becoming clearer; human intrathecal tracer magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) shows drainage to deep cervical lymph nodes; external mechanical and intrinsic physiological regulation can alter cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) drainage; aging-related lymphatic decline is a systemic vulnerability axis; phosphorylated tau 181 (pTau181) enrichment in deep cervical lymph nodes supports the central-to-cervical transport direction; and fibrotic remodeling of deep cervical lymph nodes localizes the bottleneck to the lymph node level. The core empirical gap is whether, within the same individual, a decline in investing fascia elasticity precedes or accompanies changes in the mechanical state of lymph nodes within the carotid sheath and mediates altered clearance function, while remaining statistically independent of cervical bone-ligament structural parameters and global spinal alignment parameters.

article.title: Telomere Dynamics in Congenital Heart Defects: Hidden Architects of Cardiogenesis?
article.authors: Joshi R, Nath S, Gupta S.
article.abstract: Background Congenital heart defects (CHDs) represent a significant global health burden, particularly in India, and are among the leading causes of childhood mortality. Despite growing insights into their multifactorial etiology, the molecular mechanisms linking maternal health to embryonic heart development remain elusive. Telomeres, the repetitive DNA-protein structures that cap chromosome ends, are recognized as markers of cellular aging and also as regulators of early embryogenesis. This review examines emerging evidence connecting telomere biology with the risk of CHD in offspring. Scope of review This review is aimed at mapping the existing evidence on telomere dynamics in the context of cardiogenesis and CHD. It encompasses studies involving human subjects and experimental models, focusing on telomere length (TL), telomerase activity, and telomere dysfunction in cardiac development and CHD pathogenesis. Key findings We highlight the influence of environmental stressors on telomere dynamics and chromosomal stability in gametes and early embryos. Current evidence suggests that altered telomere dynamics may influence cardiomyocyte proliferation, cellular senescence, and genomic integrity, thereby contributing to aberrant cardiac development. Studies indicate potential associations between telomere shortening, impaired telomerase activity, and increased susceptibility to CHD; however, findings remain heterogeneous and fragmented. Implications This review highlights the need to explore impaired parental telomere maintenance as a novel risk factor for improper chromosomal segregation and abnormal heart development. Understanding the role of telomere dynamics in cardiogenesis may provide novel insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying CHD. This could aid in identifying potential biomarkers for early risk assessment and open avenues for targeted therapeutic strategies aimed at modulating telomere function. Conclusion Telomere biology represents a promising yet underexplored area in CHD research. This study is among the first to conceptualize impaired parental and embryonic telomere dynamics as a unifying mechanistic link in CHD pathogenesis. This review highlights the need for comprehensive and integrative studies to elucidate potential mechanistic links in order to translate these findings into clinical applications. Understanding this telomere-CHD axis may open a new frontier for periconceptional intervention and targeted maternal care to improve overall birth outcomes.

article.title: Nutrimental Determinants of Chronological Aging and Competitiveness in the snf1Δ Warburg Model.
article.authors: Correa-Olivares A, Champagne ACL, Bertadillo-Jilote AD, Leon KIL, Garcia-Gutierrez DG, Nava GM, Sanchez-Quezada V, Madrigal-Perez LA.
article.abstract: Cancer, one of the world's leading causes of death, is characterized by a complex metabolic reprogramming that features the Warburg effect as one of its hallmarks. The Warburg effect involves increased glucose and amino acid metabolism, which promotes tumor proliferation and progression. Although cancer has historically been attributed to genetic mutations, recent studies suggest a possible metabolic origin. However, a key characteristic of cancer cells is their greater adaptability than normal cells, as evidenced by their resistance to chemotherapy, which stems from their high mutability. This underscores the need to examine the relationship between metabolic reprogramming and cancer development from both metabolic and evolutionary perspectives. In this context, Saccharomyces cerevisiae snf1∆ strain has emerged as an ideal cellular model for studying the Warburg effect. This study aimed to determine whether deletion of the SNF1 gene in S. cerevisiae affects its chronological aging and competitiveness in a glucose and amino acid-dependent manner. Herein, we provide evidence that the snf1∆ strain changes the chronological aging depending on nutrimental condition, under low-nutrient levels shortens (0.1% glucose + 0.1× amino acids), and increases under high-nutrient levels (5% glucose + 3× amino acids). Competitiveness of the snf1∆ strain in cocultivation with wild-type was also improved in 5% glucose + 3× amino acids, by approximately two orders of magnitude. These results indicate that snf1∆ strain aging and competitiveness are also sensitive to nutrimental status, as was observed in cancer cells.

article.title: Targeting protective renin-angiotensin system pathways in pulmonary emphysema: Preclinical evidence for resolving inflammation and restoring lung homeostasis.
article.authors: Magalhaes GS, Carvalho-Ribeiro IA, Cardoso LP, Gregorio JF, Neves VH, do Nascimento MD, Sánchez-Ferrer CF, Peiró C, Campagnole-Santos MJ, Dos Santos RAS, Rodrigues-Machado MG.
article.abstract: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) remains one of the leading causes of morbidity and mortality worldwide and still lacks effective disease-modifying therapies. Current pharmacological treatments primarily alleviate symptoms and reduce exacerbations, but have limited ability to prevent progressive lung destruction or promote tissue repair. Increasing evidence indicates that beyond the classical cardiovascular functions of the renin-angiotensin system (RAS), it additionally plays a central role in regulating pulmonary inflammation, oxidative stress, extracellular matrix remodelling, cellular senescence and endogenous repair mechanisms. Experimental studies have shown that both pharmacological inhibition of the ACE/Ang II/AT1 axis and activation of the protective AT2 receptor and ACE2/Ang-(1-7)/Mas pathways attenuate multiple pathological processes involved in COPD progression. In this review, we comprehensively discuss the current preclinical evidence supporting pharmacological manipulation of the RAS in experimental models of pulmonary emphysema, highlighting the anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, anti-fibrotic, pro-resolutive and regenerative mechanisms associated with these therapeutic strategies. We further discuss emerging evidence indicating that activation of protective RAS pathways not only suppresses inflammation, but also promotes tissue repair through modulating autophagy, inflammasome activation, cellular senescence and endogenous regenerative signalling. These findings collectively position protective RAS modulation as a promising disease-modifying strategy for COPD and provide a strong rationale for future translational and clinical studies aimed at restoring pulmonary homeostasis.

article.title: Dissecting the shared genetic architecture of adipose tissue aging and aging-related lipid-metabolic dysfunction: a multivariate genomic analysis.
article.authors: Li M, Yao Y, Zhao Y, Guo Q, Li C, Lv C, Zhang B, Li J, Zhao H.
article.abstract: Adipose tissue aging is increasingly recognized as a systemic process involving altered fat distribution, ectopic lipid deposition, and metabolic dysfunction, yet its shared genetic architecture remains incompletely characterized. In this study, we constructed a latent multivariate genetic phenotype of adipose tissue aging by integrating genome-wide association summary statistics for seven adipose- and metabolism-related traits, including visceral adipose tissue volume, abdominal subcutaneous adipose tissue volume, thigh subcutaneous adipose tissue volume, liver proton density fat fraction, fasting insulin, adiponectin, and leptin. Using Genomic Structural Equation Modelling, we derived a latent phenotype termed mvAdiposeAge and further characterized its genetic and biological relevance through genome-wide association analysis, FUMA-based functional annotation, MAGMA gene-level analysis, transcriptome-wide association analysis, expression fine-mapping, pathway and tissue enrichment analyses, and Mendelian randomization. The Genomic SEM model supported a shared genetic dimension linking adipose distribution, ectopic lipid accumulation, and adipose-related metabolic traits. Genome-wide analysis identified a prominent signal at chromosome 16q12.2, with rs1421085 in the FTO region emerging as the lead variant. MAGMA identified 49 FDR-significant genes, while transcriptome-wide analysis prioritized 11 genes, with FOCUS fine-mapping highlighting expression-mediated signals involving FTO, RPGRIP1L, and AKTIP. Functional enrichment implicated neurotrophin signalling, synaptic organization, cAMP signalling, immune and phagocytic processes, endocrine regulation, and metabolic pathways, with tissue enrichment suggesting prominent brain-region-specific signals. Mendelian randomization further supported positive associations of adiposity-related traits with mvAdiposeAge and an inverse association with cognitive performance. These findings highlight mvAdiposeAge as a latent genetic factor capturing shared genetic variation across adipose-related phenotypes relevant to aging and provide a framework for further investigating their systemic biological associations.

article.title: The transcription factor BCL11A restores differentiation potential to aged oligodendrocyte progenitor cells.
article.authors: Ghosh T, Baror R, Zhao C, Sharma A, Au WH, Lakatos A, Goldman N, Franklin RJM.
article.abstract: In young animals, oligodendrocyte progenitor cells (OPCs) in the CNS efficiently differentiate into myelinating oligodendrocytes (OLs), whereas ageing reduces this capacity, impairing remyelination following demyelinating injury and adaptive myelination involved in learning. To identify factors that restore resilience in aged OPCs, we developed gSWITCH (https://altoslabs.shinyapps.io/gSWITCH/, https://github.com/Tanay-math/gSWITCH), a computational pipeline that captures dynamic gene-expression patterns to identify 'switch' genes during lineage progression and ordered biological transitions, including time-series experiments. gSWITCH identified OPC-characteristic switch genes, which we compared between young and aged OPCs to determine whether their regulation is altered with ageing. This revealed several transcription factors with reduced expression in aged OPCs. Transcription-factor binding-site enrichment highlighted Bcl11a as a potential master-regulator of multiple switch genes. Bcl11a inhibition reduced OPC differentiation into OLs, whereas its overexpression in aged OPCs significantly enhanced OL differentiation without affecting proliferation. In aged mice subjected to demyelination injury in spinal cord white matter, Bcl11a overexpression increased OPC differentiation within lesions. We found that Bcl11a has undergone pervasive purifying selection throughout vertebrate evolution, preserving its amino acid sequence by eliminating deleterious mutations. Our study shows that reversing the age-related decline of this evolutionarily conserved factor in aged OPCs restores their impaired capacity for differentiation.

article.title: Rethinking why "Cognitive dysfunction" predicts some, but not all, transdiagnostic symptom dimensions in older adults: Commentary on Hoy et al. (2026).
article.authors: Grégoire C.
article.venue: Journal of psychopathology and clinical science
article.abstract: Hoy et al. (2026) wrote a brilliant article on the potential association between cognitive dysfunction and psychopathology in aging, characterized by the general p construct and spectra such as internalizing, thought disorders, and externalizing. This commentary proposes that cognitive dysfunction may lack specificity when investigating cognition in aging. I suggest that future research should further decompose cognitive dysfunction into subdomains, one of which is cognitive control processes, as they depend on frontal-related networks, which are among the first to decline with age. article.title: From aspiration to accountability: Human rights-based care and support for older persons at the UN Convention moment.
article.authors: Rabheru K, Jeste DV, Reynolds CF.
article.abstract: The emerging United Nations process toward a legally binding instrument on the human rights of older persons is not only a legal milestone; it is an accountability test for geriatric psychiatry, brain health, dementia care, mental health services, long-term care, community care, palliative care, digital systems, and implementation science. The legal protection gap has been documented through the Madrid International Plan of Action on Ageing, the Open-ended Working Group on Ageing, OHCHR analyses, Independent Expert reports, and legal scholarship. As the Human Rights Council moves this work into an Intergovernmental Working Group to elaborate a legally binding instrument, geriatric psychiatry and allied fields have a responsibility to contribute clinical, ethical, scientific, and implementation expertise. This essay argues that the future Convention should be understood not only as a legal text but as an opportunity to make dignity, agency, legal capacity, supported decision-making, brain health, mental health, care, support, participation, and freedom from discrimination real in everyday systems. Ageism causes measurable health harms; mentalism and ableism compound exclusion; dementia and cognitive impairment can trigger diagnosis-based loss of voice and agency; grief, loneliness, coercion, and institutionalization reveal failures of supportive care; and artificial intelligence can deepen or mitigate ageism, digital exclusion, and epistemic injustice. Strengths-based approaches emphasizing wisdom, resilience, community capacity, and learning health systems offer a way forward. Building on the WPA-SOAP White Paper, Leiden Summary Statement, and WHO/OHCHR tools, this essay offers an implementation-focused bridge from principle to practice and from aspiration to accountability.

article.title: Medicalising the Human Cell Atlas for musculoskeletal disease: towards a translational roadmap.
article.authors: Hourston GJM, To K, Teichmann SA, Snelling S, McCaskie A, Buckley CD.
article.abstract: The Human Cell Atlas (HCA) has fundamentally changed the way biologists describe human tissues. However, its greatest promise for musculoskeletal (MSK) practitioners lies ahead: to convert cellular maps into clinically actionable knowledge. MSK diseases are common, heterogeneous, and often insufficiently stratified by current diagnostic labels. The same label, such as rheumatoid arthritis, can conceal distinct cellular mechanisms, tissue niches, and therapeutic vulnerabilities. Conversely, apparently different disorders such as tendinopathy or fibrotic capsulitis can share convergent stromal, immune, vascular, or neuronal programmes. A MSK-HCA therefore should not be conceived as a passive reference catalogue. It should be 'medicalised': designed from the outset to connect tissue atlases with clinical phenotypes, imaging, biospecimens, genetic risk, biomarkers, perturbation experiments, and interventional trials. In this review, we describe how single-cell, single-nucleus, spatial, and multiomic approaches are beginning to map MSK tissues from development to ageing and from health to disease. We highlight examples in embryonic skeletal development, bone marrow, muscle ageing, osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, tendon disease, and inflammatory fibrosis and show how these data can reframe disease taxonomy around pathogenic cell states rather than organ-level labels alone. We propose a translational roadmap in which atlases define healthy reference coordinates, identify disease-enriched cell states, nominate biomarkers and therapeutic targets, and then learn from clinical trial outcomes. For clinicians, the MSK-HCA offers a route to mechanism-led diagnosis and patient stratification; for scientists, it provides a shared coordinate system for testing how genes, cells, and tissue microenvironments generate disease. Medicalising the HCA could make cellular medicine a practical foundation for precision rheumatology and regenerative MSK therapy.

article.title: UV-aged tire wear particles and their leachates jointly enhance antibiotic resistance gene dissemination.
article.authors: Liu X, Xu X, Yin M, Gao Y, Xin Y, Ahmad S.
article.abstract: Tire wear particles (TWPs) represent a major source of environmental microplastics, yet how ultraviolet (UV) aging influences their effects on the transfer of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) remains unclear. Here, the promoting effects and underlying mechanisms of UV-aged TWPs and their leachate on bacterial conjugative transfer were investigated. Aging significantly increased the specific surface area and oxygen-containing functional groups of TWPs, and promoted the release of heavy metal ions and organic additives into leachate. In conjugation assays, 60-day-aged TWPs enhanced the transfer frequency of plasmid RP4 by 15.3-fold; whereas the corresponding leachate alone caused a 62.0-fold increase. Mechanistically, aged TWPs acted primarily as a physical oxidative stressor, promoting conjugative transfer through reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation and disruption of cell membrane integrity. Aged leachate acted mainly as a chemical signaling stressor, inducing biofilm formation and collective behavioral responses that created a protective microenvironment conducive to plasmid exchange, although they also contributed to oxidative stress. Combined exposure further produced a response greater than that of either pathway alone, establishing a physicochemical dual-stress framework that drives ARGs transfer. Collectively, these findings suggest that environmental aging critically shapes the ecological risks of microplastics, positioning aged TWPs as potential vectors for ARGs dissemination and underscoring the need to consider both particle-associated and leachate-mediated pathways in future risk assessments.

article.title: Pathology of the intervertebral disks and other spinal lesions in 31 aging inbred mouse strains.
article.authors: Sundberg JP, Schofield PN, Garcia VN, Sundberg BA, Ackert-Bicknell CL, Ward JM.
article.abstract: In a large-scale aging study of 31 inbred strains of mice, a variety of age-related lesions arose in and around the spine (vertebrae, spinal cord, and adjacent connective and muscle tissues), including lesions of intervertebral disks, vertebrae, muscles, soft tissues, nerves, ganglia, and spinal cord that were either sporadic or strain-specific. In most cases, the mice did not present with obvious clinical signs, as many lesions were mild. Lesions included herniated or displaced intervertebral disk fragments, which appeared to be sporadic in most strains but were common in others. Fibro-osseous lesions of bones were a systemic disease in female mice with no effect on disk disease. Rhabdomyosarcomas were common in A/J mice surrounding the vertebrae but also invaded into the spinal canal, sometimes almost transecting the cord. Lymphomas affected all AKR/J mice, sometimes infiltrating into the spinal canal. Muscular dystrophy of the musculature surrounding the spine, due to mutations in the dysferlin ( Dysf ) gene, was common in A/J and SJL/J mice. Coccygeal hemivertebra was a novel strain-specific lesion only in PL/J mice. Sporadic lesions in and around the spine included hemangiosarcomas, lymphomas (both enlarged lymph nodes and invading in and around the vertebrae), schwannomas, histiocytic sarcomas, poorly differentiated sarcomas, and epidermoid/dermoid cysts. Since these strains have all been sequenced and annotated, polymorphisms in genes known to affect the pathogenesis of some of these lesions will be reported in other publications.

article.title: Self-adaptive nanophotonic metasurfaces enabling digital twins: toward continuous personalized healthcare in aging and disability.
article.authors: Taha BA, Addie AJ, Ibnaouf K, Jabir MS, Mahmood OT, Apsari R, Arsad N.
article.abstract: Continuous physiological monitoring is a prerequisite in medicine that enables early disease detection, long-term health monitoring, and individualized therapeutic interventions. Although wearable optical biosensors have evolved significantly, their long-term clinical deployment remains limited by mechanical degradation, signal drift, biofouling, energy constraints, and poor integration with intelligent healthcare infrastructure. These issues are especially acute in the aged and disabled, when constant, dependable, and tailored monitoring is critical for proactive disease treatment. As a result, next-generation sensing technologies must progress beyond passive data collection toward self-adaptive systems capable of maintaining analytical accuracy while supporting patient-specific clinical interpretation and clinician-supervised decision-making. This perspective presents an overview of self-adaptive nanophotonic metasurfaces as the sensing foundation for Living Digital Twins (LDTs) in personalized healthcare. To create an intelligent sensing ecosystem, the proposed framework combines flexible plasmonic, localized surface plasmon resonance (LSPR), surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS), artificial intelligence, internet of nano things (IoNT) connectivity, and individualized digital twin analytics. The proposed framework combines continuous multimodal biomarker sensing with patient-specific physiological modelling to support longitudinal updating of digital representations. Edge intelligence enables low-latency signal processing, while adaptive analytics may improve sensing stability, calibration, and patient-specific interpretation. The integration of adaptive nanophotonic sensing with digital twins therefore represents a prospective approach for supporting early identification of physiological deterioration, individualized risk assessment, and clinician-supervised treatment planning in aging and disabled populations.

article.title: Fatty acid synthesis system in Glaucophyta: Further evidence for the lack of chloroplast fatty acid synthesis in glaucophyte algae
article.authors: Sato N, Awai K.
article.abstract: Abstract We previously showed that the chloroplast of the glaucophyte Cyanophora paradoxa does not have fatty acid synthesis activity, based on both experimental and bioinformatic analyses. The present study was intended to extend the bioinformatic analysis to a wider range of Glaucophyta, using published genomic data. The results confirmed that the four species of Glaucophyta analyzed do not have prokaryotic acetyl-CoA carboxylase, which is found in the chloroplasts of Rhodophyta and Viridiplantae. Only the eukaryotic type of acetyl-CoA carboxylase was identified. Some components of prokaryotic fatty acid synthase (FAS II), such as acyl carrier protein (ACP), 2-oxoacyl ACP synthase (KAS I/II), and FabD, were detected in the glaucophytes, but other components especially KAS III were not detected. In contrast, the eukaryotic fatty acid synthase (FAS I) was found in Gloeochaete as well as Cyanophora. Although the genome data is still to be amended, the available evidence suggests that the lack of fatty acid synthesis in the chloroplast is a trait of not just Cyanophora but also shared by the phylum Glaucophyta. The relationship between photosynthesis and fatty acid synthesis is discussed with special attention to the origin of chloroplasts.

article.title: Coordinated adipose–liver metabolic remodelling reveals sex-specific peripheral adaptations during amyotrophic lateral sclerosis progression in TDP-43A315T mice
article.authors: Benito-Casado C, Ferrer-Donato Á, Barroso-García G, Domínguez-Vías G, Domínguez-Rubio R, Povedano M, Fernandez-Martos CM.
article.abstract: Abstract Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is increasingly recognised as a systemic disorder associated with metabolic dysfunction, although the contribution of peripheral metabolic organs and sex-dependent responses remains unclear. We investigated metabolic remodelling across white adipose tissue (WAT), brown adipose tissue (BAT) and liver, during disease progression in the TDP-43 A315T mouse model and assessed its relevance in ALS patients. Lipidomic profiling was performed in WAT from male mice, while metabolic and endocrine pathways were evaluated by RT-qPCR in BAT and liver from male and female mice. Plasma cholesterol levels were determined in ALS patients at diagnosis. The results revealed that WAT exhibited marked alterations that were detectable at the asymptomatic stage and persisted throughout disease progression. Lipid remodelling was characterised by coordinated changes affecting lipid classes, with cardiolipins predominating at early stages and triacylglycerols becoming increasingly altered as disease progressed. BAT displayed predominantly late-stage transcriptional changes in male mice, characterised by increased expression of genes associated with brown adipocyte identity, metabolic regulation and leptin signalling. Female mice developed a distinct hepatic transcriptional signature characterised by increased expression of genes associated with fatty acid uptake and utilisation, together with reduced expression of genes involved in de novo lipogenesis. Furthermore, ALS patients revealed sex-associated differences in circulating cholesterol levels at diagnosis. Overall, ALS progression is associated with extensive metabolic remodelling in peripheral tissues, with marked tissue-specific and sex-dependent responses. These findings identify peripheral metabolism as a potential contributor to disease heterogeneity and highlight metabolic pathways as promising sources of translational biomarkers and therapeutic targets.

article.title: APOE-Driven Lipid Metabolic Reprogramming Promotes Gastric Cancer Growth and Chemoresistance
article.authors: Dou X, Fu C, Wang Y, Gong Z, Liu Y, Qin S.
article.abstract: Abstract Background Apolipoprotein E (APOE) plays critical role in lipid metabolism but its function in chemoresistance of gastric cancer (GC) remains unclear. This study investigated the clinical significance of APOE in GC progression and elucidated its mechanistic role in regulating lipid metabolism and chemotherapy resistance. Methods APOE expression was analyzed in 4 published GEO datasets (GSE29272, GSE54129, GSE103236, GSE118916) and validated by immunohistochemistry (IHC) in GC tissue microarrays. Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) and correlation analyses were performed to identify lipid metabolism pathways associated with APOE . In vitro, APOE was silenced by siRNA in AGS and HGC-27 cells. Western blotting assessed the PI3K/AKT/mTOR-SREBP1-FASN signaling cascade. Cholesterol quantification, CCK-8 proliferation assay, flow cytometry apoptosis assay, and 5-fluorouracil (5-Fu) sensitivity assay were performed. Results APOE expression was significantly upregulated across 4 GC datasets ( P P P = 0.0014). GSEA revealed enrichment of lipid metabolism pathways (fatty acid, glycerophospholipid, and glycerolipid metabolism) in APOE -high tumors. APOE expression was positively correlated with SREBF1 and FASN across datasets, with IHC confirming SREBP1 and FASN co-upregulation and significant positive correlations with APOE H-score (SREBP1: r = 0.3117, P P APOE knockdown suppressed p-AKT, p-mTOR, SREBP1, and FASN, and reduced intracellular cholesterol ( P P

article.title: Engineering Nutrient-Stress Regimes for Microalgal Biodiesel Production: Biomass–Lipid Trade-Offs, Fatty-Acid Remodeling and Fuel-Quality Performance in Pediastrum duplex
article.authors: Adekanmi AA, Garuba EO, Onilude AA.
article.abstract: Abstract Rational manipulation of cultivation conditions is central to engineering microalgal processes that reconcile biomass production, lipid accumulation and biodiesel quality. However, nutrient-stress studies frequently optimise individual biological responses without resolving how cultivation variables propagate through biomass–lipid partitioning, fatty-acid composition and downstream fuel properties. This study developed an integrated bioprocess framework for evaluating nitrogen, phosphate, iron and salinity stress as controllable cultivation variables for biodiesel production from Pediastrum duplex . Biomass concentration and lipid accumulation were experimentally quantified, fatty acid methyl esters (FAMEs) were characterised by gas chromatography, and biodiesel properties were estimated from experimentally determined FAME profiles using established empirical models. Treatment effects and process-response relationships were evaluated using ANOVA, effect-size analysis, Pearson correlation, principal component analysis and hierarchical cluster analysis. Nitrogen limitation produced the highest lipid content (59.75%) but reduced biomass formation, demonstrating a pronounced biomass–lipid production trade-off. Iron limitation generated favourable combination of saturated (48.10%) and monounsaturated (49.20%) fatty acids, whereas salinity stress produced highest predicted cetane number (63.85) and flash point (225 °C). Phosphate limitation increased polyunsaturated fatty acids to 20.50%, demonstrating that cultivation conditions influenced not only lipid accumulation but also downstream fuel-quality characteristics. Multivariate analysis discriminated nutrient-specific process-response regimes and supported integrated pathway linking nutrient availability, carbon allocation, lipid accumulation, FAME remodeling and predicted biodiesel performance. The findings demonstrate that nutrient management can function as bioprocess-engineering strategy for tuning the quantity and compositional quality of lipid feedstock and provide basis for designing staged cultivation strategies that balance biomass production, lipid accumulation and biodiesel quality.

article.title: Competitive inhibition of the Nipah virus matrix protein by conivaptan: from binding pocket dynamics to protein-membrane interactions.
article.authors: Kar AP, Maity A, Bahadur RP.
article.abstract: The recurrent outbreaks of Nipah virus since its first emergence have intensified efforts to identify effective antiviral therapeutics. The matrix protein is a key structural protein that maintains virion architecture and plays a crucial role in anchoring the virus to the host plasma membrane. Binding of phosphatidylinositol-4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) to the matrix protein promotes conformational changes that facilitate membrane association and initiate viral assembly. Therefore, an effective small-molecule inhibitor should not only compete with PIP2 for binding to the Nipah virus matrix protein (NiVM) but also disrupt its interaction with the host membrane. Using virtual screening of FDA-approved drugs combined with ensemble docking, we identified conivaptan as a potential inhibitor of the Nipah virus matrix protein. The multivalent interactions of conivaptan establish stable binding within the PIP2-binding pocket while simultaneously rewiring protein-membrane interactions. In the presence of PIP2, NiVM anchors to the membrane through multiple charged residues, resulting in pronounced local bilayer deformation, an early signature of membrane remodeling. In contrast, conivaptan binding weakens membrane anchoring and preserves a more ordered and compact bilayer, thereby suppressing membrane deformation. Together, these findings identify conivaptan as a promising repurposable inhibitor of the Nipah virus matrix protein and provide a mechanistic framework for targeting virus-membrane interactions during viral assembly.

article.title: Does Exposure to Glyphosate-Based Herbicide Affect the Aerobic Metabolism, Oxidative Stress and Fatty Acid Profile of Pacú (Piaractus mesopotamicus)?
article.authors: Bonifacio AF, Marón CF, Ballesteros ML, Labuckas D, Labaque MC, Zambrano M, Filippi I, Hued AC.
article.venue: Archives of environmental contamination and toxicology
article.abstract: Glyphosate in southern South America is considered a pseudopersistent contaminant. Given Roundup ® 's multiple effects on health, reproduction, and overall species well-being worldwide, it is imperative to evaluate its effects on exposed biota. We evaluated the effects of two concentrations of Roundup Control Max ® (0.7 mg/L and 7 mg/L; the former being environmentally relevant) over 14 days of exposure on aerobic metabolism, oxidative stress, and fatty acid profiles in the economically relevant fish species Piaractus mesopotamicus, and compared them with a control experiment. The results showed no significant variation in basal or post-exercise metabolism but revealed significant differences in the delta between these parameters. Oxidative stress was elevated in the brains of exposed individuals but not in the liver. Lipid profiles did not vary significantly among individuals exposed to the herbicide. Our findings highlight this formulation's influence on a key metabolic parameter and oxidative stress. It also advances the biological and nutritional characterization of P. mesopotamicus. Further studies should continue to evaluate the effects of chronic herbicide exposure on the aerobic metabolism of this and other species.

article.title: Citalopram modulates hypothalamic appetite-related signalling and hepatic lipid metabolism in rainbow trout.
article.authors: Blanco AM, Bertucci JI, Paladea-Rojo R, Fernández-Maestú C, Bellas J, Soengas JL.
article.venue: Comparative biochemistry and physiology. Toxicology & pharmacology : CBP
article.abstract: Citalopram, a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor prescribed for depression in humans, is increasingly detected in freshwater ecosystems alongside other contaminants of emerging concern, posing risks to non-target species. Here, we investigated the impact of citalopram on appetite regulation and hepatic energy metabolism in rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss) using two exposure routes: chronic dietary administration (0.01 and 0.02 μg/g feed for 10 days) and acute intraperitoneal injection (10 μg/g bw). Plasma metabolite (glucose, lactate, triglyceride, and non-esterified fatty acids-NEFAs-) levels, mRNA abundance of appetite-regulating factors in hypothalamus and gastrointestinal tract, and hepatic enzyme activities and mRNA abundance related to glucose and lipid metabolism were assessed. Both exposure routes upregulated hypothalamic npy (neuropeptide Y) mRNA abundance-a potent orexigenic factor-, while intraperitoneal injection additionally downregulated anorexigenic pomca1 (pro-opiomelanocortin), suggesting an orexigenic nature of citalopram, though with divergent modulation of energy sensors and transcription factors (prkaa2-AMP-activated protein kinase α2, Ampkα2-, mtor-mechanistic target of rapamycin-, and creb1-cAMP response element-binding protein-). Dietary exposure increased hepatic ATP-citrate lyase (Acly) mRNA and activity, whereas intraperitoneal administration upregulated fasn (fatty acid synthase) but downregulated cpt1b (carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1) and pklr (pyruvate kinase, Pk) levels, favoring lipogenesis over fatty acid oxidation. Dietary citalopram did not affect plasma metabolites, whereas intraperitoneal injection induced hyperglycemia and reduced NEFAs. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that citalopram exposure subtly reshapes neuroendocrine appetite regulation and hepatic lipid metabolism in rainbow trout in a route-dependent manner. These alterations may have ecological implications for fish populations in polluted habitats.

article.title: The self-sufficient Aspergillus fumigatus Δ9-fatty acid desaturase SdeA requires a fused cytochrome b5 domain and hinge-dependent self-association for virulence
article.authors: Campanella, J. E. M.; Filho, G. Y.; Fabri, J. H. T. M.; Bueno, N. F.; Barbugli, P. A.; Cunha, A. F. d.; Delbaje, E.; Talachia Rosa, L.; Malavazi, I.
article.abstract: Fungal {Delta}9-fatty acid desaturases are self-sufficient enzymes in which the electron-donating cytochrome b5 (Cytb5) module is fused to the catalytic core, yet whether this covalent linkage is architecturally required has remained untested. Here we show that in the human pathogen Aspergillus fumigatus the Cytb5 module of the {Delta}9-desaturase SdeA must act in cis, within a self-associated complex organized by a hinge segment. AlphaFold3 modeling predicts a dimer in which the Cytb5 domain of one protomer approaches the other's di-iron center at a distance compatible with electron tunneling, and reciprocal co-immunoprecipitation shows that full-length SdeA self-associates in vivo. The recombinant Cytb5 module displays the spectral signatures of a genuine heme-binding redox domain. Nevertheless, deleting the Cytb5 domain, substituting its heme-coordinating histidines, or removing the 25-residue hinge each abolishes growth and virulence in Galleria mellonella without disrupting endoplasmic reticulum targeting, and a detached Cytb5-containing segment does not restore function. Hinge deletion abolishes stable SdeA self-association, identifying this segment as a structural organizer of the catalytically competent complex. Finally, we find no evidence that the sdeB locus provides a backup {Delta}9-desaturase. These results define the architectural requirements of a self-sufficient fungal desaturase and identify vulnerabilities absent from the human {Delta}9-desaturase for antifungal targeting.

article.title: Structural Determinants of the Energetic Barrier of Phospholipid Flip-Flop
article.authors: Vuorte, M. I.; Pandey, U.; Javanainen, M.
article.abstract: Spontaneous phospholipid flip-flop sets the background against which flippases, floppases, and scramblases create and dissipate membrane asymmetry. How the associated free-energy barrier depends on lipid chemistry and on the surrounding membrane remains unclear, because experiments are few and contradictory and previous simulations covered only a small part of the lipidome. Here, we calculate Martini 3 flip-flop free-energy barriers for over 700 membrane--lipid combinations, the largest such dataset to our knowledge. A systematic single component bilayer panel of five headgroups, three linkages, and 35 tail families is complemented by mixed bilayers, from binary mixtures to organelle-inspired compositions, that place the same lipid in different membranes and thus separate the effects of lipid chemistry and the membrane environment. In single component bilayers, the barrier rises with tighter tail packing and depends strongly on headgroup and tail unsaturation but only weakly on linkage. Moving a lipid into a mixed bilayer shifts its barrier as much as most headgroup substitutions do, and the shift follows the change in local tail order. Within a shared membrane, headgroup differences are mostly smaller than between single component bilayers, so part of a headgroup effect arises from the membrane that the lipid forms. A Bayesian model combining chemical descriptors with local membrane structure predicts barriers for withheld lipid families and membranes with cross-validated errors of 2.8 and 3.8 kJ/mol. The calculated trends agree qualitatively with native-lipid vesicle experiments, although Martini 3 underestimates the barrier differences between lipids, gives lower barriers than atomistic models, and overstates the effect of cholesterol.

article.title: Sustainable Feeding Strategies for Pork Quality and Healthier Traditional Products
article.authors: Leite A, Vasconcelos L, Teixeira A, Rodrigues S.
article.venue: 预印本平台（数据库未注明）
article.abstract: The growing demand for healthier and more sustainable meat products has encouraged the devel-opment of alternative feeding strategies that improve resource efficiency while potentially enhancing meat quality. Among these strategies, the incorporation of agro-industrial by-products into pig diets represents a promising approach to promoting circular economy principles and reducing dependence on conventional feed ingredients. This review critically examines the effects of sustainable feeding strategies, particularly those involving olive cake, grape pomace, tomato pomace, and citrus-derived by-products, on pork quality and their potential contribution to the development of healthier tradi-tional meat products. Available evidence indicates that these ingredients can be incorporated into pig diets at appropriate inclusion levels without substantially compromising animal performance, carcass characteristics, or the physicochemical and sensory properties of pork. Furthermore, certain dietary interventions may modify fatty acid composition, enhance antioxidant status, and improve oxidative stability, although responses depend on the composition of the by-product, dietary inclu-sion level, and experimental conditions. Importantly, some diet-induced modifications, particularly those affecting lipid composition, may persist after processing into traditional meat products, in-cluding dry-cured products. Nevertheless, the limited number of studies evaluating the entire pro-duction chain and the variability in reported results highlight the need for further research. An in-tegrated feed-to-food approach, combining nutritional, technological, sensory, environmental, and economic assessments, is essential to determine the practical applicability of these strategies. Over-all, sustainable feeding strategies offer opportunities to improve the nutritional characteristics of pork and traditional meat products while promoting resource efficiency and preserving their tech-nological quality, sensory acceptance, and cultural identity.

article.title: Therapeutic Efficacy of Indigenous Ogi Lactiplantibacillus Strains in Antibiotic-Induced Gut Dysbiosis
article.authors: Ojeniyi OJ.
article.abstract: Abstract Purpose: Broad-spectrum antibiotic administration disrupts intestinal eubiosis, leading to mucosal tissue damage, systemic inflammation, and metabolic dysregulation. This study evaluated the in vitro probiotic traits and therapeutic efficacy of indigenous Lactiplantibacillus strains isolated from 'ogi' (Lacticaseibacillus casei PJ1, Lacticaseibacillus paracasei PJ3, and Lactiplantibacillus plantarum PC1) in Wistar rat models of antibiotic-induced gut dysbiosis. Methods: In vitro auto-aggregation, co-aggregation, and gastric acid tolerance (pH 1–7) were assessed spectrophotometrically. Rats with antibiotic-induced dysbiosis were treated with single or combined probiotic regimens over 14 days. Primary outcomes measured included intestinal histopathology, tissue and serum tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) levels, body weight progression, and serum lipid profiles (Total Glycerides, LDL, HDL, Total Cholesterol). Results: All isolates demonstrated high auto-aggregation (>98%) and co-aggregation (>96%), alongside robust survival at pH 1 and pH 3. In vivo, probiotic administration significantly attenuated dysbiosis-induced intestinal mucosal lesions, preventing muscular wall degeneration and necrosis. Probiotic treatment markedly reduced intestinal and serum TNF-α concentrations (P Conclusion: Indigenous Lactiplantibacillus isolates from ogi demonstrate potent anti-inflammatory, histoprotective, and hypolipidemic properties, confirming their potential as effective biotherapeutic agents for restoring intestinal health.

article.title: GC-MS-based screening of novel biomarkers in the plasma of Aflatoxin B1-treated mouse model.
article.authors: Bhardwaj N, Babu R, Singh A.
article.venue: European journal of mass spectrometry (Chichester, England)
article.abstract: The current work investigates the novel biomarkers in the plasma of Aflatoxin B1 (AFB1)-treated mouse model. Plasma samples isolated from AFB1-treated mice (0.3 mg/kg body weight orally three times a week for four weeks) were derivatized with BSTFA with 1% TMCS for silylation. The samples were examined using gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS), and metabolites were identified by comparing the peaks in the NIST14, NIST14s, PMW_TOX2, and WILEY8 library databases available in GCMS Lab Solution software. A total of 121 peaks (33 hydrocarbons, 26 fatty acyls, 17 prenol lipids and glycerophospholipids, 8 organooxygen and oxoanionic, 9 benzene derivatives, and 28 mixed compounds) were identified in the plasma. A total of 17 compounds (13 upregulated and 4 downregulated) belonging to hydrocarbons and fatty acyls showed significant metabolic perturbations. The PCA and PLS-DA models also suggest a perfect discrimination between the metabolites in the plasma of AFB1-treated mice. The PLS-DA-VIP plot identifies the nine compounds in plasma with the highest VIP score (decane, hexatriacontane, octane, tridecane, 3-methyl heptane, octadecanoic acid, nonane, hexane, and ctricontane). AFB1 administration modulates linoleic acid metabolism, sulfur metabolism, unsaturated fatty acid biosynthesis, xenobiotic metabolism by cytochrome P450, and fatty acid biosynthesis pathways in the plasma. Undecane, octadecane, linoleic acid, and hexatriacontane have the highest AUC values that can be used for diagnostic purposes.

article.title: Tissue-Specific Regulation of Postprandial Non-Esterified Fatty Acid Metabolism in individuals with prediabetes
article.authors: Le Roux, E.; Hogan-Lamarre, S.; Lepitre, M.; Frisch, F.; Dumont, L.; Fortin, M.; Richard, G.; Noll, C.; Sarrhini, O.; Mampuya, W.; Phoenix, S.; Bouffard, L.; Guerin, B.; Turcotte, E.; Rutters, F.; Raina, P.; Despres, J.-P.; Hoeks, J.; Schrauwen, P.; Carpentier, A. C.; Blondin, D. P.
article.abstract: After a meal, it is generally assumed that tissue non-esterified fatty acids (NEFA) uptake falls in proportion of the reduction of systemic NEFA appearance from insulin-mediated suppression of adipose tissue lipolysis. Here, we combined dynamic [11C]palmitate PET/CT, stable isotope tracers, and MRI to measure palmitate uptake, oxidation, and esterification in the heart, liver, skeletal muscle, and subcutaneous and visceral adipose tissue, in the fasted state and 60min after a mixed meal in individuals with prediabetes. Net palmitate uptake decreased in all tissues, but most tissues extracted a larger fraction of circulating palmitate after the meal. The intracellular fate of palmitate differed between organs. The heart shifted toward oxidation, the liver toward esterification, maintaining VLDL-palmitate release, and this shift was smaller in individuals with more liver fat. Both adipose depots increased fractional esterification, and visceral fat almost stopped releasing palmitate. Thus, plasma NEFA overestimates the postprandial reduction in lean tissue NEFA exposure.

article.title: Evaluating associations of oxylipin metabolites and fatty acids with incident and prevalent type 2 diabetes in the Hispanic Community Health Study/Study of Latinos (HCHS/SOL).
article.authors: Downie CG, Highland HM, Howard AG, Alotaibi M, Elfassy T, Cordero C, Below JE, Carnethon M, Cheng S, Daviglus M, Garcia-Bedoya O, Kaplan R, Khambaty T, Li Y, Lilly AG, Lin DY, Long T, Penedo FJ, Petty LE, Thyagarajan B, Tien HC, Jain M, Welch BM, North KE, Avery CL.
article.abstract: Background Inflammation is a common pathological feature underlying type 2 diabetes (T2D) risk and progression. Determining the roles of fatty acids and bioactive lipid oxylipin inflammatory mediators could inform T2D preventative efforts and therapeutic targets. Methods Leveraging the Hispanic Community Health Study/Study of Latinos (HCHS/SOL), we evaluated cross-sectional and prospective associations of 81 oxylipins and polyunsaturated, monounsaturated, and saturated fatty acids with T2D. We assessed whether fatty acid levels differed at visit 2 by visit 1-prevalent T2D status and prioritized likely causal metabolites using Bayesian model averaging Mendelian randomization (MR-BMA). Results Fifty-four fatty acids and oxylipins were associated with prevalent T2D at visit 1 (15,138 participants; 2,962 T2D cases), four of which (adrenic, dihomo-gamma-linolenic, tricosanoic, and lignoceric acids) were also associated with incident T2D by visit 2 (8,548 participants; 1,376 T2D events), though effects were attenuated for adrenic and dihomo-gamma-linolenic acids upon further adjustment for impaired glucose tolerance. Sixteen out of 28 fatty acids were significantly different at visit 2 between those with and without prevalent T2D at visit 1 (9,115 participants; 2,151 T2D cases), holding visit 1-measured fatty acid levels constant. MR-BMA prioritized one diHETrE oxylipin as a likely causal risk factor for T2D. Conclusions Fatty acids and oxylipins showed complex patterns of association with T2D, including more associations likely reflecting overt disease processes in prevalent T2D, than incident risk-enhancing associations.

article.title: Pinto bean supplementation improves maternal metabolic outcomes in a high-fat diet-induced obesity model of pregnancy.
article.authors: Chandrashekar R, Olawale F, Mulakala BK, Read QD, Sutton B, Lewis S, Cerney A, Fox R, LeRoith T, Gill KK, Nanduri B, Ruebel ML, Lucas E, Yeruva L.
article.abstract: Background Maternal obesity is linked to dysregulated lipid metabolism, inflammation, and altered gut microbiota, which together can compromise placental function and fetal development. Pinto beans (PB), a fiber and polyphenol rich legume, may mitigate metabolic dysfunction during pregnancy. Methods Female C57BL/6 mice (n=20/group) were fed a control diet (CON) or high fat diet (HFD) for six weeks, randomized (n=10/group) to continue with or without 10% PB for an additional six weeks before and during pregnancy. Dams were euthanized at gestational day (GD) 17-17.5 and maternal and fetal tissues were collected. Body composition, serum lipids, maternal hepatic gene and protein expression, gut microbiota composition, placental morphology, and fetal hepatic and placental gene expression were assessed. Generalized linear and mixed models (dams as the experimental unit) approach was used for analyses. Results HFD increased % fat mass (26% vs 19%) and decreased %lean mass (74% vs 81%; both p Conclusion PB supplementation reduced serum cholesterol and triglycerides in HFD-fed dams, reduced hepatic lipogenic gene expression, and greater gut microbial richness. Placental and fetal differences were modest and sex- and diet-dependent, affecting placental necrosis.

article.title: Polygenic risk and genomic signals in premature coronary artery disease
article.authors: Laird, C.; Xing, D. G.; Abrar, M.; Sinha, S.; Dewiit, A.; White, C.; Modi, K.; Bhuiyan, M. S.; Yurdagul, A.; Kevil, C. G.; Orr, A. W.; Rom, O.; Conrad, S.; Bhuiyan, M. A. N.
article.abstract: Background: Premature coronary artery disease (pCAD) is a distinct presentation of CAD. Using the All of Us (AoU) Research Program data, we compared pCAD with later-onset CAD across cardiometabolic, polygenic, and genome-wide domains. Methods: We conducted a retrospective, cross-sectional case-case analysis of All of Us Research Program (AoU) participants with established CAD. pCAD was defined as first CAD event before age 55 years in males and before age 65 in females; later-onset CAD was defined as the first CAD event at or after age threshold. Pre-index cardiometabolic measures were extracted from electronic health records and modelled with logistic regression. Using 607,719 variants, a CAD polygenic risk score (PRS) was constructed using published summary statistics and short-read whole-genome sequencing data (srWGS). Results were standardized within self-reported race groups, and evaluated overall, by race, and with a PRS x race interaction. A case-case genome-wide association study (GWAS) compared pCAD with later-onset CAD. Results: The CAD cohort included 49,919 participants, including 18,455 with pCAD and 31,464 with later-onset CAD. Participants with pCAD had higher BMI, LDL cholesterol and diastolic blood pressure, and lower HDL cholesterol, serum calcium, and systolic blood pressure. Higher BMI and LDL cholesterol were positively associated with higher odds of pCAD, whereas higher HDL cholesterol, systolic blood pressure, and serum calcium were inversely associated. PRS was associated with greater odds of pCAD in the genomic models (OR per 1-SD higher PRS, 1.14; 95% CI, 1.12?1.17; P<0.001). Analyses stratified by race showed PRS association was present among White participants but was not observed among Black participants. In the case-case GWAS, one variant reached genome-wide significance at 2q24.3 (rs13383835; OR=1.20; 95% CI, 1.13-1.27; P=5.8x10-9). A total of 137 variants met an exploratory threshold of P<1x10-5. Conclusions: Premature onset of CAD is characterized by a distinct cardiometabolic profile driven by modifiable risk factors, greater polygenic burden, and genomic signals associated with earlier disease timing. A European-derived PRS did not transfer to Black participants, who were overrepresented in pCAD. Together, these findings support pCAD as a clinically and genetically distinct presentation of CAD and highlight the need for ancestry-specific validation of genomic risk tools in diverse cohorts.

article.title: Octyl gallate attenuates atherosclerosis by modulating PPARγ-associated cholesterol homeostasis and enhancing NRF2-NQO1 antioxidant defence.
article.authors: Hua J, Yue X, Wu C, Wang J.
article.abstract: Atherosclerosis (AS) is a vascular disease driven by dysregulated lipid metabolism, oxidative stress, and chronic inflammation. This study investigated the anti-atherosclerotic potential of octyl gallate (OG), a gallic acid derivative with anti-inflammatory and metabolic regulatory properties. In vitro , OG (20-50 μM) significantly attenuated oxidised low-density lipoprotein (ox-LDL)-induced lipid accumulation in THP-1-derived macrophages. This effect was accompanied by increased expression of the cholesterol efflux-related genes ABCA1 and ABCG1 , whereas OG had only limited effects on CD36 and SRA expression. In vivo , oral administration of OG (25 or 50 mg kg -1 ) for 3 months reduced atherosclerotic lesion formation in the aortic arch, whole aorta and aortic root of high-fat diet-fed Apoe -/- mice. OG also improved serum lipid profiles by reducing low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) and total cholesterol levels, increasing high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C) levels. In addition, OG decreased IL-1β and TNF-α expression in the aortic root. Network pharmacology, molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations identified PPARγ as a potential molecular target of OG. Further experiments demonstrated that OG enhanced the expression of PPARγ, LXRα, ABCA1, and ABCG1 in ox-LDL-treated macrophages. Moreover, OG suppressed inflammatory responses and reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation while activating the NRF2-NQO11 antioxidant system and promoting NRF2 nuclear translocation. Collectively, these findings suggest that OG may exert anti-atherosclerotic effects by coordinating macrophage lipid metabolism, redox homeostasis, and inflammatory responses through the PPARγ-LXRα-ABCA1/ABCG1 axis and the NRF2-NQO1 antioxidant pathway, respectively. These results provide experimental evidence supporting the potential of OG as a candidate compound for the prevention and treatment of AS.

article.title: Chronic progressive demyelination induces a microglial state with lysosomal dysfunction.
article.authors: Berghoff SA, Spieth L, Vitale S, Schlaphoff L, Zirngibl M, Junker N, Dean AC, Liu L, Damkou A, Roth S, Hurler CA, Hosang L, Perez Anderson K, Besson-Girard S, Reich M, Feiten A, Huber L, Müller C, Kislinger G, Dinkel L, Nkeh YB, Groh J, Williams A, Liesz A, Schifferer M, Saher G, Nave KA, Jäkel S, Tahirovic S, Giera M, Gokce O, Simons M.
article.abstract: Dysfunctional immune responses impair remyelination and contribute to neurodegeneration. While immune and metabolic responses to acute myelin injury are well characterized, myeloid cell adaptations to chronic myelin damage remain poorly understood. Here we performed a comparative analysis of genetic and toxic mouse models of acute and chronic demyelination, which identified a distinct microglial state associated with chronic demyelination, characterized by sustained pro-inflammatory activation, lysosomal lipid sequestration and reduced lipid droplet formation. Transcriptomics profiling further revealed a metabolic program marked by upregulated cholesterol synthesis and diminished sterol efflux. Treatment with a desmosterol mimetic possessing 24-dehydrocholesterol reductase inhibitor activity reversed this microglial state, attenuated pro-inflammatory signaling (including C-C Motif Chemokine Ligand 4 expression), reduced myelin damage and improved motor performance in a mouse model of leukodystrophy. Our findings uncover a pro-inflammatory microglial state characterized by lysosomal dysfunction and increased myelin reactivity, highlighting a novel therapeutic target for chronic demyelinating disorders.

article.title: Exogenous resolvin D2 alleviates diabetic neuropathic pain by regulating microglial fatty acid metabolism and phenotypic polarization.
article.authors: Ma X, Wang X, Yue L, Duan K, Hao Y, Liu X, Sun T.
article.venue: Neurotherapeutics : the journal of the American Society for Experimental NeuroTherapeutics
article.abstract: Diabetic neuropathic pain (DNP) is a common and intractable complication of diabetes with limited therapeutic options. Distinct from traditional NF-κB or MAPK inflammatory pathways, resolvin D2 (RvD2) alleviates DNP through metabolic reprogramming-a novel mechanism that remains largely unexplored. Untargeted metabolomics analysis of the spinal cord from DNP model mice and RvD2-treated mice revealed significant alterations in fatty acid oxidation (FAO)-related metabolites between the two groups. Functionally, RvD2 effectively alleviated hyperalgesia in DNP mice and ameliorated the FAO dysfunction associated with a pro-inflammatory microglial state. Mechanistically, RvD2 upregulated the expression of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha (PPARα) and carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1a (CPT1a), thereby activating the PPARα/CPT1a axis to enhance FAO. This metabolic shift consequently augmented ATP production, suppressed reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels, and diminished succinate accumulation, which in turn blocked hypoxia-inducible factor-1α (HIF-1α)-mediated pro-inflammatory signaling. Concurrently, RvD2 elevated the acetyl-CoA pool, promoting histone acetylation and chromatin accessibility at the promoters of pro-resolving polarization-related genes, which drove microglia toward a pro-resolving phenotype. Notably, the specific CPT1a inhibitor etomoxir partially reversed these protective effects of RvD2. In conclusion, RvD2 alleviates DNP by driving microglial pro-resolving polarization through a CPT1a-mediated metabolic-epigenetic axis, providing a promising therapeutic target and a potent candidate agent for the clinical management of DNP.

article.title: Isocaloric restriction normalizes body weight but not relative adiposity, adipose inflammation, or gut microbial diversity in high-fat diet-fed mice
article.authors: Eun, S.; Jeong, E.; Chae, S.; Lee, S.
article.abstract: Background/Objectives: The separate contributions of excess energy intake and diet composition to high-fat diet (HFD)-induced adiposity, adipose inflammation, and gut microbial changes are unclear. We tested whether restricting HFD intake to the energy intake of low-fat (LF)-fed mice (isocaloric restriction) prevents or reverses these outcomes. Subjects/Methods: Male C57BL/6 mice (n = 8/group) received for 12 weeks an LF diet (LF/LF) or HFD (HF/HF) ad libitum, HFD ad libitum then isocaloric HFD from week 7 (HF/IHF), or isocaloric HFD throughout (IHF/IHF). Adiposity, plasma markers, adipose and ileal gene expression, and fecal microbiota (16S rRNA sequencing, n = 4/group) were assessed. Results: Final body weight in IHF/IHF did not differ from LF/LF (difference 0.1 g, 95% CI -6.5 to 6.7; P > 0.99) and was lower than in HF/HF (-8.2 g, -14.7 to -1.6; P = 0.011). Switching to isocaloric feeding reduced weight gain during weeks 6-12 (HF/IHF vs HF/HF, -6.4 g, -9.8 to -3.1; P < 0.001). IHF/IHF mice had lower glucose (P = 0.031) and cholesterol (P = 0.005) than HF/HF mice. However, visceral fat relative to body weight remained higher than in LF/LF in IHF/IHF (+1.5 percentage points, 0.04 to 2.9; P = 0.042) and HF/IHF (+1.8, 0.4 to 3.3; P = 0.008). Adipose Tnf expression remained elevated in HF/IHF (log2 difference 2.2, 0.2 to 4.2; P = 0.025), and fecal phylogenetic diversity was lower in IHF/IHF than in LF/LF (Faith's PD -3.1, -5.9 to -0.4; P = 0.024). Ileal barrier genes and plasma lipopolysaccharide-binding protein were unchanged. Conclusions: Limiting HFD energy intake normalized body weight, glycemia, and plasma lipids but not relative adiposity, adipose Tnf expression, or the loss of gut microbial diversity. Diet composition affects these outcomes independently of energy intake, so normal body weight does not indicate their reversal.

article.title: Pantoea ananatis-triggered systemic resistance requires root sensing through the LORE receptor kinase in Arabidopsis.
article.authors: Duchateau S, Crouzet J, Cordelier S, Touchard M, Schellenberger R, Borrego C, Villaume S, Guise JF, Esmaeel Q, Groleau MC, Cloutier M, Gauthier C, Dhondt-Cordelier S, Mazeyrat-Gourbeyre F, Baillieul F, Ranf S, Déziel E, Aziz A, Dorey S.
article.abstract: Systemic immunity induced by beneficial bacteria enhances plant resilience to subsequent pathogen attacks. However, the mechanisms by which plants perceive these bacteria and translate this perception into a systemic response remain poorly understood. The Brassicaceae LIPOOLIGOSACCHARIDE-SPECIFIC REDUCED ELICITATION (LORE) receptor kinase is the direct sensor of bacterial medium-chain-length 3-hydroxy fatty acids (mc-3-OH-FAs) and 3-(3-hydroxyalkanoyloxy)alkanoic acids (HAAs), both of which activate local Brassicaceae immunity. Here, we show that the HAA-producing bacterium Pantoea ananatis BRT175 can colonize Arabidopsis thaliana roots independently of the production of HAAs, but these compounds induce a lore-dependent local immune response in roots. P. ananatis triggers induced systemic resistance (ISR) against the necrotrophic fungus Botrytis cinerea, but not against the hemibiotrophic bacterium Pseudomonas syringae pv. tomato DC3000. This ISR can be mimicked by HAAs or 3-hydroxy-decanoic acid (3-OH-C10), the strongest agonist of LORE. Both bacterium- and 3-hydroxylated fatty acid MAMP-induced ISR against B. cinerea rely on LORE-mediated sensing, involve salicylic acid, jasmonic acid/ethylene signaling pathways, and activate similar defense gene expression profiles in infected leaves. Our results demonstrate that lipidic microbe-associated molecular patterns (MAMPs) produced by beneficial microorganisms are necessary and sufficient to trigger rhizobacteria-mediated ISR and could differentially activate systemic resistance against biotrophic and necrotrophic pathogens.

article.title: Differential responsiveness to stromal fibroblasts in highly invasive lung cancer cells is associated with free fatty acid receptor 1 (FFAR1) and FFAR4 signaling.
article.authors: Nagano S, Kusumoto Y, Tamura M, Shimomura N, Isa E, Amano H, Kawamoto M, Ishida M, Yanome M, Kano N, Tsujiuchi T.
article.abstract: Solid tumors contain cancer cells and stromal cells that interact within the tumor microenvironment and influence malignant progression. However, whether the interaction between cancer cells and stromal cells changes as the malignant potential of cancer cells increases remains unclear. This study investigated the interaction between lung cancer cells and fibroblasts and examined the involvement of free fatty acid receptors (FFARs). Highly invasive A549-M8 cells derived from parental A549 cells were compared with A549 cells. Cells were cultured with 3T3 fibroblast supernatant or co-cultured with 3T3 cells, and proliferation, motility, invasion, and cisplatin (CDDP) sensitivity were evaluated. The effects of FFAR1 and FFAR4 activation were assessed using the respective agonists TUG-770 and TUG-891. A549-M8 cells exhibited greater motility and invasion and higher cell viability following CDDP treatment than A549 cells. Co-culture with 3T3 cells increased FFAR1 expression in both cell types and reduced FFAR4 expression in A549-M8 cells. 3T3 cell supernatant increased A549-M8 cell proliferation and cell viability following CDDP treatment, whereas these responses were limited in A549 cells. TUG-770 enhanced motility, invasion, and cell viability following CDDP treatment, whereas TUG-891 suppressed motility, invasion, and cell viability following CDDP treatment. Notably, the responses to 3T3 cells were stronger in A549-M8 cells, and 3T3 cell motility was also higher when co-cultured with A549-M8 cells than with A549 cells. These findings suggest that highly invasive A549-M8 cells exhibit greater responsiveness to stromal fibroblast-derived factors than parental A549 cells, while co-culture experiments indicate reciprocal effects between A549-M8 and 3T3 cells. FFAR1 and FFAR4 signaling is associated with these differential responses.

article.title: Identification of metabolic risk phenotypes among U.S. adolescents: A machine learning analysis of NHANES 2017-2023.
article.authors: Antunez Martinez OF.
article.abstract: Background Adolescent metabolic risk is multidimensional and may not be fully characterized by individual anthropometric or biochemical indicators considered separately; however, evidence regarding data-derived metabolic-risk phenotypes among adolescents remains limited. Purpose To identify metabolic risk phenotypes among U.S. adolescents using unsupervised machine learning and examine demographic and socioeconomic factors associated with phenotype membership. Methods Data from adolescents aged 12-17 years participating in the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) 2017-March 2020 and 2021-2023 cycles were analyzed. K-means clustering was performed among 848 adolescents with complete data for seven anthropometric and cardiometabolic variables. Logistic regression examined sociodemographic factors associated with elevated metabolic-risk phenotype membership. Results A two-cluster solution yielded the highest silhouette coefficient (0.289), identifying a lower metabolic-risk phenotype (n = 580, 68.4%) and an elevated metabolic-risk phenotype (n = 268, 31.6%). The elevated-risk phenotype was characterized by substantially higher BMI and waist circumference, together with higher triglycerides and LDL-C cholesterol, lower HDLC, and modestly higher glycated hemoglobin. In the adjusted logistic regression analysis (n = 763), older age was associated with greater odds of elevated-risk phenotype membership (aOR = 1.18, 95% CI 1.07-1.29), whereas income-to-poverty ratio was associated with lower odds (aOR = 0.78, 95% CI 0.70-0.87). Conclusions Unsupervised machine learning identified two exploratory metabolic-risk phenotypes characterized by concurrent differences in adiposity, lipid, and glycemic measures. The findings provide an exploratory basis for investigating multidimensional cardiometabolic assessment approaches relevant to pediatric nursing. Independent replication and longitudinal validation are needed to determine their prognostic and clinical utility.

article.title: Altered Sphingolipid–N-Acylethanolamine Signaling Reveals Peripheral Lipid Remodeling in First-Episode Schizophrenia
article.authors: Zheng F, Liu M, Qin X, Zhao H, Zhu Y, He Y, Zhou F, Sun Z.
article.abstract: Abstract Background Lipid abnormalities have been reported in schizophrenia, but little is known about changes in sphingolipids and N-acylethanolamines (NAEs) early in the illness or their trajectories during antipsychotic treatment. We examined plasma lipid-related metabolites in first-episode schizophrenia and their associations with clinical symptoms, cognitive performance, and short-term treatment. Methods Targeted plasma metabolomic profiling was performed in 55 individuals with first-episode schizophrenia and 80 healthy controls. Sixty-seven metabolites were quantified. Clinical symptoms and cognitive function were assessed using the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS) and the MATRICS Consensus Cognitive Battery (MCCB). Thirty-five patients had paired plasma samples at baseline and Week 8. Between-group differences, clinical correlations, metabolite correlation patterns, receiver operating characteristic analyses, and longitudinal changes were examined. Results Twenty of the 67 metabolites remained significantly different between patients and controls after false discovery rate (FDR) adjustment. Six of seven sphingolipid and NAE metabolites examined in detail were higher in patients. Plasma sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) was positively correlated with negative symptoms (r = 0.42) and PANSS total scores (r = 0.46), and negatively correlated with processing speed (r = − 0.47) and the MCCB composite score (r = − 0.44).
